citation_details.description: The authors identify this as the closest related work but note key differences, such as the current paper's analysis of finite buffers, which were not covered by Gurvich and Whitt. They also highlight that their technical treatment requires uniform estimates over scenarios, distinguishing it from the cited work.
citation_details.context: As far as our convergence results and RSP are concerned, the closest work is by Gurvich and Whitt [11], where a parallel server system, with multiple classes as well as multiple server pools, is considered in the HW regime, under the fixed queue and idleness ratio policy. This policy aims at keeping queue lengths as well as idleness levels at the different server pools at predetermined fixed ratios. When specialized to the case of a single server pool, and equal queue length ratios, this setting is similar to one of the two settings studied in this paper, namely, SLQ. There are, however, two important differences in terms of the technical treatment. First, as already mentioned, the estimates required to deduce the main result must be uniform over scenarios. A second difference is that finite buffers are not covered by Gurvich and Whitt [11]. Although it may seem that this aspect requires only simple adaptations to cover convergence results, this is not the case. In fact, diffusion limits do not always exist under our assumptions, as is the case under SLQ if the buffers are of equal size (this issue is developed further in Atar and Saha [4]). Hence, considerations beyond the infinite buffer model are necessarily significant here.

citation_details.parsed_title: Optimal learning in experimental design using the knowledge gradient policy with application to characterizing nanoemulsion stability
citation_details.description: The authors introduce the Knowledge Gradient with Discrete Priors (KGDP) method from [14] for handling nonlinear models. They then highlight its primary limitation, which is the reliance on a small, fixed set of parameter candidates that is not practical for high-dimensional problems.
citation_details.context: While KGDP presents an approach to handle nonlinear parametric models, one of its biggest limitations is that it starts with a limited number of parameter candidates, one of which is required to be the truth (or a close approximation of the truth). Moreover, the complexity of KGDP grows quickly as the number of candidates increases. In the experiments described in [14], KGDP can handle at most tens of candidates. In higher dimensional applications (more than four or five dimensions), a few dozen candidates are unlikely to be close to the truth in all dimensions, a well-known result of the curse of dimensionality.

citation_details.parsed_title: Optimal learning for stochastic optimization with nonlinear parametric belief models
citation_details.description: The paper describes the resampling algorithm from [30] as an effective extension to KGDP that is asymptotically optimal. However, it identifies a key gap in this prior work: its inability to handle continuous, multidimensional alternatives, which is the central problem the current paper aims to solve.
citation_details.context: The resampling algorithm is asymptotically optimal in terms of finding both the true parameter $\theta^{*}$ and the best alternative out of a finite set [30], supported by encouraging experimental testing showing a fast rate of convergence. However, the resampling algorithm, as with the original KGDP, can only handle a finite set of alternatives $x\in \mathcal{X}$ , which introduces a limitation similar to the original assumption in KGDP of a finite set of parameters $\theta$ . Specifically, if the controls $x$ are continuous with more than four or five dimensions, a finite set of alternatives (numbering in the tens) is not going to do a good job of capturing the optimal solution. In the remainder of the paper, we propose and analyze a way to extend the resampling algorithm of [30] to handle control vectors $x$ and parameters $\theta$ that are both multidimensional and continuous.

citation_details.parsed_title: An analysis of mixed integer linear sets based on lattice point free convex sets
citation_details.description: The authors state that Andersen, Louveaux, and Weismantel [2] showed that families of polyhedral lattice-free sets with bounded max-facet-width yield polyhedral closures. The current paper's results generalize this finding.
citation_details.context: Andersen, Louveaux, and Weismantel [2] generalize the result in [1] and show that, as in the case of split sets, families of polyhedral lattice-free sets with bounded max-facet-width yield polyhedral closures. Split sets are maximal convex lattice-free sets with max-facet-width one. Averkov [3] gave a short proof of a stronger version of this result using the Gordan-Dickson lemma. He showed that for a given rational polyhedron $P$ , any arbitrary family $\mathcal{L}$ of polyhedra with bounded max-facet-width has a finite subfamily $\mathcal{L}'$ such that for any $L \in \mathcal{L}$ , there exists $L' \in \mathcal{L}'$ satisfying $\mathrm{conv}(P \setminus L') \subseteq \mathrm{conv}(P \setminus L)$ (for any set $S$ , $\mathrm{conv}(S)$ stands for the convex hull of $S$ ). When the elements of $\mathcal{L}$ are lattice-free sets, this result implies that all cuts for a rational polyhedron $P$ obtained from a set $L \in \mathcal{L}$ are dominated by cuts for $P$ obtained from some $L' \in \mathcal{L}'$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: On the polyhedrality of cross and quadrilateral closures
citation_details.description: The authors cite their own prior work [9] which established that any family of 2-branch split sets has a finite dominating subfamily. The current paper extends this result from 2-branch to the more general t-branch split sets.
citation_details.context: Basu, Hildebrand, and Köppe [5] showed that the triangle closure (points satisfying cuts obtained from maximal lattice-free triangles) of the two-row continuous group relaxation is a polyhedron. Note that, in the context of the two-row continuous group relaxation, the triangle closure is contained in the split closure. We showed [9] that the quadrilateral closure of the two-row continuous group relaxation is a polyhedron. This result follows from the study of an alternative generalization of split cuts, called multibranch split cuts. Li and Richard [13] defined 2-branch split cuts, i.e., cuts that are obtained by considering the union of two split sets simultaneously. These cuts are called cross cuts in Dash, Dey, and Günlük [7] (a cross set is the union of two split sets). In [9] we generalized Averkov's result and showed that given an arbitrary family $\mathcal{C}$ of 2-branch split sets, $\mathcal{C}$ has a finite subfamily $\mathcal{C}'$ such that cuts defined by the 2-branch split sets in $\mathcal{C}'$ imply all cuts defined by 2-branch split sets in $\mathcal{C}$ .

citation_details.description: The authors cite [4] as a foundational reference for the definition of the trust-region subproblem (TRS) and for a comprehensive discussion on trust-region methods. It is also mentioned for its specific suggestion on choosing the matrix B in the ellipsoidal norm.
citation_details.context: The trust-region subproblem (TRS) [4], [26, Chap. 4] is to $$ \underset {\| p \| _ {B} \leq \Delta} {\text{minimize}} g ^ {\top} p + \frac {1}{2} p ^ {\top} A p, \tag{1} $$ where $A, B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ are symmetric, $g \in \mathbb{R}^n$ , $\Delta > 0$ , and $B$ is symmetric positive definite. Trust-region methods are a popular approach to dealing with general nonlinear optimization problems to minimize $f(x)$ , in which each iteration requires an (approximate) solution for TRS (1). In a trust-region method, the objective function of TRS (1) is a quadratic model of $f$ near the current approximate solution $\tilde{x}$ , in which $A$ is the Hessian and $g$ is the gradient of $f$ at $\tilde{x}$ . Note that we allow for the constraint $\|p\|_B \leq \Delta$ in an ellipsoidal norm, defined by $\|p\|_B = \|B^{1/2}p\| = \sqrt{p^\top Bp}$ for a positive definite matrix $B$ , not necessarily equal to the identity $I$ . An appropriate and nontrivial choice $B \neq I$ can be important, for example, when working in a properly scaled trust region to solve the nonlinear problem efficiently [23]. For example, in [4] it is argued that a good choice would be to take $B = |A|$ , the Hermitian polar factor [17] of $A$ . For more on trust-region methods and TRS, see the book [4].

citation_details.context: Readers are also referred to Asmussen (1987), and Kaspi and Rubinovitch (1988) for additional examples and references on Harris recurrence, and to Asmussen (1990), Bélisle, Romeijn and Smith (1990), Sigman (1988), Kaspi and Mandelbaum (1992) and Meyn and Down (1992) for some more recent applications.

citation_details.parsed_title: Markov decision processes with arbitrary reward processes
citation_details.description: The authors mention that Yu et al. studied a similar model with a fixed transition matrix and adversarial rewards, developing a more computationally efficient algorithm. Their analysis uses a similar concept of mixing time and achieves results that hold with high probability.
citation_details.context: Following our initial publication, Yu et al. [20] studied a similar model where the transition matrix is known and stationary and the rewards are chosen by an adversary. Their algorithm is based on following the perturbed leader and is computationally more efficient. In their analysis they use a similar notion of mixing time and obtain similar dependence. An advantage of their algorithm is that the results hold with high probability.

citation_details.parsed_title: A production-transportation problem with stochastic demand and concave production costs
citation_details.description: The paper is cited as an example of a practical problem in production-transportation planning that can be modeled as a DC (difference of two convex) programming problem, which the authors' proposed method is designed to solve.
citation_details.context: Many practical problems can be modelled as a DC programming problem where the explicit DC decompositions of the objective and/or constraint functions are readily available. These problems include production-transportation planning [15], location planning [31], engineering design [22], cluster analysis [4, 30], clusterwise linear regression analysis [6], and supervised data classification [1], to name a few.

citation_details.parsed_title: Notions of maximality for integral lattice-free polyhedra: The case of dimension three
citation_details.description: The authors cite this paper as part of recent work focused on classifying maximal lattice-free sets. They note that this line of work has not yet produced a complete classification for dimensions n ≥ 3, highlighting a research gap that motivates their approximation-based approach.
citation_details.context: Recent work has focused on this classification [1, 4, 5, 15], and the classification was given for $n = 2$ in [15]. However, a classification is not known for any $n \geq 3$.

citation_details.parsed_title: On the relative strength of split, triangle and quadrilateral cuts
citation_details.description: This paper is cited for its result showing that the split closure provides an infinitely bad approximation of the corner polyhedron in two dimensions. This finding serves as a baseline inapproximability result that the current work builds upon and analyzes.
citation_details.context: In [9], it was shown that $\rho(\mathcal{L}_2^2,\mathcal{L}_*) = \infty$, and in [2], this inapproximability result was generalized to show that $\rho(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{L}_*) = \infty$ whenever $\mathcal{B}$ only contains lattice-free sets with nontrivial lineality space.

citation_details.parsed_title: Maximal lattice-free convex sets in linear subspaces
citation_details.description: This work is referenced as a source for the characterization of maximal lattice-free sets. This characterization is a fundamental concept that underpins the theoretical framework of the paper.
citation_details.context: A characterization of maximal lattice-free sets was given by Lovász [17]; see also [3] and [10].

citation_details.parsed_title: Minimal inequalities for an infinite relaxation of integer programs
citation_details.description: The authors cite this work for the foundational result that any lattice-free set is contained within a maximal one. This theorem justifies the paper's focus on cuts generated from maximal lattice-free sets, as they are the strongest.
citation_details.context: It is known that every lattice-free set is a subset of a maximal lattice-free set [11].

citation_details.parsed_title: Scalar Labelings for Homotopy Paths
citation_details.description: The author cites Garcia and Gould [6] as an example of a restart method that does not require an extra dimension. The paper suggests its own proposed method should be comparable in performance to this class of algorithms.
citation_details.context: Hence the method here (and that in [21]) should be comparable to those restart methods that do not require an extra dimension—see Garcia and Gould [6], van der Laan and Talman [8], [9] and Tuy [22]; also Todd [20].

citation_details.parsed_title: On the Convergence Rate of Algorithms for Solving Equations that are Based on Methods of Complementary Pivoting
citation_details.description: The paper refers to Saigal [11] for a discussion on rapid convergence and acceleration techniques. These techniques are applicable when dealing with continuously differentiable functions, a property relevant to the zero-finding problems discussed.
citation_details.context: For a discussion of the rapid convergence and acceleration techniques possible with a continuously differentiable function but not with point-to-set mappings, see Saigal [11] and Saigal and Todd [14].

citation_details.parsed_title: The Computation of Fixed Points and Applications
citation_details.description: The author cites [17] as a foundational reference for the simplicial or fixed-point algorithms that are the subject of the paper. The paper also refers to specific chapters in this work for definitions of the triangulations it uses.
citation_details.context: We consider the simplicial or fixed-point algorithms [1]–[5], [10], [12], [15], [17] that find an approximate zero of a continuous function $f \colon R^n \to R^n$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: A two-sided relaxation scheme for mathematical programs with equilibrium constraints
On the solution of a minimum weight elastoplastic problem involving displacement and complementarity constraints
citation_details.description: The authors acknowledge the work of Ferris and Tin-Loi [18] for presenting an explicit formulation with complementarity constraints for structural optimization. citation_details.context: Ferris and Tin-Loi [18] present an explicit formulation to find minimum-weight solutions for truss-like structures with complementarity constraints that incorporate inelastic behavior. We consider structures with a greater number of degrees of freedom than trusslike structures have. However, this work demonstrates the use of complementarity constraints in explicit structural optimization problems.

citation_details.parsed_title: Nonlinear conjugate gradient methods
citation_details.description: The paper cites this work as a source for a recent review on nonlinear conjugate gradient methods, providing background context for the field.
citation_details.context: More recent reviews on nonlinear conjugate gradient methods can be found in Dai [5] and Hager and Zhang [19].

citation_details.parsed_title: The complexity of optimizing over a simplex, hypercube or sphere: A short survey
citation_details.description: This citation is a review paper that provides theoretical context on the complexity of polynomial optimization, covering hardness theorems and approximation schemes.
citation_details.context: The review [14] places these results in the context of complexity theory with an overview of hardness theorems and approximation schemes for polynomial optimization on standard domains.

citation_details.parsed_title: Lasserre hierarchy for large scale polynomial optimization in real and complex variables
citation_details.description: This work is cited as a recent approach for SOS optimization in the specific case of low-degree polynomials with a large number of variables, a different setting from the one primarily addressed in the paper.
citation_details.context: Optimization over the cone $\Sigma_{n,2d}$ for low $d$ and large $n$ is also an interesting and active area of research; recent approaches to problems of this type include [67] and [26].

citation_details.parsed_title: Optimal designs for rational function regression
citation_details.description: This work is cited as an example of an application of sum-of-squares optimization in the area of design of experiments, highlighting the broad relevance of the problem class being addressed.
citation_details.context: These problems are fundamental in many areas of applied mathematics and engineering, including discrete geometry [4, 5], probability theory [7], control theory [25], signal processing [16], power systems engineering [19], computational algebraic geometry [32, 27], design of experiments [47], and statistical estimation [2].

citation_details.parsed_title: Semi-infinite programming using high-degree polynomial interpolants and semidefinite programming
citation_details.description: This work is cited as evidence for the impracticality of the standard SDP-based approach for high-degree polynomials. It demonstrates the limitations in memory usage and computation time that the current paper aims to overcome.
citation_details.context: The impracticality of the SDP-based approach for problems involving high-degree polynomials was demonstrated recently in [48]. In a family of small examples with two WSOS cone constraints (for $n = 1$ , $m = 2$ , and increasing $d$ ), the largest instance that could be solved with the 32 GB of available memory using several popular semidefinite programming solvers had $2d = 1100$ , even though the original SOS optimization problem (before the semidefinite programming reformulation) is a convex optimization problem with only $2d + 1$ variables. The increase in the running times as $d$ increases was also found to be prohibitive in practice, with the largest "solvable" instances requiring several hours of computation.

citation_details.parsed_title: Sum-of-Squares Optimization without Semidefinite Programming
Using SeDuMi 1.02, a MATLAB toolbox for optimization over symmetric cones
Worst-case evaluation complexity for unconstrained nonlinear optimization using high-order regularized models
citation_details.description: The authors identify this work as a significant theoretical contribution that established evaluation complexity bounds for a regularization method using arbitrary degree models for unconstrained problems.
citation_details.context: A theoretically significant step was made in [6] for unconstrained problems, where evaluation complexity bounds were obtained for convergence to first-order stationary points of a simplified regularization method using models of arbitrary degree.

citation_details.parsed_title: Trust-region and other regularization of linear least-squares problems
Sharp worst-case evaluation complexity bounds for arbitrary-order nonconvex optimization with inexpensive constraints
citation_details.description: This reference provides the foundational framework that the current paper extends. The authors highlight that a key limitation of this prior work is its assumption of exact function and derivative evaluations, which their new algorithm addresses.
citation_details.context: Even more recently, [12] proposed a conceptual unified framework subsuming all known results for regularization methods, establishing an upper evaluation complexity bound for arbitrary model degree and also, for the first time, for arbitrary orders of optimality. This paper additionally covers unconstrained problems and problems involving "inexpensive" constraints, that is, constraints whose evaluation/enforcement cost is negligible compared to that of evaluating the objective function and its derivatives. It also allows for a full range of smoothness assumptions on the objective function. Finally it proves that the complexity results obtained are optimal in the sense that upper and lower evaluation complexity bounds match in order. In [12], all the abovementioned results are established for versions of the regularization algorithms, where it is assumed that objective function values and values of its derivatives (when necessary) can be computed exactly.

citation_details.parsed_title: Trust-Region Methods
citation_details.description: The authors state that their adaptive method for handling inexactness is inspired by a dynamic accuracy trust-region scheme described in this reference.
citation_details.context: The present paper proposes an extension of the unifying framework of [12] for unconstrained or inexpensively constrained problems that allows inexact evaluations of the objective function and of the required derivatives in an adaptive way inspired by the trust-region scheme of [16, section 10.6].

citation_details.parsed_title: On the complexity of matrix rank and rigidity
citation_details.description: The authors cite this work to support the statement that computing the rigidity of a matrix is generally an intractable problem. This fact highlights the difficulty of a special case of the paper's decomposition problem, motivating their tractable convex optimization approach.

citation_details.parsed_title: Fast and Simple PCA via Convex Optimization
citation_details.description: The authors cite Garber and Hazan [9] for their work on analyzing the convergence rate of SVRG for a specific class of nonconvex problems. This work is then presented as part of a body of literature that is limited to the Euclidean search space, which the current paper aims to address.
citation_details.context: Garber and Hazan [9] analyzed the convergence rate of SVRG when $f$ is a convex function that is the sum of nonconvex (but smooth) terms, and they applied their result to the principal component analysis (PCA) problem.

Second-order analysis for control constrained optimal control problems of semilinear elliptic systems

citation_details.description: The paper cites this work as a good reference for proximal point algorithms, a broad class of algorithms applicable to optimization problems on metric spaces.

citation_details.parsed_title: Optimization problems with perturbations: A guided tour
citation_details.description: This work is cited as a key reference for the concept of sensitivity in optimization problems. The authors state that this concept is essential for formulating the predictor steps in their proposed algorithm.
citation_details.context: In the case of parametric NLPs, the notion of sensitivity, how the optimal solution and objective value change as a parameter in an optimization problem is subject to small perturbations [3], is essential for formulating appropriate predictors.

citation_details.parsed_title: On the accurate identification of active constraints
citation_details.description: The authors use the robust active set estimator from this paper to identify the active constraints in their algorithm. This estimator is a key component of the proposed path-following procedure.

citation_details.parsed_title: Stabilized sequential quadratic programming for optimization and a stabilized Newton-type method for variational problems
citation_details.description: This paper is cited as an example of a perturbed Newtonian method that has recently demonstrated the possibility of achieving fast local convergence for optimization problems with weak constraint qualifications. This provides context for the current paper's goal of handling dual-degenerate problems.
citation_details.context: We note that even achieving fast local convergence for problems under weak constraint qualification conditions has just fairly recently shown to be possible, under perturbed Newtonian methods. (See, for instance, [14, 37], and [16] for a complete algorithm.)

citation_details.parsed_title: Solution sensitivity for Karush-Kuhn-Tucker systems with non-unique Lagrange multipliers

citation_details.context: New sensitivity theory has been developed after this book appeared, however, particularly for degenerate problems (see, e.g., [22]).

citation_details.context: This necessitates the analysis framework of inexact Newton methods [4]. (See also [11, 23] for contemporary frameworks.)

citation_details.context: For a further discussion of these classes, see Marshall and Shaked (1982, 1986) and Ohi and Nishida (1982).

citation_details.parsed_title: Integer knapsacks: Average behavior of the Frobenius numbers
citation_details.description: This paper is cited as a source for previously established upper bounds on the average value of the Frobenius number. This result for the special case of m=1 serves as a baseline that the current work aims to generalize.
citation_details.context: Upper bounds for the average value of $\mathrm{F}(\pmb{a})$ have been obtained in Aliev and Henk [4] and Aliev, Henk, and Hinrichs [5].

citation_details.parsed_title: Self-dual smooth approximations of convex functions via the proximal average
citation_details.description: The paper's proposed regularizations for monotone operators are inspired by the self-dual smoothing techniques for convex functions from the cited work. This reference provides the foundational concepts and specific theorems on which the paper's methods are based.
citation_details.context: Both regularizations of monotone operators given in sections 3 and 4 originate and are motivated from self-dual smoothing or regularizing convex functions [9], [26].

citation_details.parsed_title: The kernel average for two convex functions and its applications to the extension and representation of monotone operators
citation_details.description: The author cites this work as an example of the application of self-dual regularization to convex functions. This establishes the background for the paper's main contribution, which is to extend this idea to monotone operators.
citation_details.context: The idea of self-dual regularization is very important in optimization. It has been used for convex functions; see [9], [15], [26].

citation_details.parsed_title: Monotone operators and the proximal point algorithm
citation_details.description: The author refers to Rockafellar's observation that the proximal point algorithm converges at a linear rate. This is used to characterize the speed of convergence for the iterative schemes proposed in the paper.
citation_details.context: As observed by Rockafellar [35], $x_{\gamma}^{n} \to x_{\gamma}$ as fast as a linear rate when $n \to \infty$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: Jointly constrained biconvex programming
citation_details.description: The authors cite this work as part of a common solution methodology for bilinear problems, which involves constructing polyhedral relaxations using envelopes for each bilinear term.
citation_details.context: A common solution methodology is to construct polyhedral relaxations using envelopes of each bilinear term [3] within a spatial branch-and-bound framework [16].

citation_details.parsed_title: Bidimensional packing by bilinear programming
citation_details.description: The authors cite this paper as an example of an application for continuous and mixed integer bilinear problems, highlighting the broad relevance of the problem class being studied.
citation_details.context: Continuous and mixed integer bilinear problems find many applications [19, 25, 26, 30, 22, 31, 12] and have been fairly well studied in literature.

citation_details.parsed_title: Strong valid inequalities for orthogonal disjunctions and bilinear covering sets
citation_details.description: This work is referenced as a method for constructing tighter relaxations for bilinear problems by using convex envelopes of the entire bilinear function.
citation_details.context: Tighter relaxations can be constructed using convex envelopes of the entire bilinear function [34, 33].

citation_details.parsed_title: Stochastic approximation over multidimensional discrete sets with applications to inventory systems and admission control of queueing networks
citation_details.description: The author cites Lim [14] as a motivating application for studying stochastic approximation in nonsmooth settings. The cited work proposes a methodology for optimization over discrete parameters by applying SA to a piecewise linear, and thus nondifferentiable, extension of the cost function.
citation_details.context: Another application which motivates the study of SA in the nonsmooth setting arises in the optimization problems over discrete parameters. Lim [14] proposes several methods to find the minimizer of a cost function over a set of integer points, which proceed by constructing an extension of the cost function from a discrete domain to a continuous domain using the piecewise linear interpolation, and applying SA to the extended function. By the nature of the piecewise linear interpolation, the extended function is nondifferentiable so one needs to investigate the behavior of SA in the nonsmooth setting to analyze the methods proposed by Lim [14].

citation_details.parsed_title: On Triangulations for Computing Fixed Points
citation_details.description: The paper cites the Union Jack triangulation from [33] as an example of a triangulation method that satisfies the properties required for the proposed piecewise linear approximation.
citation_details.context: For example, Kuhn's triangulation [24] and the Union Jack triangulation [33], [34] with the integral vertex set have the above property.

citation_details.parsed_title: Contingent derivatives of set-valued maps and existence of solutions to nonlinear inclusions and differential inclusions
citation_details.description: The author states that their contribution rests on differentiation tools developed in Aubin's work. These tools, particularly the concept of the contingent derivative, are foundational to the paper's approach for deriving optimality conditions.
citation_details.context: The contribution in this paper differs in several significant respects from all the approaches alluded to above. It rests on tools of differentiation recently developed in Rockafellar (1985, 1988, 1989a, b, 1990) and Aubin (1981, 1983, 1990). Our main result is that for a large class of nonsmooth problems of the type (P), we give first-order necessary conditions of optimality, in terms of generalized first derivatives of the subgradient operator $\partial F$ , the latter being expressed by the set-valued map whose graph is the contingent cone to the graph of $\partial F$ , namely the contingent derivative.

citation_details.parsed_title: Lipschitz Behavior of Solutions to Convex Minimization Problems
citation_details.description: The paper's contribution is built upon the differentiation tools developed in Aubin's work. These tools are used to establish the theoretical framework for analyzing nonsmooth control problems.
citation_details.context: The contribution in this paper differs in several significant respects from all the approaches alluded to above. It rests on tools of differentiation recently developed in Rockafellar (1985, 1988, 1989a, b, 1990) and Aubin (1981, 1983, 1990). Our main result is that for a large class of nonsmooth problems of the type (P), we give first-order necessary conditions of optimality, in terms of generalized first derivatives of the subgradient operator $\partial F$ , the latter being expressed by the set-valued map whose graph is the contingent cone to the graph of $\partial F$ , namely the contingent derivative.

citation_details.parsed_title: Proto-Differentiability of Set-valued Mappings and its Applications in Optimization
citation_details.description: The paper adopts the concept of a function being "twice epi-differentiable" from Rockafellar's work. This definition is a key element of the theoretical framework used to derive the main results.
citation_details.context: According to Rockafellar (cf. Rockafellar 1989a for example), the function $F$ is said to be twice epi-differentiable at $x_0$ relative to $y_0$ if and only if the family of convex functions $\varphi_t$ Mosco-converges (as $t \downarrow 0$ ) (cf. Attouch 1984 for the precise definition). The limit function is ten denoted by $F_{x_0, y_0}''$ and is called the second order epi-derivative of $F$ at $x_0$ relative to $y_0$ . Using the subdifferential convergence theorem of Attouch (cf. Attouch 1984, Theorem 3.66), one shows that the Mosco-convergence of the family of functions $\varphi_t$ (as $t \downarrow 0$ ) is equivalent to the convergence (in the Painlevé-Kuratowski sense) of the family of sets $[(graph(\partial F) - (x_0, y_0)) / t]_{t > 0}$ , as $t \downarrow 0$ (cf. Rockafellar 1989a).

citation_details.parsed_title: Second-order Optimality Conditions in Nonlinear Programming Obtained by way of Epi-derivatives
citation_details.description: The author refers to Rockafellar's work for the theoretical result that the contingent derivative is the subdifferential of the second-order directional epi-derivative. This relationship is a crucial component of the paper's methodology.
citation_details.context: The contribution in this paper differs in several significant respects from all the approaches alluded to above. It rests on tools of differentiation recently developed in Rockafellar (1985, 1988, 1989a, b, 1990) and Aubin (1981, 1983, 1990). Our main result is that for a large class of nonsmooth problems of the type (P), we give first-order necessary conditions of optimality, in terms of generalized first derivatives of the subgradient operator $\partial F$ , the latter being expressed by the set-valued map whose graph is the contingent cone to the graph of $\partial F$ , namely the contingent derivative. This result is based on a symmetry condition for contingent derivatives (cf. Definition 2.1). It uses (among other things) the subdifferential convergence theorem of Attouch (cf. 1984, Theorem 3.66), which yields the contingent derivative as the subdifferential of the second-order directional epi-derivative (cf. Rockafellar 1985 for details).

[3]).

citation_details.description: The paper cites this work to provide the formal definition of strong metric regularity for a set-valued mapping. This concept is foundational for the subsequent analysis connecting full stability and the properties of subdifferential mappings.
citation_details.context: Recall [3] that a set-valued mapping $F: \mathbb{R}^n \Rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ is strongly metrically regular at $(\bar{x}, \bar{y}) \in \operatorname{gph} F$ if the inverse mapping $F^{-1}$ admits a Lipschitzian single-valued localization around $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ , i.e., there are neighborhood $U$ of $\bar{x}$ and $V$ of $\bar{y}$ and a single-valued Lipschitz continuous mapping $f: V \to U$ such that $f(\bar{y}) = \bar{x}$ and $F^{-1}(y) \cap U = \{f(y)\}$ for all $y \in V$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: Convergence conditions for Newton-type methods applied to complementarity systems with nonisolated solutions
citation_details.description: This work is cited as a source establishing the strong local convergence properties of the LP-Newton method. Specifically, it provides the theoretical basis that the method achieves local quadratic convergence even for problems with non-differentiability and nonisolated solutions.
citation_details.context: We emphasize that the LP-Newton method has very strong local convergence properties. In particular, the assumptions for local quadratic convergence to a solution of (1.1) neither imply differentiability of $F$ nor require the solutions to be isolated; see [8, 13]. This combination of difficulties is very challenging, and other methods require stronger assumptions; see the discussion in [8]. For example, even for the special case of KKT systems (or, in fact, for the even more special case of optimization), other Newton-type methods developed for degenerate problems of this specific structure need assumptions that require the primal part of the solution to be isolated, e.g., [11, 12, 16, 17, 22]; see also [18, Chapter 7]. This is in addition to classical methods such as sequential quadratic programming, for which both primal and dual solutions must be (locally) unique [18, Chapter 4]. By contrast, for the LP-Newton method applied to a KKT system, neither primal nor dual solutions have to be isolated.

citation_details.parsed_title: Diffusion Approximations for Optimal Filtering of Jump Processes and for Queueing Networks
citation_details.description: The author cites Johnson [16] for generalizing heavy traffic results to a network with two customer types under a priority discipline. Johnson's work showed that the system's limiting behavior is effectively one-dimensional, a phenomenon later called 'state space collapse'.
citation_details.context: The heavy traffic research cited so far applies to networks with a single customer type. Johnson [16] has generalized Reiman's result to a network with two customer types, one of which has preemptive-resume priority over the other at all stations. Under this discipline, the high priority customers are completely unaffected by the low priority customers. As a result, their queue length processes vanish in the usual heavy traffic normalization, a phenomenon already observed in single-station priority systems (see Harrison [4] and Whitt [23]). Thus, in the limit, each station can be represented in one dimension rather than two. Johnson also considers single-station models with two or more customer types under FCFS and processor sharing disciplines. In both cases he obtains a heavy traffic result for the total queue length process, and then shows that a fixed fraction of the limit process corresponds to customers of a particular type. Thus, the limiting behavior of the system is effectively one-dimensional. This phenomenon, in which the limit process for a queueing system can be defined on a state space of smaller dimension than the original system, has been called "state space collapse" by Reiman [20]. His paper treats a number of other queueing systems for which the heavy traffic limit is a one-dimensional reflected Brownian motion.

Assuming that the cost-to-go functions are discrete $L^{\natural}$ -convex (classes of discrete convex functions are discussed later in this subsection), Chen, Dawande, and Janakiraman [5] propose a pseudopolynomial-time approximation scheme that satisfies an arbitrary prespecified additive error guarantee. citation_details.parsed_title: A fully polynomial time approximation scheme for single-item inventory control with discrete demand

citation_details.context: The approximation scheme discussed in this paper relies on the concept of $K$ -approximation sets and functions, introduced in [14]. Intuitively, a $K$ -approximation function (with $K = 1 + \epsilon > 1$ ) is a function that has a relative error of at most $K - 1$ (i.e., $\epsilon$ ) with respect to a given function. A $K$ -approximation set is a set of points that induces a $K$ -approximation function via linear interpolation. A $K$ -approximation set of a function with codomain $[1, U]$ can be constructed with $O(\log_K U)$ points because we can allow the function values to increase by roughly a factor $K$ between two consecutive points. The papers [14, 13] define $K$ -approximation sets for functions over discrete domains.

citation_details.context: In [13] the authors emphasize the need for stability analysis of the feasible set for an infinite-dimensional optimization problem arising in the optimal control of a system of $n$ water reservoirs $R_1, R_2, \ldots, R_n$ . The model is based on the realistic assumption that if more raining water flows into the reservoirs than they can hold, the rest can be sold to a neighboring dry region, provided that the demand of the region is satisfied. Conversely, if the inflows are short, and the reservoirs have free capability for additional water, some water can be bought from outside to meet the inner demand. In this problem a set of decision variables consists of the rates $x_i(t)$ at which water is fed from $R_i$ at time $t$ (we assume that $x_i, i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$ , are continuous functions in the operating interval of time $[a, b]$ ), and a second group of variables $y_i, i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$ , provides the "selling" rate of water from $R_i$ at $t$ , which is given by $dy_i(t)$ (now it makes sense to require that functions $y_i, i = 1, 2, \ldots, n$ , are of bounded variation, since these planned inflows $(dy_i(t) > 0)$ or outflows $(dy_i(t) < 0)$ take place in punctual instants of time in $[a, b]$ ). Constraints come from the need of satisfying the overall demand at each instant $t \in [a, b]$ and not exceeding the capability of each reservoir along all the operating time. Since the raining inflows and demand are necessarily uncertain, it is a crucial issue to study the stability of this problem with respect to perturbations of the uncertain data.

citation_details.parsed_title: Optimal multiple stopping and valuation of swing options
citation_details.description: The authors identify several limitations in the work of Carmona and Touzi [11], noting that its results rely on restrictive assumptions such as continuous sample paths and finite moments. The current paper aims to overcome these limitations by providing a more general framework.
citation_details.context: Our result here is, however, stronger than theirs in several directions. Carmona and Touzi [11] show it when (i) the payoff process has a.s. continuous sample paths, (ii) its supremum over the entire horizon has some finite high-order moment, and (iii) it is adapted to a left-continuous filtration, all of whose martingales must also have continuous sample paths. They impose those conditions in order to make sure that Snell envelopes have a.s. continuous sample paths and are left-continuous in expectation. Their first and third conditions disallow jump processes, which we also come across in the literature as proper models for the underlayers in pricing certain financial options in energy markets. Moreover, their second condition excludes general payoff functions that are encountered in the ever-expanding world of complex compounded financial and real options. Since Carmona and Touzi [11] focus exclusively on pricing multiple-exercise put options (namely, options with bounded terminal payoff functions), this compromise in their treatment of the general optimal multiple-stopping problem is suitable for their purpose and allows them to avoid technical difficulties, which they call "beyond the scope of [their] paper." In this paper, one of our purposes is to price multiple-exercise options with general payoff processes, and we are able to prove the key result, namely the reduction of general optimal multiple-stopping problems to a sequence of ordinary optimal stopping problems, for payoff processes (i) with càdlàg (right continuous with left limits) sample paths, (ii) without any conditions on the moments of the supremum of the payoff process, and (iii) adapted to any filtration satisfying the usual conditions.

citation_details.description: The authors discuss the analysis of the random pursuit (RP) algorithm from [40], which proved linear convergence for strongly convex functions. They point out that this analysis is not generalizable to their context as it relies on line searches, thus creating a gap that their new methodology aims to fill.
citation_details.context: Later on, Stich, Müller, and Gartner analyzed the simple random pursuit (RP) where $\mathbf{Y}_{t+1}$ is a random direction and $\sigma_t$ is the result of a line search in the $\mathbf{Y}_{t+1}$ direction [41, 40]. Assuming exact or approximate line search, they proved the linear convergence of RP for strongly convex functions. They experimentally compared RP to an accelerated version of RP, to Nesterov's schemes, and to a classical CB-SARS [37, 35, 11]. The accelerated RP and Nesterov's schemes need as input some constants related to the function (i.e., they are not tested in a black-box setting). Concluding their observations on the performance of the CB-SARS, the authors emphasize "that the performance of the adaptive step-size ES scheme [the classical CB-SARS] is remarkable given the fact that it does not need any function-specific parametrization. A comparison to the RP shows that it needs four times fewer function evaluations on functions $f_2 - f_4$ " [40]. The main reason is the saved expenses due to the omitted line searches. The theoretical analysis in [40] heavily relies on the control of the $f$ -decrease at each iteration with the assumption of exact line search (or with a controlled error in the case of approximate line search). We believe that the authors' analysis, however, is difficult to generalize to our context. We resort thus to a different approach that can prove in particular the linear convergence of the CB-SARS algorithm experimented in the aforementioned paper (for which the authors stress the remarkable performance) [5].

citation_details.parsed_title: Randomized methods for linear constraints: Convergence rates and conditioning
Random algorithms for solving convex inequalities
citation_details.description: The authors identify [27] as a closely related work but point out its limitations, such as assuming a fixed set representation and only analyzing projections onto a single set. They also note that [27] lacks a theoretical basis for certain choices like non-uniform sampling or significant extrapolation, which the current paper addresses.
citation_details.context: The papers most closely related to our work are [23, 24, 27]. Although these papers also consider general convex feasibility problems, they assume a fixed representation for the set $\mathcal{X}$ , given either in terms of finite intersection of simple convex sets [23] or in terms of functional constraints [24, 27]. They also state that choices for the probabilities of sampling sets other than the uniform one may lead to better projection schemes, without any theoretical justification, however. For such fixed representations, [23, 24, 27] analyze only random projection algorithms that require projection onto a single set at each iteration, i.e., $N = 1$ . Finally, they do not consider extrapolation $\alpha_{k} > 2$ in the convergence analysis, i.e., their convergence results are derived for a diminishing step size, constant step size $\alpha \in (0,2)$ , or an ideal constant step size that depends on the radius of a ball contained in the feasible set $\mathcal{X}$ . Note that our general convergence results for $N = 1$ recover the main convergence rates from [23, 24, 27]; see section 6.3 for a detailed comparison.

citation_details.parsed_title: Multi-item lot-sizing with joint set-up cost
citation_details.description: The authors describe the work of Anily et al. [4], which solves a special case of the lot-sizing problem by proposing an extended linear programming formulation. This method's applicability is limited by its reliance on a monotonicity assumption for holding costs, a constraint the current paper's method does not have.
citation_details.context: In a recent paper, Anily et al. [4] have considered the same model with time-dependent cost parameters, but with the additional monotonicity assumption on the holding costs. In particular, the assumption is that the items are indexed, such that each item has higher holding costs than all items of smaller index, uniformly for all periods. Specifically, $h_{1t} \leq h_{2t} \leq \dots \leq h_{Nt}$ , for all periods $t = 1, \ldots, T$ . For this problem, they have proposed an extended linear programming formulation with $O(N \times T^2)$ constraints and variables that solves the problem to optimality. This implies that this special case is polynomially solvable.

citation_details.parsed_title: A Scalable Bounding Method for Multi-Stage Stochastic Integer Programs
citation_details.description: The authors state that the current paper builds upon their previous unpublished work [40]. In that work, they extended bounding methods to multistage stochastic programs and showed that using any partition of the scenario set is sufficient for producing valid bounds.
citation_details.context: This paper extends our previous work on two-stage stochastic mixed-integer programs (SMIPs) [39] and builds on our unpublished work on multistage stochastic programs [40], which sparked a flurry of recent activity in the literature [7, 31, 32, 47]. Considering two-stage SMIPs with a discrete scenario set, Sandikci, Kong, and Schaefer [39] demonstrate how to generate bounds for the optimal objective value by solving smaller problems, called group subproblems, each formulated over a subset of scenarios of a given size $b$ , and prove that these bounds monotonically improve with $b$ . Formulating the group subproblems in [39] requires identifying a reference scenario to be included in each subproblem. These bounds are calculated by taking an expectation of group subproblem objective values over all subsets of size $b$ , which may be computationally challenging for large scenario sets. In [40], we extend the bounds in [39] to multistage SMIPs and note that any partition of the scenario set is sufficient to produce legitimate bounds, which helps avoid the computational challenges encountered in [39].

citation_details.parsed_title: Inventory control for spectrally positive Lévy demand processes
citation_details.description: The authors cite Yamazaki [52] for generalizing previous inventory models to spectrally positive Lévy demand processes. They also note that Yamazaki used smooth and continuous pasting conditions to find the optimal policy, a technique which the current paper states is not applicable to their own model.
citation_details.context: Bensoussan et al. [12] and Benkherouf and Bensoussan [11] studied a stochastic inventory model where the demand is a mixture of a Brownian motion and a compound Poisson process; the optimal policy for this model is of the $(s,S)$ type again. Using the fluctuation theory of Lévy processes, Yamazaki [52] generalized their results to spectrally positive Lévy demand processes. In these papers, the optimal ordering policies are obtained by solving a set of quasi-variational inequalities (QVIs) deduced from the Bellman equation. For computing the optimal parameters, one needs to impose additional smoothness conditions at the reorder and order-up-to levels. This technique, widely known as smooth pasting, is essential to solving a Brownian control problem by the QVI approach. Smooth pasting is also used by Yamazaki [52] to obtain the optimal $(s,S)$ policy when the Lévy demand process is of unbounded variation; a set of weaker conditions, referred to as continuous pasting conditions, is imposed in the same paper when the Lévy demand process is of bounded variation. See Dixit [19] for a comprehensive account of smooth pasting and its applications.

citation_details.parsed_title: Semidefinite representation of convex sets
citation_details.description: The authors state a theorem from Helton and Nie's work concerning a version of Putinar's Positivstellensatz for matrix polynomials with degree bounds. This theorem is a key theoretical tool used in the paper's analysis.
citation_details.context: THEOREM 2.11 (Helton and Nie [HN1]). Fix $C, d, k, m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ and fix any norm on the vector space $\mathbb{R}[\underline{X}]_d^{k \times k}$ . Let $\underline{g} \coloneqq (g_1, \ldots, g_m) \in \mathbb{R}[\underline{X}]^m$ such that $M(\underline{g})$ is Archimedean. Then there exists $d \in \mathbb{N}_0$ such that every symmetric $H \in \mathbb{R}[\underline{X}]_d^{k \times k}$ satisfying $\| H \| \leq C$ and $H \succeq \frac{1}{C}$ on $S(\underline{g})$ satisfies $H \in M_d^{k \times k}(\underline{g})$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: On the Lasserre hierarchy of semidefinite programming relaxations of convex polynomial optimization problems
citation_details.description: The paper credits Lasserre with a foundational observation for handling nonnegative linear polynomials on the set S(g). This idea, which involves considering supporting hyperplanes, is a precursor to the methods discussed in the paper.
citation_details.context: Lasserre [L2] made a first key observation to deal with this problem: He considered without loss of generality only such $f \in \mathbb{R}[\underline{X}]_1$ nonnegative on $S(\underline{g})$ that vanish in at least one point $u \in S(\underline{g})$ (and whose real zero set therefore defines a supporting hyperplane at the point $u$ of the convex set $S(\underline{g})$ unless $f = 0$ ).

citation_details.parsed_title: Ergodic, primal convergence in dual subgradient schemes for convex programming
citation_details.description: The paper discusses [8] as a work addressing problems with nonsmooth dual functions where an approximate primal solution is formed via running averages. citation_details.context: At one extreme are results for problems with a nonsmooth dual function (see, e.g., [14, 8]), which in general allow the primal problem to also be nonsmooth and have nonlinear constraints. For these problems, one typically applies the subgradient method to the dual problem and forms running averages of the generated primal iterates to construct an approximate primal solution. Such an approximate primal solution converges asymptotically to the primal optimal set if the subgradient iterations use a diminishing step-size [8] and has guaranteed bounds on suboptimality and infeasibility when a constant step-size is used [14].

citation_details.parsed_title: Robust optimization—Methodology and applications
citation_details.description: This paper is cited as a key reference for the robust optimization approach, which addresses uncertainty by finding a single solution that is feasible for all parameter realizations within a given set. This approach is presented as an alternative to stochastic optimization that is significantly more tractable.
citation_details.context: More recently, the robust optimization approach has been considered to address optimization under uncertainty and has been studied extensively (see Ben-Tal and Nemirovski [4, 5, 6], El Ghaoui and Lebret [17], Goldfarb and Iyengar [19], Bertsimas and Sim [11, 12]). In a robust optimization approach, the uncertain parameters are assumed to belong to some uncertainty set, and the goal is to construct a single (static) solution that is feasible for all possible realizations of the uncertain parameters from the set and optimizes the worst-case objective.

citation_details.context: Bertsimas and Goyal [10] analyze the performance of static robust solution in two-stage stochastic problems for perfectly symmetric uncertainty sets such as ellipsoids and norm-balls. We consider a generalized notion of symmetry of a convex set introduced in Minkowski [25], where the symmetry of a convex set is a number between 0 and 1. The symmetry of a set being equal to one implies that it is perfectly symmetric (such as an ellipsoid). We show that the performance of the static robust and the finitely adaptable solutions for the corresponding two-stage and multistage stochastic optimization problems depends on the symmetry of the uncertainty set. This is a two-fold generalization of the results in Bertsimas and Goyal [10].

citation_details.parsed_title: Potential games
citation_details.description: This paper is cited for introducing the class of finite games that have the finite improvement property (FIP), where every improvement path is guaranteed to be finite. These games, known as potential games, use a potential function to track payoff changes, which provides the conceptual framework for analyzing convergence to equilibria.
citation_details.context: In a seminal paper [40], Monderer and Shapley identified the class of finite games in which every improvement path is guaranteed to be finite, and coined this property as the finite improvement property (FIP). These are games with which one can associate a generalised ordinal potential, a function on the set of joint strategies that properly tracks the qualitative change in players' payoffs resulting from a strategy change. Thus the FIP not only guarantees the existence of Nash equilibria but also ensures that it is possible to reach it from any initial joint strategy by a simple update dynamics amounting to a local search. This makes the FIP a desirable property. An important class of games that have the FIP are the congestion games that, as already noted in [45], actually have an exact potential, a function that exactly tracks the quantitative difference in players' payoffs.

citation_details.parsed_title: Worst-case evaluation complexity for unconstrained nonlinear optimization using high-order regularized models
citation_details.description: The authors state that [3] demonstrated improved complexity for regularization methods using higher-order derivatives. The current paper generalizes the methods from [3] to allow for arbitrary Taylor models, regularization powers, and levels of smoothness.
citation_details.context: An important related question and extension were answered in [3]: if higher-order derivatives are available, can one improve the complexity of regularization methods? It was shown in [3] that if one considers approximately minimizing an $(r - 1)$ th-order Taylor model of the objective regularized by the (weighted) $r$ th power of the (Euclidean) norm of the step in each iteration (so $r = p + 1$ ), the complexity of the resulting adaptive regularization method is $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-\frac{r}{r - 1}})$ evaluations to obtain (1.2), under the assumption that the $(r - 1)$ th derivative tensor is globally Lipschitz continuous. The method proposed in [3] measures the progress of each iteration by comparing the Taylor model decrease (without the regularization term) to that of the true function decrease and only requiring mild approximate (local) minimization of the regularized model. Here, we generalize these higher-order regularization methods from [3] to allow for an arbitrary local Taylor model, an arbitrary regularization power of the step, and varying levels of smoothness of the highest-order derivative in the Taylor model.

citation_details.parsed_title: Worst-case evaluation complexity of regularization methods for smooth unconstrained optimization using Hölder continuous gradients
citation_details.description: The authors describe their previous work in [11], which analyzed regularization methods for objectives with Hölder-continuous gradients using first-order models. The current paper generalizes the approach from [11] to use higher p-th order Taylor models.
citation_details.context: In [11] we considered regularization methods applied to nonconvex objectives with Hölder-continuous gradients (with unknown exponent $\beta_{1} \in (0,1]$ ) that employ a first-order quadratic model of the objective regularized by the $r$ th power of the step. We showed that the worst-case complexity of the resulting regularization methods varies depending on $\min\{r,1 + \beta_{1}\}$ . In particular, when $1 < r \leq 1 + \beta_{1}$ , the methods take at most $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-\frac{r}{r - 1}})$ evaluations/iterations until termination, and otherwise at most $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-\frac{1 + \beta_{1}}{\beta_{1}}})$ evaluations/iterations to achieve the same condition. The latter complexity bound reflects the smoothness of the objective's landscape, without prior knowledge or use of it in the algorithm, and is independent of the regularization power. Here we generalize the approach in [11] to $p$ th-order Taylor models and find that similar bounds can be obtained.

citation_details.parsed_title: Regularized Newton Methods for Minimizing Functions with Hölder Continuous Hessians
citation_details.description: The paper identifies [19] as proposing a universal cubic regularization scheme whose complexity adapts to the objective's smoothness. The authors' work generalizes the approach from [19] from a specific case to a broader framework with varying model order, regularization power, and smoothness.
citation_details.context: Recently, Grapiglia and Nesterov [19] proposed a new cubic regularization scheme that yields a universal algorithm in the sense that its complexity reflects the (possibly unknown or even absent) degree of sufficient smoothness of the objective; the approach in [19] addresses the case when $p = 2$ , $r = 3$ , and $\beta_{2} \in [0,1]$ in our framework. Our ARp algorithm includes a modification in a similar (but not identical) vein to that in [19]. In particular, our approach checks a theoretical condition that carefully monitors the length of the step on each iteration on which the objective is sufficiently decreased. The technique in [19] is different in that it requires a specific/new sufficient decrease condition of the objective on each iteration that makes progress. We generalize the approach in [19] and achieve complexity bounds with similar universal properties for varying $r$ , $p$ , and unknown $\beta_{p} \in [0,1]$ , provided $r \geq p + \beta_{p}$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: Portfolio-Selection with Transactions Costs
citation_details.description: The authors describe the work of Magill and Constantinides as the closest related research, noting its use of dynamic programming for a model with proportional transaction costs but no fixed costs. They highlight that this prior work also concluded that the optimal portfolio is piecewise constant.
citation_details.context: The work that comes closest to ours in this sense is that of Magill and Constantinides [12]. In this paper the risky assets are of the log-normal type, and the riskless asset earns interest at a constant rate. The variable costs are proportional to the value of the transaction, and the fixed cost is not present. The control variables are the portfolio vector and consumption, and the authors are mostly interested in the decreasing absolute risk aversion utility. The method of solution is to employ dynamic programming on a system with perturbed diffusion coefficients. It is concluded that the optimal portfolio is piecewise constant and some computational formulas are obtained.

While all these approaches prove exactness results under suitable assumptions, they suffer from the drawback that the resulting penalized subproblems are nonsmooth NEPs and therefore difficult to solve numerically.

citation_details.parsed_title: On the multiplier-penalty-approach for quasi-variational inequalities
citation_details.description: The paper acknowledges [20] for presenting an augmented Lagrangian method for the general class of quasi-variational inequalities (QVIs), but identifies a gap. The authors argue that the general QVI framework in [20] is less effective for GNEPs than their direct approach, as it lacks GNEP-specific constraint qualifications and a focus on feasibility.
citation_details.context: An improved version of that method can be found in [20], also for QVIs. Since the GNEP is a special instance of a QVI, these two papers also discuss the GNEP within their general QVI framework. Here, we apply the augmented Lagrangian idea directly to GNEPs. It turns out that the corresponding results are significantly stronger than or simply different from those that arise from the QVI framework in [20, 22]. In particular, no GNEP-tailored constraint qualifications are considered in [20, 22], and the feasibility issue, which plays a central role in this paper, is not discussed there as a separate topic.

citation_details.context: Ai and Zhang [2] derived easily verifiable conditions to characterize when the CDT problem has no duality gap, which is equivalent to when the SDP relaxation of the CDT problem is tight since the Lagrangian dual problem coincides with the SDP relaxation (see [22]). citation_details.parsed_title: A note on polynomial solvability of the CDT problem
citation_details.description: The authors acknowledge Bienstock's [5] work for proving the polynomial-time solvability of the CDT problem. However, they highlight that this algorithm is considered impractical and difficult to implement, which motivates their paper's goal of developing a more practical algorithm.
citation_details.context: In general, however, the complexity of the CDT problem had been open for a long time until Bienstock [5] recently proved its polynomial-time solvability. Bienstock's proof in fact provides a polynomial-time algorithm for general quadratic optimization problems with an arbitrary fixed number of quadratic constraints. His algorithm makes a sequence of calls to a polynomial-time feasibility algorithm based on Barvinok's construction [3]; the length of the sequence is polynomial in the number of bits in the data and $\log \epsilon^{-1}$ . The algorithm returns an $\epsilon$ -feasible solution with $\epsilon$ -accuracy, that is, a solution guaranteed to satisfy the relaxed constraints: $x^{\top}Q_{i}x + 2q_{i}^{\top}x + \gamma_{i} \leq \epsilon$ , and in exact arithmetic the solution has objective value within $\epsilon$ from the optimal. Unfortunately, however, Bienstock's polynomial-time algorithm does not appear to be very practical, because the polynomial-time feasibility algorithm looks difficult to implement. To the best of our knowledge, no polynomial-time algorithm for the CDT problem has been implemented and used to solve large-scale instances.

citation_details.parsed_title: Approximations of dynamic programs I
citation_details.description: The authors cite White [42, 43] as a survey of techniques for computing approximate value functions. They also note that this work is part of a body of literature limited to MDPs with discrete spaces or bounded cost functions, a restriction the current paper aims to overcome.
citation_details.context: Various methods have been developed to compute approximate value functions and near optimal policies. A partial list of these techniques is as follows: approximate dynamic programming, approximate value or policy iteration, simulation-based techniques, neuro-dynamic programming (or reinforcement learning), state aggregation, etc. For rather complete surveys of these techniques, we refer the reader to Fox [17], White [42, 43], Langen [28], Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis [6], Ren and Krogh [32], Ortner [30], White [40, 41], Bertsekas [3], Dufour and Prieto-Rumeau [14, 15], and references therein. With the exception of Dufour and Prieto-Rumeau [15] and Ortner [30], these papers in general study either the finite horizon cost or the discounted infinite horizon cost. Also, the majority of these results are for MDPs with discrete (i.e., finite or countable) state and action spaces, or a bounded one-stage cost function (e.g., Fox [17], White [42, 43], Van Roy [37], White [40, 41], Cavazos-Cadena [9], Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis [6], Ren and Krogh [32], Ortner [30], Bertsekas [3]).

citation_details.parsed_title: Approximations of dynamic programs II
citation_details.description: The authors reference White [43] as a survey and as an example of prior work limited to discrete spaces or bounded costs. They also highlight it as a result that only approximates the value function without providing a method to compute near-optimal policies.
citation_details.context: Various methods have been developed to compute approximate value functions and near optimal policies. A partial list of these techniques is as follows: approximate dynamic programming, approximate value or policy iteration, simulation-based techniques, neuro-dynamic programming (or reinforcement learning), state aggregation, etc. For rather complete surveys of these techniques, we refer the reader to Fox [17], White [42, 43], Langen [28], Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis [6], Ren and Krogh [32], Ortner [30], White [40, 41], Bertsekas [3], Dufour and Prieto-Rumeau [14, 15], and references therein. With the exception of Dufour and Prieto-Rumeau [15] and Ortner [30], these papers in general study either the finite horizon cost or the discounted infinite horizon cost. Also, the majority of these results are for MDPs with discrete (i.e., finite or countable) state and action spaces, or a bounded one-stage cost function (e.g., Fox [17], White [42, 43], Van Roy [37], White [40, 41], Cavazos-Cadena [9], Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis [6], Ren and Krogh [32], Ortner [30], Bertsekas [3]). Those that consider general state and action spaces (see, e.g., Dufour and Prieto-Rumeau [13, 14, 15], Bertsekas [3], Chow and Tsitsiklis [11]) assume in general Lipschitz type continuity conditions on the components of the control model to provide a rate of convergence analysis for the approximation error. Some of the results only consider approximating the value function and do not provide a procedure to compute near optimal policies (e.g., Langen [28], White [43], Dufour and Prieto-Rumeau [14]).

citation_details.context: Due to its success, many improvements and generalizations of Feasibility Pump, both for MILPs and mixed integer nonlinear programs (MINLPs), have been studied [AB07, BFL07, BCLM09, FS09, SLR13, DFLL10, BEET12, DFLL12, BEE+14]. However, the focus of these improvements has been on the projection and rounding steps or generalizations for MINLPs; to the best of our knowledge, they use essentially the same randomization step as proposed in the original algorithm [FGL05] (and its generalization to the general integer MILP case of [BFL07]). We note that some approaches avoid the randomization step altogether; see [BCLM09] for convex MINLPs and [GMSS17] for MILPs.

citation_details.context: However, the focus of these improvements has been on the projection and rounding steps or generalizations for MINLPs; to the best of our knowledge, they use essentially the same randomization step as proposed in the original algorithm [FGL05] (and its generalization to the general integer MILP case of [BFL07]).

citation_details.context: Rockafellar [23] introduced the proximal point algorithm for the minimization of (deterministic) lower semicontinuous proper convex functions.

citation_details.parsed_title: Multistage stochastic decomposition: A bridge between stochastic programming and approximate dynamic programming
citation_details.description: The authors cite Higle and Sen [30] as an example of a prior work that implemented quadratic regularization in stochastic decomposition. They point out that this method is limited by its reliance on a scenario tree, which restricts its use to problems with short time horizons.
citation_details.context: The same idea has also been implemented in the two-stage and multistage versions of the stochastic decomposition method developed by Higle and Sen [9, 30], as well as the decomposition work of Morton [16]. All of these methods utilize a scenario tree, either explicitly or implicitly (when indexing regularization terms by the entire history $H_{t}$ ), and consider separate incumbent solutions for every parent node in the scenario tree. That limits their applicability to problems with short time horizons.

citation_details.context: The inf-compactness condition holds when $f(x, \cdot, \xi)$ is uniformly coercive or strongly convex. Moreover, in the case when $G(x, y, \xi) = y$ , the condition is implied by some kinds of monotonicity of $H(x, \cdot, \xi)$ . For instance, if $\Xi$ is bounded and $H(x, \cdot, \xi)$ is an $R_0$ function for every $(x, \xi) \in \mathcal{X} \times \Xi$ ; that is, if, for any sequence $\{y^k\}$ with $\lim_{k \to \infty} \| y^k \| = +\infty$ , $\lim_{k \to \infty} \inf_{k \to \infty} \min_{k \to \infty} \{y_1^k, \ldots, y_m^k\} / \| y^k \| \geq 0$ , and $$ \lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} \inf \min \left\{H _ {1} \left(x, y ^ {k}, \xi\right), \dots, H _ {m} \left(x, y ^ {k}, \xi\right)\right\} / \| y ^ {k} \| \geq 0, $$ there exists an index $j$ such that $\{y_j^k\} \to +\infty$ and $\{H_j(x,y^k,\xi)\} \to +\infty$ . In such a case, the feasible set of problem (3.3) is uniformly bounded for $t \in [0, +\infty)$ ; see [23] for more details.

citation_details.context: For Nesterov's accelerated algorithm (NS) and FISTA algorithm, if we set $F = f + g$ , it is proven that the objective function $F(x_{n}) - \min F$ enjoys an inverse quadratic order of convergence rate $O(n^{-2})$ asymptotically when $b \geq 3$ . citation_details.context: The convexification procedure from [16] plays an important role in this work, although for our ends we will need to enhance it in several directions. citation_details.context: The level-set techniques discussed above find an $\epsilon$ -feasible and $\epsilon$ -optimal solution to (1)-(2), that is, the terminal solution may not be feasible. citation_details.parsed_title: Radial Subgradient Method
citation_details.description: The authors identify Grimmer's work [14] as an extension of a method that emphasizes feasibility but point out its limitations. They note its line search can be challenging for general problems and its complexity cannot be improved by smoothness or strong convexity.
citation_details.context: The radial subgradient method proposed by Renegar [35] and extended by Grimmer [14] also emphasizes feasibility. This method avoids projection and finds a feasible and $\epsilon$ -relative optimal solution by performing a line search at each iteration. This line search, while easy to execute for some linear or conic programs, can be challenging for general convex programs (1)-(2). Moreover, it is unknown whether the iteration complexity of this approach can be improved by utilizing the potential smoothness and strong convexity of the objective function and constraints. In contrast, the feasible level-set approach in this paper avoids the need for line search, in addition to projection, and its iteration complexity leverages the strong convexity and smoothness of the objective and constraints when these properties are true.

citation_details.description: The authors cite Rockafellar [21] for proposing the proximal point method, a classical iterative scheme for solving the monotone inclusion problem. This method and its convergence properties form the foundational framework for the methods discussed in the paper.
citation_details.context: A broad class of optimization, saddle point, equilibrium, and variational inequality (VI) problems can be posed as the monotone inclusion problem, namely: finding $x$ such that $0 \in T(x)$ , where $T$ is a maximal monotone point-to-set operator. The proximal point method, proposed by Rockafellar [21], is a classical iterative scheme for solving the monotone inclusion problem which generates a sequence $\{x_{k}\}$ according to $$ x _ {k} = (\lambda_ {k} T + I) ^ {- 1} (x _ {k - 1}). $$ It has been used as a generic framework for the design and analysis of several implementable algorithms. The classical inexact version of the proximal point method allows for the presence of a sequence of summable errors in the above iteration, i.e., $$ \left\| x _ {k} - \left(\lambda_ {k} T + I\right) ^ {- 1} \left(x _ {k - 1}\right) \right\| \leq e _ {k}, \quad \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} e _ {k} < \infty. $$ Convergence results under the above error condition have been established in [21] and have been used in the convergence analysis of other methods that can be recast in the above framework.

citation_details.context: An asynchronous implementation of a proximal bundle method is provided in [8], where bundle solutions are implicitly regularized in the objective function. citation_details.parsed_title: Monotone operators and the proximal point algorithm
citation_details.description: The paper identifies this as the seminal work by Rockafellar that introduced two inexact versions of the proximal point algorithm in Hilbert spaces. The authors summarize Rockafellar's criteria for inexactness and his convergence results, which form the foundation for their own analysis on Hadamard manifolds.
citation_details.context: In particular, in his seminal work [51], Rockafellar developed two inexact versions of the proximal point algorithm to generate the sequences ${z^{k + 1}}$ by using two approximate rules $z^{k + 1} \approx (\mathbf{I} + c_k T)^{-1}(z^k)$ . One criterion adopted by Rockafellar is $$ \left\| z ^ {k + 1} - \left(\mathbf {I} + c _ {k} T\right) ^ {- 1} \left(z ^ {k}\right) \right\| \leq \varepsilon_ {k}, \quad k = 0, 1, \dots, \tag {1.3} $$ while the other is $$ \mathrm {d} \left(0, S _ {k} \left(z ^ {k + 1}\right)\right) \leq \frac {\varepsilon_ {k}}{c _ {k}}, \quad k = 0, 1, \dots, \tag {1.4} $$ where each $S_{k}(\cdot) \coloneqq T(\cdot) + c_{k}^{-1}(\cdot - z^{k})$ and the real sequence ${\varepsilon_k}$ satisfies $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \varepsilon_k < \infty$ . As shown in [51], that criterion (1.4) implies criterion (1.3). Under the assumption that the solution set of (1.1) is nonempty and the regularized parameters ${c_{k}}$ are bounded away from zero, it is proved in [51] that the sequence ${z^{k}}$ generated by (1.3) (and so by (1.4)) with any initial point $z^{0}$ converges weakly to a solution of (1.1); furthermore the convergence rate is at least linear if $T^{-1}$ is additionally assumed to be Lipschitz continuous at 0.

citation_details.description: The author discusses Del Pia's work [6], which uses mesh partitions and linear underestimators, but notes its limitation. The approach is ineffective when the number of integer variables is not fixed, as its flatness-based algorithm can generate an exponential number of subproblems.
citation_details.context: In [6, 7] Del Pia employs mesh partitions and linear underestimators in concave mixed-integer quadratic programming. He gives an algorithm that finds an $\epsilon$ -approximate solution in polynomial-time, provided that the number of negative eigenvalues and the number of integer variables are fixed. Vavasis' technique is not directly applicable to the mixed-integer setting since the midpoint of two feasible points is generally not feasible. To obtain the desired bound, these algorithms decompose the original problem into a fixed number of subproblems. The geometry of the mixed-integer points guarantees that in each subproblem the midpoint is feasible and this is used to obtain the desired bound. The decomposition approaches introduced in [6, 7] are not effective if the number of integer variables is not fixed. The flatness-based algorithm described in [6] could yield an exponential number of subproblems, and their constraint matrices can have subdeterminants larger than those of the original constraint matrix.
