citation_details.parsed_title: Optimal multiple stopping of linear diffusions
citation_details.description: The authors position their work against Carmona and Dayanik [12], noting that while it extended multiple stopping problems, its formulation requires a positive refracting time between stops. The current paper addresses this gap by allowing zero refracting time, which is more realistic for order placement but requires a different solution technique.
citation_details.context: The theoretical and numerical aspects of optimal multiple stopping problems were first discussed in Carmona and Touzi [13], in the context of swing options. That work has been extended in Carmona and Dayanik [12] and Zeghal and Mnif [31] to more general payoff processes. Differing from the formulations in Carmona and Touzi [13], Carmona and Dayanik [12], and Zeghal and Mnif [31], we do not impose the assumption that two consecutive stopping times must be separated by a positive refracting time interval; instead we allow two consecutive stopping times to take exactly the same value. In Carmona and Touzi [13] the assumption of a strictly positive refracting time is enforced to prevent the original multiple stopping problem from degenerating to a single stopping problem. However, in the context of an optimal order placement problem, multiple stopping times taking the same value corresponds to the strategy of cancelling multiple limit orders at exactly the same time, which is common in practice. Therefore, it is important for us to allow zero refracting time period between consecutive stopping times. Similar to Carmona and Touzi [13], Carmona and Dayanik [12], and Zeghal and Mnif [31], we shall show that our newly proposed optimal multiple stopping problem can also be reduced to a sequence of recursively defined optimal single stopping problems. However, under our formulation, each optimal single stopping problem has an exponentially distributed random maturity. For each optimal single stopping problem, if the stopping time $\tau$ occurs before the random maturity, the order would be executed as a market order at the best-bid price; otherwise, the order would be placed as a limit order at the best-ask price. In particular, the payoff is nonzero when the random maturity occurs before the stopping time $\tau$ . Due to this nonzero payoff at the random maturity before $\tau$ , an extra transformation is required to convert each optimal single stopping problem into a canonical form commonly found in the literature, such as that in Peskir and Shiryaev [28] (see Equation (29)). Techniques developed in Carmona and Touzi [13], Carmona and Dayanik [12], and Zeghal and Mnif [31] to characterize the optimal stopping region rely crucially on the supermartingale property of the value function of each optimal single stopping problem (see Proposition 3 in Carmona and Touzi [13]). However, in our formulation, the original value function of each optimal single stopping problem does not satisfy the supermartingale property (see Equation (36)). Therefore, in our case techniques developed in Carmona and Touzi [13], Carmona and Dayanik [12], and Zeghal and Mnif [31] cannot be directly applied.

citation_details.context: Hassin and Zemel [HZ] studied the probabilistic version of the transportation problem where the underlying graph is complete and the edge capacities are random variables. A collection of random variables {c_k: k \in K} is said to be proper with respect to a constant \alpha if, for each y \geq 0 and each k \in K , \operatorname{Prob}[c_k \geq y|S] \leqslant \alpha y . Here S represents any conditioning event concerning the variables {c_l: l \in K, l \neq k} . Hassin and Zemel considered the case where the edge capacities form a proper collection and the supplies/demands are bounded from above. In effect, the "properness" condition requires that each edge capacity be positive. This means that the underlying graph must be complete. Under these assumptions, they presented an algorithm which, with high probability, computes a feasible flow in linear time.

citation_details.parsed_title: Altruism, selfishness, and spite in traffic routing
citation_details.description: The authors discuss the work by Chen and Kempe [4], which models player altruism, to show the implications of their own findings. They explain that their negative result demonstrates a limitation in the model from [4], as the price of anarchy becomes unbounded if any fraction of players are purely selfish.
citation_details.context: Most notably in this context is the very recent work by Chen and Kempe [4], who introduce a new network routing game with nonatomic players that is capable to model the players' degree of altruism. Every player $i$ has an altruism level $\beta_{i}$ and the utility function is a linear combination of a selfish part (player $i$ 's latency) and an altruistic part (the average latency of all players). By varying $\beta_{i}$ from 1 to 0 to -1, player $i$ 's degree of altruism ranges from altruistic to selfish to spiteful, respectively. The authors show, among other results, that if all players have a uniform altruism level of $\beta > 0$ , i.e., there are no entirely selfish players, then the price of anarchy is bounded by $1 / \beta$ for arbitrary networks and semiconvex latency functions. On the other hand, our negative result implies that if the players who are entirely selfish $(\beta_{i} = 0)$ only control a nonzero fraction of the overall demand, then the price of anarchy is unbounded, even for single-commodity networks and independently of the altruism levels of the nonselfish players $(\beta_{i} \neq 0)$ . In fact, based on this negative result, Chen and Kempe [4] restrict their analysis of the price of anarchy for nonuniform altruism levels to parallel-arc networks.

citation_details.context: Also, using $\bar{x} = 0$ , it is shown in Freund and Vera [5] that a favorable value of $\mathcal{C}(d)$ implies favorable geometry of $S$ , namely, favorable values of $R/r$ , $R$ , and $1/r$ , and that a converse of this statement holds under an assumption of "conic curvature" defined and shown in Belloni and Freund [1].

citation_details.parsed_title: Coherent Continuous Systems and the Generalized Functional Equation of Associativity
citation_details.description: The author cites this paper as a related work, alongside Mak [21], which shows that strict essentiality is a crucial assumption for deriving closure properties for weak separability. This prior work serves as a baseline against which the author contrasts their own paper's weaker assumptions.
citation_details.context: In Mak [21], strict essentiality for all variables is crucial in deriving closure properties for weak separability [21, p. 259]; see also [22].

citation_details.parsed_title: Trust-Region Methods
citation_details.description: The authors cite this work as a foundational and comprehensive reference for the trust-region methodology. This methodology is the basis for the model-based algorithms being analyzed in the paper.
citation_details.context: These algorithms are based on the well-known trust-region methodology (see Conn, Gould, and Toint [5] for an extensive coverage).

citation_details.parsed_title: Wedge trust region methods for derivative free optimization
citation_details.description: The authors cite Marazzi and Nocedal [17] as part of a list of researchers who have developed model-based algorithms for derivative-free optimization. This reference helps to establish the body of existing work and methodology in the field.
citation_details.context: Pioneered by Winfield [33, 34] and Powell [23, 24, 25, 26, 27], they have been developed, for constrained and unconstrained problems, by a number of authors (see Conn and Toint [13], Conn, Scheinberg, and Toint [6, 7, 8], Marazzi and Nocedal [17], Colson [2], Colson and Toint [3, 4], Vanden Berghen and Bersini [30], Oeuvray [20], Driessen [14], Conn, Scheinberg, and Vicente [9, 10, 11], Oeuvray and Bierlaire [22], Wild [31], or Wild, Regis, and Shoemaker [32]).

citation_details.parsed_title: Exact penalty functions in nonlinear programming
citation_details.description: The authors cite this work for the technique of using squared-slack variables to eliminate inequality constraints from a nonlinear programming problem. This reformulation is a foundational step in deriving the exact differentiable penalty function used in the paper.
citation_details.context: To derive the EDPF used in this work, we first note that one can eliminate the inequality constraints of the NLP (1.1) by using squared-sack variables $z \in \mathcal{R}^n$ [28, 6].

citation_details.parsed_title: Strategyproof approximation of the minimax on networks
citation_details.description: The authors mention that Alon et al. have studied the facility location problem on a circle topology, which is a different setting from the line topology focused on in the current paper.
citation_details.context: In addition, some consideration has been given in literature to the circle topology, by Alon et al. [1, 2].

citation_details.parsed_title: Robust optimization: Methodology and applications
Learning noisy functions via interval models
citation_details.description: The author cites this work as an example where Random Convex Programs (RCPs) are applied to identification and prediction problems, thereby establishing the practical relevance of the paper's topic.
citation_details.context: RCPs also arise naturally in identification and prediction problems [7, 13], as well as in pattern analysis and data classification problems.

citation_details.parsed_title: A sample approximation approach for optimization with probabilistic constraints
citation_details.description: The author describes a method from the cited paper for approximating chance constraints via empirical counterparts. The author then highlights a limitation of this approach, noting that its theoretical bounds depend on restrictive hypotheses like a finite search domain or Lipschitz continuity.
citation_details.context: Also, in [27] the authors propose a method of approximation of chance constraints based on replacing the true probability with its empirical counterpart, and then they provide results on the probability with which the empirical program yields upper and lower bounds on the original CCP. These bounds require introduction of some hypotheses such as finite cardinality of the search domain or uniform Lipschitz continuity of $f$ with respect to $x$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: Approximations to solutions to systems of linear inequalities
citation_details.description: The paper cites Hoffman's foundational result on error bounds for affine functions. This work is later grouped with other results that are characterized as being limited by their reliance on the assumptions of a closed cone and a pre-assumed nonempty solution set, which the current paper aims to relax.
citation_details.context: In this case, the most important and celebrated result regarding the error bound is due to Hoffman, who proved that if $F$ is affine and the solution set $S$ is nonempty, then there exists $c > 0$ such that (1.2) holds with $e(\cdot) = \mathrm{d}(F(\cdot),\mathbb{R}_{-}^{m})$ and $U = X$ (see [6, 7]).

citation_details.parsed_title: Global error bounds for piecewise convex polynomials
citation_details.description: The paper includes [10] in a list of established extensions of Hoffman's error bound to convex inequalities. The authors later group these works as being limited by assumptions (e.g., a closed cone and nonempty solution set) that their new approach will drop.
citation_details.context: Extensions of Hoffman's result to convex inequalities have been well established in the literature; see, for example, [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 19, 20, 28] and references therein.

citation_details.parsed_title: Global error bounds with fractional exponents
citation_details.description: The paper lists [17] as a related work on global error bounds for nonconvex inequalities. This body of work, which follows a discussion of papers [13, 14], is implicitly characterized as being limited by the presence of an unknown fractional exponent in the error bound.
citation_details.context: Other related works in this direction can be found in [15, 17, 18, 27].

citation_details.parsed_title: Stochastic dominance and moments of distributions
citation_details.description: The paper cites this work for a theorem that establishes a necessary condition for nth-degree stochastic dominance based on the moments of the distributions. This theorem is used as a basis for discussing the properties of traditional stochastic dominance.
citation_details.context: The following theorem (Fishburn 1980b, O'Brien 1984) provides a necessary condition on moments for $n$ th-degree stochastic dominance: see also Lemma 5 in §5.

citation_details.parsed_title: Matching, matroids, and extensions
citation_details.description: The author lists this paper as an example of related work in the context of the weighted $C_k$-free 2-factor problem and its polyhedral structures. No specific details about the paper's contribution are provided.
citation_details.context: Related work also appears in Cunningham [2], Hell et al. [14], and Russell [20].

citation_details.parsed_title: Duality gap estimation of linear equality constrained binary quadratic programming
citation_details.description: The authors state that their proposed technique for reducing the duality gap is a generalization of the methods found in the cited work. The paper notes that reference [29] specifically addressed binary quadratic programs.
citation_details.context: The gap reduction technique proposed in this paper can be viewed as a generalization of the results in [22], [29] where binary quadratic programs are considered.

citation_details.parsed_title: Strong duality for the CDT subproblem: A necessary and sufficient condition
citation_details.description: This work is cited as an example of research providing conditions under which the Shor relaxation for the Two-Trust-Region Subproblem (TTRS) is tight, meaning there is no optimality gap.
citation_details.context: There are a variety of results (see, for example, [1] and [3]) that give conditions under which the Shor relaxation for TTRS is in fact tight, i.e., $v(x^{*}) = z(x^{*},X^{*})$

citation_details.parsed_title: A note on polynomial solvability of the CDT problem
citation_details.description: This paper is referenced for describing a polynomial-time algorithm to solve the TTRS, which is noted as an alternative to other methods that are not provably polynomial-time.
citation_details.context: This method is not provably polynomial time, but a polynomial-time algorithm for TTRS based on methods for polynomial equations [2] is described in [4].

citation_details.parsed_title: Second-order-cone constraints for extended trust-region subproblems
citation_details.description: This work provides the baseline method using SOC-RLT constraints, which the current paper's KSOC approach is shown to be stronger than. The computational experiments are performed on instances that this baseline method failed to solve.
citation_details.context: For the general case of TTRS, in which the Shor relaxation may not be tight, the approach taken in [7] is to start with $\mathrm{TTRS}_{\mathrm{SDP}}$ , and then add violated SOC-RLT constraints based on the SOC constraints of the problem as in Example 2 of section 1. After each constraint addition the problem is resolved and an attempt is made to generate another violated SOC-RLT constraint. This process continues until either no violated constraint can be found, or 25 SOC-RLT constraints are added.

citation_details.parsed_title: Trust Region Methods
citation_details.description: This reference is cited to establish that the TTRS problem originates as a subproblem within the broader field of trust-region methods for nonlinear optimization.
citation_details.context: The TTRS, also referred to as the Celis-Dennis-Tapia problem [8], arises as a direction-finding subproblem in certain trust-region-based methods for nonlinear optimization [9].

citation_details.parsed_title: Alternative theorems for quadratic inequality systems and global quadratic optimization
citation_details.description: This paper is mentioned as part of the body of literature that has investigated and established optimality conditions for the TTRS problem.
citation_details.context: Optimality conditions for TTRS are considered in [5], [6], [11], and [13].

citation_details.parsed_title: Investigations into the Efficiency of the Fixed Point Algorithms
citation_details.description: The author cites this work as a study on the efficiency of algorithms that use the triangulation I, which is one of the triangulations employed in the current paper.
citation_details.context: One of the triangulations we shall use in this paper is $I$ , proposed by Kuhn [6] and studied by Saigal [12], Todd [21] in relation to the efficiency of algorithms implemented on this triangulation.

citation_details.parsed_title: Sharp uniform convexity and smoothness inequalities for trace norms
Models for minimax stochastic linear optimization problems with risk aversion
citation_details.description: This paper is cited as an example of a traditional robust optimization approach. The authors contrast these traditional methods with their own, noting that traditional approaches require knowledge of the functional form, which represents a gap their method addresses.
citation_details.context: The concept of functionally robust optimization was first proposed by Hu, Li, and Mehrotra [26] in a newsvendor problem for the unknown mathematical form of a price-demand function, which is different from traditional robust approaches requiring the knowledge of the functional form, e.g., [3, 4, 5, 10, 17, 52, 54].

citation_details.parsed_title: A convex analytic approach for risk-aware Markov decision processes
citation_details.description: This paper is cited as an example of a prior work on optimization models using stochastic dominance. The authors list it to establish the context and show the breadth of existing research in this area.
citation_details.context: For the last decade, optimization models using stochastic dominance have been the subject of theoretical considerations and practical applications in areas such as business, finance, energy, and transportation; see, e.g., [11, 14, 16, 22, 24, 29, 35, 40, 45, 50, 58].

citation_details.parsed_title: New formulations for optimization under stochastic dominance constraints
citation_details.description: This work is referenced as an example of the theoretical and practical application of optimization models with stochastic dominance constraints. The authors include it in a list to demonstrate the significant body of existing research in this domain.
citation_details.context: For the last decade, optimization models using stochastic dominance have been the subject of theoretical considerations and practical applications in areas such as business, finance, energy, and transportation; see, e.g., [11, 14, 16, 22, 24, 29, 35, 40, 45, 50, 58].

citation_details.parsed_title: Optimality conditions for the minimization of quadratic 0-1 problems
citation_details.description: The author cites this work to identify specific theorems (2.15 and 2.21) as incorrect. The paper's main construction serves as a direct counterexample to the cited work's claims about the polynomial-time termination of certain local search methods.
citation_details.context: This also provides a counterexample to [2, Theorems 2.15 and 2.21], which state, incorrectly, that a particular 1-flip (respectively, 2-flip) local search method terminates in no more than $n$ iterations (resp., $O(n^2)$ iterations) for every $n$ -variable problem.

citation_details.parsed_title: Separating clique trees and bipartition inequalities having a fixed number of handles and teeth in polynomial time
citation_details.description: The paper cites Carr [5] for providing a partial result on the separation of comb inequalities. Specifically, Carr's work offers an exact separation method when the number of teeth is fixed.
citation_details.context: A partial result, obtained by Carr [5], gives an exact separation method under the assumption that the number of teeth is fixed.

citation_details.parsed_title: Computing all small cuts in undirected networks
citation_details.description: The authors state that the algorithm from Nagamochi [25] can be used to enumerate the set of all small cuts (the set $\mathcal{A}$) within a specific time complexity, which is a step in their proposed separation algorithm.
citation_details.context: Using the algorithm of Nagamochi [25], it is possible to completely enumerate $\mathcal{A}$ in $O(m^{2}n + n^{h + r + 2}m)$ , where $m$ is the number of edges in $G$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: Differential Inclusions: Set-Valued Maps and Viability Theory
citation_details.description: The paper cites this work to support the well-established result that the differential inclusion under study admits at least one solution through any initial point, given that the set-valued map is 'standard'. This existence theorem is a foundational piece of the methodology.
citation_details.context: Under the above assumptions, it is well known (see Aubin and Cellina [1]) that (4) admits at least one solution (i.e. an absolutely continuous mapping $\mathbf{x}:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}^m$ such that $\dot{\mathbf{x}} (t)\in F(\mathbf{x}(t))$ for almost every $t$ ) through any initial point.

citation_details.description: The paper is cited as an example of prior work that analyzed the complexity of quadratic penalty methods for convex problems. This highlights a research gap, as the current paper extends this analysis to the more general nonconvex setting.
citation_details.context: Finally, complexity analysis of first-order quadratic penalty methods for solving special convex instances of (1) where $h$ is an indicator function was first studied in [17] and further analyzed in [4, 20, 23].

citation_details.context: As in the latter work, our AIPP method also uses the idea of solving a sequence of convex proximal subproblems by an ACG method, but solves them in a more relaxed manner and, as a result, achieves the complexity bound (6), which improves the one in [5] by a factor of $\log (M / \rho)$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: On the complexity of the hybrid proximal extragradient method for the iterates and the Ergodic mean
citation_details.description: This paper is referenced for its study of Hybrid Proximal Extragradient (HPE) methods. The authors mention it to provide context for related approaches involving inexact proximal point methods.

citation_details.parsed_title: An accelerated hybrid proximal extragradients method for convex optimization and its implications to second-order methods
citation_details.description: This work is cited as an example of a previously proposed inexact proximal point method that uses an ACG variant to solve subproblems. This shares a core methodological concept with the authors' proposed algorithm.
citation_details.context: Also, inexact proximal point methods and HPE variants of the ones studied in [21, 30] for solving convex-concave saddle point problems and monotone variational inequalities, which inexactly solve a sequence of proximal subproblems by means of an ACG variant, were previously proposed by [11, 12, 16, 22, 27].

citation_details.parsed_title: Behavior of Accelerated Gradient Methods Near Critical Points of Nonconvex Functions
citation_details.description: This paper is mentioned as a related study that analyzes the behavior of accelerated gradient methods for unconstrained nonconvex problems, particularly near saddle points.

citation_details.parsed_title: A Solvable One-Dimensional Model of a Diffusion Inventory System
citation_details.description: The author states that as one product's inventory level approaches infinity, the optimal policy for the two-product system converges to the optimal policy for the one-dimensional problem, which was solved in reference [5].
citation_details.context: PROPOSITION 2.1. When one of the product inventory levels goes to infinity, the optimal policy converges to the optimal policy of the one-dimensional inventory problem [5].

citation_details.parsed_title: Mixed-integer sets from two rows of two adjacent simplex bases
citation_details.description: The authors cite this work to situate their own contribution within recent efforts to strengthen inequalities from group relaxations. It is mentioned as a related but distinct approach, highlighting a research gap that the current paper addresses.
citation_details.context: Very recently Andersen, Louveaux, and Weismantel [1] have considered the effect of adding bounds on the continuous nonbasic variables y and Dey and Wolsey [14] have examined how inequalities can be strengthened when some of the nonbasic variables are integers.

citation_details.parsed_title: Maximal lattice-free convex sets in linear subspaces
citation_details.description: This paper is cited as a supporting reference for a key theoretical result about maximal S-free convex sets being polyhedra. This result, primarily attributed to [7], removes technical conditions from an earlier version of the authors' own proof, strengthening their paper's foundation.
citation_details.context: Basu et al. [7] recently showed that the above mentioned technical conditions are not necessary (see also Basu et al. [6]).

citation_details.parsed_title: Minimal inequalities for an infinite relaxation of integer programs
citation_details.description: The authors credit Basu et al. [7] for providing a proof of a fundamental theorem that links minimal valid functions to maximal S-free convex sets. This theorem is a cornerstone of the theoretical framework used in the paper.
citation_details.context: If π: R^m → R is a minimal valid function for R(f, S) , then P(π) is a maximal S -free convex set. A very elegant proof of this fact is given by Basu et al. [7].

citation_details.parsed_title: Minimal valid inequalities for integer constraints
citation_details.description: Borozan and Cornuéjols [10] are credited with defining the set P(π) for the continuous group problem. This definition is a key methodological tool that the current paper adopts and generalizes.
citation_details.context: The definition of inequalities and their hierarchy were introduced for the group problem in Gomory and Johnson [18] and that of P(π) for the continuous group problem was defined in Borozan and Cornuejols [10] (also see Andersen et al. [2]).

citation_details.parsed_title: On the facets of mixed integer programs with two integer variables and two constraints
citation_details.description: This work is cited as a baseline for understanding extreme inequalities in the simpler, unconstrained 2D case. The current paper extends this type of analysis to the more general constrained setting.
citation_details.context: In two dimensions, maximal lattice-free polyhedra generating extreme inequalities for continuous group relaxations are well understood; see Andersen et al. [2] and Cornuéjols and Margot [13].

citation_details.parsed_title: The Generalized Gradient of a Marginal Function in Mathematical Programming
citation_details.description: The author cites this paper as an example of recent progress in the area of estimating the generalized or Clarke's directional derivative of a marginal function.
citation_details.context: Also the problem of estimating the generalized or Clarke's directional derivative of $\varphi$ has received a great deal of attention in recent years and some progress in this area can be found in [7, 13, 18].

citation_details.parsed_title: Refined MDP-based branch-and-bound algorithm for the Hamiltonian cycles problem
citation_details.description: The authors use the geometric properties of the Hamiltonian polytope's extreme points, which were developed and proven by Ejov et al. [4], as a foundation for their own analysis.
citation_details.context: Ejov et al. [4] proved the following results that reveal interesting geometric properties of extreme points of polytope $\mathcal{H}_{\beta}$ . More precisely, as stated below, they showed that the extreme points of the polytope $\mathcal{H}_{\beta}$ possess a specific structure.

citation_details.parsed_title: Global regularity theorems
citation_details.description: The paper cites this reference for a result (Lemma 3.1) that provides a bound on the Hausdorff distance between feasible sets of the continuous relaxation of the recourse problem. This lemma is a methodological tool used to prove the properties of the value function for mixed-integer convex recourse problems.
citation_details.context: LEMMA 3.1 (see [5, Corollary 5]). Assume that $C_{rel}(t) \neq \emptyset$ holds for any $t \in \mathbb{R}^k$ and that $C_{rel}(0)$ is compact. Let $t_1, \ldots, t_k$ denote the components of $t \in \mathbb{R}^k$ , then for any $r > 0$ , $$ K(r):= \sup_{t:||t|| < r, y\notin C_{rel}(t)}\frac{\inf\left\{\|y - y^{\prime}\| \mid y^{\prime}\in C_{rel}(t)\right\}}{\max\left\{g_{j}(y) - t_{j} \mid j = 1,\ldots,k\right\}} $$ is finite and such that $$ d _ {\infty} \left(C _ {r e l} (t), C _ {r e l} \left(t ^ {\prime}\right)\right) \leq K (r) \| t - t ^ {\prime} \| $$ holds for any $t, t' \in \mathbb{R}^k$ satisfying $\|t\|, \|t'\| < r$ . Here, $d_{\infty}$ denotes the Hausdorff distance.

citation_details.parsed_title: Regularization vs. relaxation: A conic optimization perspective of statistical variable selection
citation_details.description: The authors note that the minimax concave penalty (MCP) and the reverse Huber penalty, two existing penalties, can be derived using the perspective relaxation method from the cited work.
citation_details.context: Note that the two last penalties can also be derived using perspective relaxation [9].

citation_details.parsed_title: Nearly unbiased variable selection under minimax concave penalty
citation_details.description: This paper is cited as the source of the minimax concave penalty (MCP), which is listed among a variety of existing continuous nonconvex penalties that approximate the $\ell_0$-norm and are analyzed in the current work.
citation_details.context: Among the variety of $\ell_0$ -like continuous penalties, one can find the nonnegative garrote [4], log-sum penalty [6], capped- $\ell_1$ [33], $\ell_p$ -norms $(0 < p < 1)$ [12], ratio $\ell_1 / \ell_2$ [25], smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD) [11], minimax concave penalty (MCP) [31], and the reverse Huber penalty [24].

citation_details.parsed_title: On optimal solutions of the constrained $\ell_0$ regularization and its penalty problem
citation_details.description: This work is cited to support the statement that $\ell_0$-constrained and $\ell_0$-regularized problems are not entirely equivalent, highlighting a known complexity in the field.
citation_details.context: However, due to their nonconvexity, $\ell_0$ -constrained and $\ell_0$ -regularized (1) problems are not (completely) equivalent [21, 32].

citation_details.parsed_title: Multi-stage convex relaxation for learning with sparse regularization
citation_details.description: This paper is referenced as the origin of the capped-$\ell_1$ penalty, which is included in a list of state-of-the-art continuous penalties that the authors' analysis encompasses.
citation_details.context: Among the variety of $\ell_0$ -like continuous penalties, one can find the nonnegative garrote [4], log-sum penalty [6], capped- $\ell_1$ [33], $\ell_p$ -norms $(0 < p < 1)$ [12], ratio $\ell_1 / \ell_2$ [25], smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD) [11], minimax concave penalty (MCP) [31], and the reverse Huber penalty [24].

citation_details.parsed_title: An axiomatic approach to location on networks
citation_details.description: The authors cite Holzman [9] for its finding that minimizing the sum of squared costs is a unique solution with desirable axiomatic properties on a tree. This is presented as an example of other measures in the literature, motivating future work on generalizing the paper's results.
citation_details.context: Third, recall that many measures were featured in the literature. For example, minimizing the sum of squared costs is known to be the unique solution that satisfies desirable axiomatic properties when the graph is a tree (Holzman [9]). Can our results be generalized in a way that captures multiple measures? In more detail, Marsh and Schilling [13] provide a framework in which the different equity measures can be organized; this framework consists of three dimensions. One could hope for a result that relates feasible SP approximation ratios to the parameters along the different dimensions.

citation_details.parsed_title: A linearization method for nonsmooth stochastic programming problems
citation_details.description: The paper notes that its proposed methods are geometrically similar to stochastic subgradient methods, such as the one in [58]. These methods are described as fitting a convex expected value function by taking the maximum of a set of hyperplanes.
citation_details.context: Geometrically, our proposed methods are similar to cutting plane methods, like L-shaped decomposition [72, 74, 38] and stochastic subgradient methods [58], which fit a convex expected value function through the maximum of a set of hyperplanes.

citation_details.parsed_title: Trust Region Methods
citation_details.description: The authors cite this work to draw a parallel between the update rule in their SD algorithm and the traditional update rule in trust region methods. They highlight that their method is different because it uses value function approximations rather than true function values.
citation_details.context: Moreover, this update rule is also closely related to the traditional update rule in trust region methods (see Conn, Gould, and Toint [6]) except that the functions used in measuring reductions are value function approximations instead of the true function values.

citation_details.parsed_title: Inexact bundle methods for two-stage stochastic rogramming
citation_details.description: The paper positions the Stochastic Decomposition (SD) algorithm as a type of inexact bundle method, as described in [19]. This is because SD uses a combination of exact and inexact subgradients from sample functions to build its approximations.
citation_details.context: We begin by observing that SD can be seen as one of the inexact bundle methods (see Oliveira, Sagastizábal, and Scheimberg in [19]) in which SD at each iteration utilizes an exact subgradient of a random sample function and inexact subgradient approximations of all other sample functions in the construction of value function approximations.

citation_details.parsed_title: Convergence of stationary points of sample average two-stage stochastic programs: A generalized equation approach
citation_details.description: The authors reference a specific lemma from this paper to support one of their technical assumptions. The cited work provides a sufficient condition for the local Lipschitz continuity of the optimal value function, which is used in the convergence rate analysis.
citation_details.context: Moreover, it is worth noticing that a sufficient condition for the local Lipschitz continuity of the optimal value function was presented in Lemma 5.1 in [21].

citation_details.parsed_title: Monotone operators and the proximal point algorithm
citation_details.description: The paper cites Rockafellar [23] as the foundational source for the definition of the proximal mapping point. This concept is a core component of the stochastic proximal mapping used in the authors' algorithm.
citation_details.context: In addition, the projection operator onto a set $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is defined by $$ P _ {X} (x) \triangleq \operatorname * {a r g m i n} _ {z \in X} \| z - x \| ^ {2}, \tag {1} $$ and the proximal mapping point (see Rockafellar [23]) with respect to a convex function $g$ is defined by $$ T _ {\alpha g} ^ {X} (x) \triangleq \operatorname * {a r g m i n} _ {z \in X} \left\{\alpha g (z) + \frac {1}{2} \| z - x \| ^ {2} \right\}. \tag {2} $$

citation_details.parsed_title: Differentiability properties of metric projections onto convex sets
citation_details.description: The paper is cited as one of several references concerning the differentiability of the metric projection operator. This is part of a literature review establishing the existing work that the current paper builds upon.
citation_details.context: As a first step towards the sensitivity analysis of the above variational inequality, one would consider a slight perturbation of the point $x \in \mathrm{H}$ , replacing it by $x(t) \in \mathrm{H}$ , where $t \in \mathbb{R}_+$ is a parameter. The behavior of $y(t) = \mathrm{proj}_{ \mathrm{C}}(x(t))$ is well studied in the literature and is naturally connected to the differentiability properties (in some general sense) of the projection operator $\mathrm{proj}_{ \mathrm{C}}$ . We mention for instance the work of Zarantonello [29] who had shown the existence of directional derivatives for $\mathrm{proj}_{ \mathrm{C}}$ at the boundary of C. However, it is well known that outside the set C the directional differentiability of $\mathrm{proj}_{ \mathrm{C}}$ is not guaranteed (see [27] for a counterexample in $\mathbb{R}^2$ ). On the other hand, Haraux [5] and Mignot [11] published two fundamental papers where the conical differentiability of the projection operator is proved under a polyhedric (also called density) assumption. In that case, an asymptotic development of $y(t)$ at $t = 0$ can be obtained and the derivative $y'(0)$ can be expressed as the projection of $x'(0)$ onto a closed subset of the tangent cone of C at $y(0)$ . We also refer the reader to [4, 6, 28] for other references concerning the differentiability of the metric projection operator.

citation_details.context: There is a certain overlap of ideas and results herein with the paper [6] by Bauschke, Bolte, and Teboulle. For starters, the relative smoothness condition definition in the present paper in Definition 1.1 is equivalent to the (LC) condition in [6] except that [6] also requires the reference function $h(\cdot)$ to be essentially smooth and strictly convex, which we do not need in this paper. The main developments in [6] are based on generalizing a key descent lemma and applying this generalization to tackle (additive) composite optimization problems using the primal gradient scheme (called the NoLips Algorithm in [6]) with associated complexity analysis involving a symmetry measure of the Bregman distance $D_{h}(\cdot,\cdot)$ . These results are then illustrated in the application of composite optimization to Poisson inverse problems. While the NoLips Algorithm in [6] is structurally the same as Algorithm 1 herein, they are both instantiations of the standard primal gradient scheme; however, as will be seen in section 3 here, we do not need any symmetry measure in constructing step sizes or in the complexity analysis.

The problem in [8] can be formulated as the following constrained $\ell_1$ -penalized maximum likelihood estimation problem: $$ \left. \max _ {X \in S ^ {n}} \left\{\log \det X - \langle S, X \rangle - \sum_ {(i, j) \notin V} \rho_ {i j} | X _ {i j} |: X _ {i j} = 0, \forall (i, j) \in V \right\}, \quad \right. \tag {5} $$ where $V$ is as in (4) and ${\rho_{ij}}_{(i,j)\notin V}$ is a set of nonnegative parameters. Lu proposed adaptive first-order (adaptive spectral projected gradient and adaptive Nesterov's smooth) methods for the problem (5). His methods consist of solving a sequence of unconstrained penalty problems of the following form: $$ \max _ {X \in \mathcal {S} ^ {n}} \log \det X - \langle S, X \rangle - \sum_ {i, j} \rho_ {i j} | X _ {i j} | $$ where the set of moderate penalty parameters ${\rho_{ij}}_{(i,j)\in V}$ is adaptively adjusted until a desired approximate solution is found.

citation_details.parsed_title: A restricted Lagrangean approach to the traveling salesman problem
citation_details.description: The author cites this work as an example of a successful application of ascent direction methods to the traveling salesman problem. This supports the argument that these methods are effective for various combinatorial optimization problems.
citation_details.context: So-called ascent direction methods do produce series of monotonically increasing lower bounds. These are iterative problem-specific approximation algorithms that exploit the structure of the problem and the formulation. An ascent direction algorithm is in general much faster than the subgradient method, but it cannot be guaranteed to produce lower bounds that are as good. Many success stories of Lagrangian relaxation are nonetheless attributed to ascent direction methods. They have shown to be successful for many combinatorial optimization problems, including plant location problems [3,6,14], the traveling salesman problem [2,4] the generalized assignment problem [10], and the set covering problem [11]. These applications indicate that the gain in speed over the subgradient method compensates the possible loss in lower quality more than sufficiently.

citation_details.parsed_title: A dual algorithm for the one-machine scheduling problem
citation_details.description: The author notes that while using the subgradient method with time-indexed formulations can produce strong lower bounds, the computational time required is substantial. This is cited as a limitation of that approach.
citation_details.context: Integer linear programming formulations are predominantly cast in terms of linear ordering variables $x_{jk}$ that take the value 1 if job $J_{j} (j = 1, \dots, n)$ completes before job $J_{k} (k = 1, \dots, n, k \neq j)$ , and the value 0 otherwise, or in terms of time-indexed variables $x_{jt}$ that take the value 1 if $J_{j} (j = 1, \dots, n)$ completes at time $t$ , and the value 0 otherwise. Note that the second type of formulation requires a pseudopolynomial number of variables. As to the design of ascent direction algorithms, it seems that the first type of formulation is suitable for precedence-constrained scheduling problems only [16,26]. The second type of formulation does not seem to allow the kind of analysis required to develop fast ascent direction algorithms; the subgradient method is the only practical approach to deal with the Lagrangian dual problem. This gives generally very strong lower bounds, but the time needed to compute them is substantial [7]. For a specific single-machine scheduling problem, Dyer and Wolsey [5] show that Lagrangian bounds obtained from time-indexed formulations are stronger than those obtained from logical formulations in terms of the job completion times $C_{1}, \ldots, C_{n}$ . In many applications, however, logical formulations are easier to handle in that good Lagrangian lower bounds can quickly be obtained one way or the other, such as by elegant $O(n)$ single-pass methods, as proposed by Hariri and Potts [15] and Potts and Van Wassen-hove [27,28], by ascent direction algorithms, as we will show in this paper, or by more opportunistic approaches, as applied in [36].

citation_details.parsed_title: Validation of subgradient optimization
citation_details.description: The author cites this work to support the claim that the subgradient method has known downsides, such as non-monotonic lower bounds, zigzagging behavior, and slow convergence. This highlights a limitation of a common alternative approach.
citation_details.context: For any application, there are several issues to take care of, including dealing with the Lagrangian dual problem. This is the problem of finding the Lagrangian multipliers that give the best Lagrangian lower bound. The subgradient method is frequently used to solve this problem, since it is always easy to implement. The downside of this iterative method, however, is that it does not produce a series of monotonically increasing lower bounds. It is known for its zigzagging in the beginning and slow convergence at the end (see, e.g., [19]).

citation_details.parsed_title: Stronger Lagrangian bounds by use of slack variables: applications to machine scheduling problems
citation_details.description: The paper describes this work as presenting a general technique using slack variables to improve Lagrangian lower bounds for various problems, including the one being studied. It is mentioned as an alternative bounding method and its strength is compared to other existing bounds.
citation_details.context: Various lower bounds have been proposed for the machine scheduling problem under consideration. Potts [26] proceeds from a formulation in terms of linear ordering variables and presents an ascent direction algorithm to compute a Lagrangian bound; this algorithm is time-consuming, however, requiring $\Omega(n^4)$ time per iteration. Queyranne and Wang [31] proceed from a logical formulation of the problem and obtain their bound by solving the problem as a linear program to which they add three types of facet-defining inequalities; see also Queyranne and Wang [30]. Hoogeveen and Van de Velde [20] present a general technique to improve Lagrangian lower bounds by use of slack variables. They present various applications, including the problem under consideration. As to the quality of the bounds, Queyranne and Wang [31] prove that Hoogeveen and Van de Velde's bound is no stronger than theirs. Also, Wolsey [38] and Queyranne and Schulz [29] show that the linear programming bound obtained from the linear ordering formulation, of which Potts's Lagrangian bound is an approximation from below, is no weaker than Queyranne and Wang's bound. As to the speed by which the bounds can be computed, we note that the linear programming bounds are time-consuming; in contrast, our ascent direction algorithm is fast.

citation_details.parsed_title: A successive projection method
citation_details.description: The authors note that Han [11] independently re-proved the finite-dimensional version of Dykstra's algorithm, apparently without being aware of the original work.
citation_details.context: In related work, we note that Han [11] (apparently unaware of Dykstra's algorithm) reproved the finite-dimensional version. Iusem and De Pierro [14] applied Han's (i.e. Dykstra's) algorithm to prove a finite-dimensional variant thereof, and also gave a convergence proof for the case when the intersection of the convex sets is empty. Gaffke and Mathar [9] gave a duality proof of the convergence of Dykstra's algorithm, which also provided some motivation for Dykstra's algorithm. Bauschke and Borwein [1] generalized the results of Iusem and De Pierro to infinite-dimensional spaces, and also considered the case when the distance between the convex sets is not attained. When $C$ is a "polyhedron" (i.e., all the $C_i$ are closed half-spaces) and $X$ is Euclidean $n$ -space, Dykstra's algorithm reduces to Hildreth's algorithm [12]. Linear convergence of Hildreth's algorithm was established by Iusem and De Pierro [13] using methods of optimization theory. More generally, the authors of this paper [7] gave sharper bounds than those of [13] on the rate of convergence of Dykstra's algorithm when $C$ is a polyhedron in any Hilbert space.

citation_details.parsed_title: Two-stage integer programs with stochastic right-hand sides: a superadditive dual approach
citation_details.description: This paper is presented as a key predecessor that developed a value-function-based approach for two-stage linear integer programs with stochastic right-hand sides. The authors state that their solution approach directly extends this methodology to the more general case of stochastic quadratic integer programs.
citation_details.context: Kong et al. [35] considers a class of stochastic programs with stochastic right-hand sides, pure-integer first- and second-stage problems that have linear objective functions in both stages, i.e. $\Lambda = \Gamma = 0$ in (P1). Similar to Ahmed et al. [9], their approach is based on an equivalent variable transformation that uses the value functions in both stages. Moreover, superadditive duality properties are exploited to characterize value functions efficiently. citation_details.context: The Steiner tree packing problem, as introduced in [12], can be stated as follows. Given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ with edge capacities $c_{c} \in \mathbb{N}$ for all $e \in E$ and a list of node sets $\mathcal{N} = \{T_{1}, \ldots, T_{N}\}$ , $N \in \mathbb{N}$ , find Steiner trees $S_{k}$ for $T_{k}$ , $k = 1, \ldots, N$ , such that each edge $e \in E$ is contained in at most $c_{e}$ of the edge sets $S_{1}, \ldots, S_{N}$ . Every collection of Steiner trees $S_{1}, \ldots, S_{N}$ with this property is called a Steiner tree packing. If a weighting of the edges is given in addition and a (with respect to this weighting) minimal Steiner tree packing must be found, we call this the weighted Steiner tree packing problem.

citation_details.parsed_title: Efficient branch-and-bound algorithms for weighted MAX-2-SAT
citation_details.description: The paper, which is the cited work itself, proposes exact branch-and-bound algorithms for MAX-2-SAT. The methodology is based on three types of lower bounds derived from a directed graph representing clause conflicts, with two of these bounds using a set covering formulation.
citation_details.context: Abstract MAX-2-SAT is one of the representative combinatorial problems and is known to be NP-hard. Given a set of $m$ clauses on $n$ propositional variables, where each clause contains at most two literals and is weighted by a positive real, MAX-2-SAT asks to find a truth assignment that maximizes the total weight of satisfied clauses. In this paper, we propose branch-and-bound exact algorithms for MAX-2-SAT utilizing three kinds of lower bounds. All lower bounds are based on a directed graph that represents conflicts among clauses, and two of them use a set covering representation of MAX-2-SAT. Computational comparisons on benchmark instances disclose that these algorithms are highly effective in reducing the number of search tree nodes as well as the computation time.

Their computational experiments revealed that the bounds obtained are strong compared to bounds obtained from other mixed integer programming formulations.
