citation_details.parsed_title: Limiting behavior of the affine scaling continuous trajectories for linear programming problems
citation_details.description: Adler and Monterio are cited for having proved the global convergence for the continuous version of the affine scaling method without requiring nondegeneracy assumptions. This is presented as a key prior result in the field.
citation_details.context: For the continuous version of the method, the global convergence was shown by Adler and Monterio [3] without assuming nondegeneracy conditions.

citation_details.parsed_title: A variation on Karmarkar's algorithm for solving linear programming problems
citation_details.description: Barnes's paper is cited as providing one of the first proofs of global convergence for the affine scaling method. However, the author notes that this proof relies on strong assumptions of both primal and dual nondegeneracy, which the current work aims to remove.
citation_details.context: Since the papers by Barnes [4] and Vanderbei et al. [21] appeared with (independent) proofs of global convergence assuming both primal and dual nondegeneracy assumptions, several researchers have dealt with this problem.

citation_details.parsed_title: Conial projection algorithms for linear programming
citation_details.description: The paper is cited as a reference for the established equivalence between Karmarkar's method and the affine scaling method for homogeneous problems. This equivalence forms the basis of the author's analysis.
citation_details.context: ...on the basis of the equivalence between Karmarkar's method and the affine scaling method applied to homogeneous problems [5, 8, 16, 17, 23].

citation_details.parsed_title: A new polynomial-time algorithm for linear programming
citation_details.description: Karmarkar's 1984 paper is cited as the seminal work that introduced the projective scaling method for linear programming. This work spurred the development of numerous related methods, including the affine scaling method.
citation_details.context: Since Karmarker [9] proposed the projective scaling method for linear programming in 1984, a number of interior point methods have been proposed and implemented.

citation_details.parsed_title: On the convergence of the affine-scaling algorithm
citation_details.description: The author acknowledges that Tseng and Luo's result is superior for not requiring degeneracy conditions, but highlights its limitation of having a problem-dependent and impractically small step-size bound. This sets up the contribution of the current paper, which proves convergence with a constant step-size.
citation_details.context: Tseng and Luo's result surpasses the other results in view of the conditions on degeneracy, however, their step-size bound for the global convergence depends on the problem and usually it cannot but be estimated by a quantity of O(2^{-L}) .

citation_details.parsed_title: Equivalent differentiable optimization problems and descent methods for asymmetric variational inequality problems
citation_details.description: The author cites Fukushima [9] for formulating asymmetric variational inequality problems (VIP) as differentiable optimization problems, mentioning it as a relevant equation-based method in the literature.
citation_details.context: More recently, Fukushima [9] formulated asymmetric VIP as differentiable optimization problems.

citation_details.parsed_title: Finite-dimensional variational inequality and nonlinear complementarity problems: a survey of theory, algorithms and applications
citation_details.description: Paper [10] is cited as a comprehensive survey covering the theory, algorithms, and applications of VIP and NCP. The authors refer to it for foundational knowledge and to avoid repeating well-established results.
citation_details.context: The paper [10] provides an extensive survey on the theory, algorithms and applications for finite-dimensional VIP and nonlinear complementarity problems (NCP).

citation_details.parsed_title: A new continuation method for complementarity problems with uniform $P$ -functions
citation_details.description: This work is cited for providing results on the limiting behavior of perturbed nonlinear complementarity problems (NCP) for the specific case of NCPs with a uniform P-function. It is part of the literature on path-following methods that motivates the current paper.
citation_details.context: Similar results were also obtained for the NCP with uniform $P$ -function [12] and the NCP with $P_0$ -function [14].

citation_details.parsed_title: A polynomial-time algorithm for a class of linear complementarity problems
citation_details.description: The author credits Kojima et al. [15] with developing the first polynomial path-following interior-point algorithm for monotone linear complementarity problems (LCP), presenting it as a key development in the field.
citation_details.context: For a monotone LCP, Kojima et al. [15] first developed a polynomial path-following interior-point algorithm based on the above idea.

citation_details.parsed_title: Nonlinear complementarity as unconstrained and constrained minimization
citation_details.description: Paper [19] is mentioned for extending a previous result to formulate the nonlinear complementarity problem (NCP) as an unconstrained optimization problem, which is noted within a review of related equation-based methods.
citation_details.context: The result was further extended in [19] to formulate NCP as unconstrained optimization problems.

citation_details.parsed_title: Stable monotone variational inequalities
citation_details.description: This paper is cited for extending previous results concerning the properties of perturbed complementarity problems to the broader class of monotone and general variational inequalities.
citation_details.context: These results were then extended to both monotone and general variational inequalities [22].

citation_details.parsed_title: NE/SQP: A robust algorithm for the nonlinear complementarity problem
citation_details.description: The author refers to paper [24] as a survey on the topic of nondifferentiable equation formulations for VIP-related problems, providing context on a related research direction.
citation_details.context: Nondifferentiable equation formulations of VIP-related problems have attracted much attention in recent years due to the theoretical development of Newton's method when applied to a system of non-Fréchet differentiable equations. See [24] for a brief survey.

citation_details.parsed_title: Sensor network localization, Euclidean distance matrix completions, and graph realization
citation_details.description: This reference is cited as an example of prior work that considered a variant of the problem formulation and applied a primal-dual interior-point method to solve it.
citation_details.context: In [11, 19], a variant of (1) and (2) is considered whereby |·| is replaced with |·|2 , and a primal-dual interior-point method is applied to solve the SDP and its dual in a certain reduced/projected form. Simulation results with up to m = 20 sensors are reported.

citation_details.parsed_title: Theory of semidefinite programming for sensor network localization
citation_details.description: This work is cited for a theorem that proves the condition for unique localizability in the noiseless case, which is that all individual traces of an interior solution must be zero.
citation_details.context: So and Ye [32, Theorem 2] proved in the case of υ sdp = 0 that the sensors are “uniquely localizable” if and only if, for any interior solution Z (equivalently, Z has maximum rank), all individual traces of Z are zero, i.e., Y = X T X .

citation_details.parsed_title: A coordinate gradient descent method for nonsmooth separable minimization
The traveling salesman problem on a graph and some related integer polyhedra
The traveling salesman problem in graphs with some excluded minors
Edmonds polytopes and weakly Hamiltonian graphs
citation_details.description: The author cites Chvátal [6] as part of a body of work that introduced effective classes of valid inequalities, such as comb inequalities, for the Traveling Salesman Problem. These inequalities are noted for their effectiveness in strengthening linear programming relaxations, a core concept in the paper's methodology.
citation_details.context: Instead of searching for violated inequalities among subtour elimination constraints only, other classes of valid inequalities have been considered, such as comb and clique tree inequalities, and have been found to be effective in strengthening the linear programming relaxation (Chvátal [6], Grötschel [15], Grötschel and Padberg [16], Padberg and Hong [30], Grötschel and Pulleyblank [17], Padberg and Rinaldi [31]).

citation_details.parsed_title: The traveling salesman problem on a graph and some related integer polyhedra
citation_details.description: This work is cited as a foundational study on the graphical relaxation of the traveling salesman polyhedron. The authors note that this approach led to the discovery of new valid inequalities for the TSP, providing a methodological basis for their own investigation into the CVRP.
citation_details.context: For instance, the study of the graphical relaxation of the traveling salesman polyhedron (Cornuejols, Fonlupt and Naddef [7], Fleischmann [11], Fonlupt and Naddef [12], Naddef and Rinaldi [27, 28]) has lead to the discovery of new valid inequalities and facets for the TSP, such as the path inequalities and the path-tree inequalities.

citation_details.parsed_title: A new class of cutting planes for the symmetric traveling salesman problem
citation_details.description: The work by Fleischmann [11] is cited as part of the foundational research on the graphical relaxation of the traveling salesman polyhedron. This line of research is noted for successfully identifying new inequalities, providing a methodological precedent for the current paper.
citation_details.context: For instance, the study of the graphical relaxation of the traveling salesman polyhedron (Cornuejols, Fonlupt and Naddef [7], Fleischmann [11], Fonlupt and Naddef [12], Naddef and Rinaldi [27, 28]) has lead to the discovery of new valid inequalities and facets for the TSP, such as the path inequalities and the path-tree inequalities.

citation_details.parsed_title: A note on some computationally difficult set covering problems
citation_details.description: The author cites Avis [1] to provide historical context on the difficulty of solving the A_45 set covering problem. The citation notes a previous successful attempt by H. Ratliff, which took a significant amount of time on hardware of that era, establishing it as a computationally hard problem.
citation_details.context: Avis [1] reports that $A_{45}$ was solved in 1979 by H. Ratliff, requiring over two and a half hours on an Amdahl V7 computer.

citation_details.parsed_title: Experimental results on Hillier's linear search
citation_details.description: The paper cites Jeroslow and Smith [13] as an example of prior work that extended Hillier's interior point method for integer programming. Their work involved creating a hybrid method by embedding Hillier's technique into a branch-and-bound framework, which improved performance over a standard branch-and-bound algorithm.
citation_details.context: Jeroslow and Smith [13] embedded phases one and two of Hillier approximation technique inside a simple branch-and-bound scheme and report significant improvement of the hybrid method over a pure branch-and-bound implementation.

citation_details.parsed_title: Penalty for zero-one integer equivalent problem
citation_details.description: The author cites this work as an additional reference supporting the established relationship between zero-one integer programming and concave programming. This connection is a foundational concept for the paper's own approach, which involves solving a nonconvex (concave) optimization problem.
citation_details.context: The relationship between zero-one integer programming (with objective function) and concave programming under linear constraints was first pointed out by Raghavachari [23]. (See also [3] and [14].)

citation_details.parsed_title: Stability of the linear complementarity problem at a solution
citation_details.description: The author identifies the concept of a 'stable solution' from Ha [6] as a key tool for their analysis. This concept is noted as a generalization of Robinson's 'strongly regular' solution.
citation_details.context: The tool for the combined analysis is the concept of a stable solution of a linear complementarity problem. This concept is defined in [6]; it generalizes Robinson's notion of a strongly regular solution (specialized to the linear complementarity problem).

citation_details.parsed_title: Finite-dimensional variational inequality and nonlinear complementarity problems: A survey of theory, algorithms and applications
citation_details.description: The author cites Harker and Pang [7] to support the established equivalence between the affine variational inequality problem and the linear complementarity problem. This equivalence allows the author to generalize their results.
citation_details.context: As a consequence of the equivalence between the affine variational inequality problem and the linear complementarity problem (see [7]), it is possible to generalize Theorem 1 to the problem VI(K,q,M) when K and M are kept fixed and q is slightly perturbed.

citation_details.parsed_title: On the convergence of iterative methods for symmetric linear complementarity problems
citation_details.description: The author positions their work by reviewing recent literature, noting that Iusem [9] established what was then the most general convergence result for iterative methods for the symmetric linear complementarity problem.
citation_details.context: Independently, De Pierro and Iusem, and Iusem wrote the papers [4, 9]; their joint paper [4] proved essentially the same result as Luo and Tseng did; the other one established a result which is by far the most general among all the existing convergence results for the symmetric problem (under the assumption of exact solutions for the subproblems).

citation_details.parsed_title: Locally unique solutions of quadratic programs, linear and nonlinear complementarity problems
citation_details.description: The author refers to Mangasarian [16] for providing a characterization of when a solution to a complementarity problem is locally unique. This is presented as part of the theoretical background on solution properties.
citation_details.context: In the paper [16], Mangasarian has derived a characterization for a solution z* to be locally unique.

citation_details.parsed_title: Generalized polymatroids and submodular flows
citation_details.description: The author refers to an algorithm by Frank and Tardos to implement a subroutine for intersecting and crossing supermodular functions, noting the number of calls to a submod-minimizer it requires.
citation_details.context: If $p$ is intersecting supermodular, then an algorithm of Frank and Tardos [24] requires $n$ calls of a submod-minimizer. The same paper includes an algorithm for the case when $p$ is crossing supermodular, and this algorithm requires $n^2$ calls of a submod-minimizer.

citation_details.parsed_title: Structures of polyhedra determined by submodular functions on crossing families
citation_details.description: The author cites Fujishige for developing an elegant necessary and sufficient condition that determines when a base-polyhedron defined by a crossing submodular function is non-empty.
citation_details.context: It is a non-trivial task to characterize the situation when $B(b)$ is non-empty for a crossing submodular function $b$ but Fujishige [26] developed an elegant necessary and sufficient condition.

citation_details.parsed_title: About strongly polynomial time algorithms for quadratic optimization over submodular constraints
Optimal flows in networks with multiple sources and sinks
citation_details.description: The author states that the paper develops an algorithmic solution for a discrete counterpart to the lexicographic flow problem introduced in Megiddo's work.
citation_details.context: An algorithmic solution to a discrete counterpart of Megiddo's lexicographic flow problem [43,44] is also developed.

citation_details.parsed_title: M-convex function minimization by continuous relaxation approach-Proximity theorem and algorithm
Discrete convex analysis
citation_details.description: The author cites this work as the source for the term 'M-convex set,' which is defined as the set of integral elements of an integral base-polyhedron.
citation_details.context: In discrete convex analysis [46,47], the set $B$ of integral elements of an integral base-polyhedron $B$ is called an M-convex set.

citation_details.parsed_title: Discrete Convex Analysis
citation_details.description: The paper refers to this work to state that minimizing the square-sum over an M-convex set is a special case of M-convex function minimization, for which a finite local improvement algorithm exists.
citation_details.context: Minimizing the square-sum $W(z)$ over an M-convex set is a special case of minimizing an M-convex function, for which a local improvement algorithm works (in finite steps) [47].

citation_details.parsed_title: A faster strongly polynomial time algorithm for submodular function minimization
citation_details.description: The author points to Orlin's work for a significantly more efficient algorithm for the submodular function minimization subroutine, stating its computational complexity.
citation_details.context: The complexity of a significantly more efficient algorithm, due to Orlin [49], is $O(n^{6})$ (where $n = |S|$ ) and this algorithm calls $O(n^{5})$ times a routine which evaluates the submodular function in question.

citation_details.parsed_title: Interior-point method for nuclear norm approximation with application to system identification
citation_details.description: The authors describe an interior-point method from Liu and Vandenberghe for a nuclear norm approximation problem. This customized method improved iteration complexity and was capable of solving problems with matrices up to 350x350.
citation_details.context: Recently, Liu and Vandenberghe [29] proposed an interior-point method for another nuclear norm approximation problem $$ \min \| \mathcal {A} (x) - B \| _ {*}, \tag {1.14} $$ where $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $$ \mathcal {A} (x) = x _ {1} A _ {1} + x _ {2} A _ {2} + \dots + x _ {p} A _ {p} $$ is a linear mapping from $\mathbb{R}^p$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ . The equivalent SDP formulation of (1.14) is $$ \min _ {x, W _ {1}, W _ {2}} \frac {1}{2} \left(\operatorname {T r} \left(W _ {1}\right) + \operatorname {T r} \left(W _ {2}\right)\right) \\ \left[ \begin{array}{l l} W _ {1} & (\mathcal {A} (x) - B) ^ {\top} \end{array} \right] \tag {1.15} $$ $$ \text {s. t.} \left[ \begin{array}{c c} W _ {1} & (\mathcal {A} (x) - B) ^ {\top} \\ \mathcal {A} (x) - B & W _ {2} \end{array} \right] \succeq 0. $$ Liu and Vandenberghe [29] proposed a customized method for computing the scaling direction in an interior point method for solving the SDP (1.15). The complexity of each iteration in their method was reduced from $O(p^6)$ to $O(p^4)$ when $m = O(p)$ and $n = O(p)$ ; thus they were able to solve problems up to dimension $m = n = 350$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: Analysis of mathematical programming problems prior to applying the Simplex Algorithm
citation_details.description: The authors cite this work as an example of an approach to make a matrix sparser. This method involves logically analyzing the matrix structure and variable bounds to identify and remove fixed variables and redundant rows.
citation_details.context: Several approaches have been proposed to make $A$ sparser. One approach is to logically analyze the structure of $A$ together with any bounds on the variables in order to identify implicitly or explicitly fixed variables and redundant rows (see, e.g., Brearily et al., 1975).

citation_details.parsed_title: Making sparse matrices sparser: Computational results
citation_details.description: The authors acknowledge that the algorithm implemented in McCormick (1990) reduces solution times for linear programs. However, they highlight its primary limitation: the algorithm was too slow, with preprocessing time negating the time saved, thus motivating the present work.
citation_details.context: The computational results in McCormick (1990) shows that pre-processing matrices with SPARSE does reduce the solution time for solving linear programs. However, SPARSE was too slow; the time saved was not appreciably more than the time used in preprocessing.

citation_details.parsed_title: On the basic theorem of complementarity
citation_details.description: The paper cites Eaves [1] for the statement of the Basic Theorem of Complementarity. This theorem provides the theoretical foundation for an existence theorem used to prove the convergence of the proposed algorithm.
citation_details.context: In Gowda and Pang [4] an existence theorem is given based on the Basic Theorem of Complementarity as stated in Eaves [1].

citation_details.parsed_title: The basic theorem of complementarity revisited
citation_details.description: The authors apply an existence theorem from Gowda and Pang [4] to prove the convergence of their algorithm. They state that their problem's homotopy set is a special case covered by the theorem in the cited work, allowing them to adopt its convergence conditions.
citation_details.context: In Gowda and Pang [4] an existence theorem is given based on the Basic Theorem of Complementarity as stated in Eaves [1]. They relate their result on the existence of a solution to the stationary point problem on a polytope which takes our homotopy set $\mathcal{H}(t)$ , $t\geqslant 0$ , as a special case. Therefore the algorithm converges under the same condition.

citation_details.parsed_title: A note on the prize-collecting traveling salesman problem
citation_details.description: The authors state they can create a better TSP-approximator by employing linear programming techniques similar to those used by Bienstock et al. for the prize-collecting TSP. This work provides a methodological foundation for their improved approximator.
citation_details.context: We can give an even better TSP-approximator by using linear programming techniques in the spirit of Bienstock et al. [11] for the prize-collecting TSP.

citation_details.parsed_title: Survivable networks, linear programming relaxations and the parsimonious property
citation_details.description: The authors apply a specific result from Goemans and Bertsimas to justify adding certain constraints to their linear programming relaxation. This result is a key step in their proof for the (2,3)-TSP-approximator, as it allows them to modify the LP without changing the objective function's value.
citation_details.context: By a result of Goemans and Bertsi-mas [12] (see also [11]), the value of the objective function is unchanged if we include the constraints

citation_details.parsed_title: The traveling-salesman problem and minimum spanning trees: part II
citation_details.description: The author cites this work as an example of a successful algorithm for the traveling salesman problem. It is mentioned as one of the methods that implicitly handles the difficulties associated with loop constraints or integer value requirements.
citation_details.context: In fact, the only algorithms which have had any reasonable success have been those which implicitly account for one or the other difficulty [2, 4, 5, 7].

citation_details.parsed_title: Convergence behaviour of some interior-point algorithms
citation_details.description: The authors cite this paper to support a statement within a proof, asserting that at any interior-point iteration, key variables are bounded away from zero and infinity. This established convergence behavior is used to analyze the properties of the $\Theta_i$ matrix as the quadratic term $Q_i$ approaches infinity.
citation_details.context: At any interior-point iteration, there exists a constant $\varepsilon$ , where $0 < \varepsilon < 1$ , such that $\varepsilon < s_i < 1 / \varepsilon$ , $\varepsilon < w_i < 1 / \varepsilon$ , $\varepsilon < x_i < 1 / \varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon < z_i < 1 / \varepsilon$ [21].

citation_details.parsed_title: Criteria for quasi-convexity and pseudoconvexity: Relationships and comparisons
citation_details.description: The author presents Theorem 1 as a generalization of a result (Theorem 2.2) from Crouzeix and Ferland [1] for the nondifferentiable case. The paper also notes that a property from the original theorem, which applied to differentiable functions, is not applicable in this new context.
citation_details.context: The following theorem (which generalizes a result of Crouzeix and Ferland [1, Theorem 2.2]) provides a sufficient condition for quasiconvex functions to be pseudoconvex.

citation_details.parsed_title: Optimizing over the subtour polytope of the travelling salesman problem
citation_details.description: The author cites this work as defining the subtour polytope of the traveling salesman problem. It is used as an example of a combinatorial problem with an exponential number of constraints where the simplex algorithm can be applied by using an oracle.
citation_details.context: Algorithms for finding violated subtour elimination constraints of the traveling salesman polytope can be modified to serve as oracles for problem STEP, allowing the simplex algorithm to be used to optimize over the subtour polytope as defined in Boyd and Pulleyblank (1990) in spite of an exponential number of constraints.

citation_details.parsed_title: Steepest-edge simplex algorithms for linear programming
citation_details.description: This work is cited as providing extensive computational evidence that the steepest edge pivot rule significantly reduces the number of pivots required by the simplex algorithm, supporting its practical effectiveness.
citation_details.context: Recent extensive computational results supporting this claim have been obtained by Bixby (1991) and by Forrest and Goldfarb (1991).

citation_details.parsed_title: A practicable steepest-edge simplex algorithm
citation_details.description: The author includes this paper in a list of foundational works on the steepest edge pivot rule, establishing it as a well-known and long-used method in large-scale linear programming.
citation_details.context: Steepest edge and its variants have been known and used for decades in the solution of large-scale linear programs and many papers have been written on the subject, including Crowder and Hattingh (1974), Dickson and Frederick (1960), Goldfarb and Reid (1977), Harris (1973), Kuhn and Quandt (1963), and Wolfe and Cutler (1963).

citation_details.parsed_title: Parametric linear programming and anti-cycling pivoting rules
citation_details.description: The author introduces the parametric simplex algorithm from this paper as a method guaranteed to resolve degeneracy. The paper's author analyzes this algorithm, notes its similarities to steepest ascent, and identifies a lack of formal analysis on the need for lexicography, which the current paper then addresses.
citation_details.context: In 1988 Magnanti and Orlin proposed a parametric simplex algorithm for solving linear programs that is guaranteed to resolve degeneracy. Interestingly, the geometry of this parametric algorithm and the steepest ascent algorithm share many similarities. The most notable manifestation of these similarities is that they both dictate the leaving constraint with complete freedom maintained in the choice of entering constraint. One major difference between the two algorithms is that the parametric algorithm must make allowances for the potential use of lexicography. Magnanti and Orlin seem aware that the use of lexicography remains unlikely, even when the feasible region of the linear program is degenerate, but they provide no formal analysis to quantify this notion.

citation_details.parsed_title: On the solution of highly degenerate linear programs
citation_details.description: This work is cited to provide a concrete example of the practical problems caused by degeneracy. It showed that a simple pivot rule failed on a real-world problem, whereas a more sophisticated rule succeeded, motivating the paper's focus on effective pivot rules.
citation_details.context: Ryan and Osborne (1988) reported that due to degeneracy they were unable to solve an airline crew scheduling problem after approximately 2000 iterations when using a pivot rule based solely on reduced cost information, but that they solved the problem in 436 iterations using Wolfe's rule (1963).

citation_details.parsed_title: Compact formulations as union of polyhedra
citation_details.description: The paper notes that its compact formulation in Theorem 5 is an instance of a known principle, observed in works like [8], where compact formulations are derived as a union of polyhedra for related problems.
citation_details.context: Theorem 5 is a case when a compact formulation can be obtained as a union of polyhedra as observed for related polyhedra without cardinality constraints [1,8,16].

citation_details.parsed_title: Valid inequalities for mixed integer linear programs.
citation_details.description: The paper cites a theorem from [9] concerning the union of polyhedra to support the proof of its own Theorem 5, which establishes a compact extended formulation.
citation_details.context: The theorem now follows from Theorem 2.1 of [3] on union of polyhedra (see also Theorem 4 in [9]).

citation_details.parsed_title: Concavity and efficient points of discrete distributions in probabilistic programming
citation_details.description: The paper describes a prior approach by Dentcheva et al. [10] that uses (1-τ)-efficient points to create reformulations and derive bounds for chance-constrained programs, setting a context of existing methods in the field.
citation_details.context: Dentcheva et al. [10] use $(1 - \tau)$ -efficient points to obtain various reformulations for chance-constrained programming with discrete random variables and to derive valid bounds on the optimal objective function value.

citation_details.parsed_title: Mixing mixed-integer inequalities
citation_details.description: The paper credits Günlük and Pochet [11] with introducing the foundational concept of the mixing set and its initial valid inequalities, which is the central structure being studied and extended in the current work.
citation_details.context: Günlük and Pochet [11] first introduced the mixing set and gave valid inequalities that define the convex hull of feasible solutions.

citation_details.parsed_title: A sample approximation approach for optimization with probabilistic constraints
citation_details.description: The paper cites Luedtke and Ahmed [13] as an example of a sample approximation approach that justifies the analysis of the special case with equal scenario probabilities, which arises from such sampling methods.
citation_details.context: For example, Luedtke and Ahmed [13] give a sample approximation approach to get bounds for chance-constrained programs in which the original distribution is replaced by an empirical distribution obtained by independent Monte-Carlo sampling.

citation_details.parsed_title: An integer programming approach for linear programs with probabilistic constraints
citation_details.description: The paper highlights a limitation of the work in [14], noting that its extended formulation is of exponential size, which the current paper improves upon by proposing a compact, polynomial-size alternative.
citation_details.context: This is in contrast to an exponential extended formulation proposed in [14].

citation_details.parsed_title: MIP reformulations of the probabilistic set covering problem
citation_details.description: The paper cites [21] to provide an example of a recent application of chance-constrained programming, specifically for probabilistic set covering. This helps to motivate the relevance and importance of the general problem class being studied.
citation_details.context: Some recent applications of chance-constrained programs with discrete distributions are probabilistic set covering [5,21], probabilistic lot/batch sizing [4,15], and probabilistic production and distribution planning [12].

citation_details.parsed_title: The mixing-MIR set with divisible capacities.
citation_details.description: The paper mentions [25] as an example of prior research that extended the basic mixing set, in this case to include divisible capacities. This places the current paper's own contributions within the broader context of ongoing research on mixing set structures.
citation_details.context: Because this is a fundamental substructure arising in different contexts, various extensions of the mixing set has been studied, such as the continuous mixing set [16,23], mixing set with flows [7] and mixing set with divisible capacities [25].

citation_details.parsed_title: Convergence of some algorithms for convex minimization
citation_details.description: The authors identify an oversight in a proposition from the cited paper, which deals with the convergence of algorithms for convex minimization. They argue that the proposition's proof requires a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, a condition not explicitly stated in the hypotheses, and proceed to provide a counterexample.
citation_details.context: In [1], Correa and Lemaréchal deal with convergence of some algorithms for convex minimization. In particular, their Proposition 4.3 helps to establish the convergence of certain bundle methods. However, there is an oversight in the hypotheses: the Hilbert space $X$ appearing in it must be assumed finite-dimensional (as is done in several other places in that paper).

citation_details.parsed_title: A dual method for discrete Chebychev curve fitting
citation_details.description: The authors state they will use the dual method algorithm from Armstrong and Kung to solve the linear programming formulation of the Chebychev curve fitting subproblems. The paper also notes that penalty calculations are based on a modification of the ratio procedures described in this work.
citation_details.context: The algorithm of Armstrong and Kung [3,4] will be used to solve (3).

citation_details.parsed_title: Experiments in mixed-integer linear programming using pseudocosts
citation_details.description: The authors tested a branching strategy based on a modification of the pseudocost procedure from Gauthier and Ribiere [10]. This approach was evaluated but was not found to be significantly better than the other branching rules considered.
citation_details.context: The pseudocost procedure of [10] was modified to the problem at hand and used to choose the parameter to restrict.

citation_details.parsed_title: Greedy algorithm and symmetric matroids
citation_details.description: The paper credits Bouchet [5] for independently introducing the concept of delta-matroids. The rank functions of delta-matroids are provided as an example of bisubmodular functions.
citation_details.context: Examples of bisubmodular functions include the rank functions of delta-matroids introduced independently by Bouchet [5] and by Chandrasekaran and Kabadi [7].

citation_details.parsed_title: On submodular function minimization
citation_details.description: This work is cited for providing the first combinatorial pseudopolynomial algorithm for minimizing integer-valued submodular functions. This algorithm built upon earlier work and established a framework used by subsequent algorithms.

In particular, the last years have seen the development and implementation of several "trust-region methods" for its solution (see, for instance, [3-5,7,9,24]). Trust-region methods are iterative numerical algorithms in which the objective function $f(x)$ is approximated in a suitable neighbourhood of the current iterate (the trust region) by a model whose values are easy to compute. A step is then chosen in the intersection of this neighbourhood and $X$ that sufficiently reduces the value of this model. The true objective function is computed at the resulting trial point: if it has also decreased sufficiently, the trial point is accepted as the new iterate. The trust region is then increased if the objective function value was well predicted by the model, or decreased otherwise.

citation_details.context: It achieves $\mathbf{O}(\sqrt{n} L)$ -iteration complexity, the best known theoretical result up to date (see Kojima, Mizuno, and Yoshise [3]), where $L$ is the binary data length of rational $(M, q)$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: Convergence behavior of interior-point algorithms
citation_details.description: The author uses the definition of a 'maximal' feasible point from Guler and Ye to characterize points in the feasible set. This concept is fundamental to the paper's analysis of the algorithm's limit points and convergence behavior.
citation_details.context: If $\operatorname{LCP}(M, q)$ is feasible but not necessarily has a feasible interior, then a point $(x, s) \in \mathcal{F}$ is maximal if and only if the number of positive components in $(x, s)$ is maximal (see Guler and Ye [4]).

citation_details.parsed_title: Error bounds for monotone linear complementarity problems
citation_details.description: The author explicitly bases the proof of Theorem 4 on the error bounds for monotone LCPs developed by Mangasarian and Shiau. This result is used to analyze the properties of the approximate solution generated by the algorithm in an ill-posed case.
citation_details.context: The proof is based on the error bounds result for the monotone LCP, described by Mangasarian and Shiau [6] (also see [5] and [2]).

citation_details.parsed_title: A quadratically convergent predictor-corrector method for solving linear programs from infeasible starting points
citation_details.description: The author cites Potra's work as an example of other existing interior-point algorithms that can start from an infeasible point. This serves to position the current paper's algorithm within the broader landscape of related research.
citation_details.context: For other interior-point infeasible starting algorithms, see Mizuno, Jarre and Stoer [7] and Potra [9], and references therein.

citation_details.parsed_title: Some perturbation theory for linear programming
citation_details.description: The author applies the concept of an 'ill-posed' problem from Renegar's perturbation theory to classify a specific outcome of their algorithm. This provides a theoretical framework for understanding cases where the LCP is sensitive to data errors.
citation_details.context: Corollary 3 indicates that $\operatorname{LCP}(M, q)$ , characterized in case (B.c), is ill-posed (Renegar [10]).

citation_details.parsed_title: Blocking and anti-blocking pairs of polyhedra
citation_details.description: The authors identify Fulkerson's theory of blocking and anti-blocking polyhedra as the origin of the questions investigated in the paper. They clarify that the dominant and submissive of the matching polyhedron correspond to the blocking and anti-blocking polyhedra, respectively.
citation_details.context: These questions were first investigated by Fulkerson in connection with his theory of blocking and anti-blocking polyhedra. (The "blocking polyhedron" associated with perfect matchings of $G$ is $\operatorname{dom}(P)$ , while $\operatorname{sub}(P)$ is the “anti-blocking polyhedron”.)

citation_details.parsed_title: Transportation problems which can be solved by the use of Hirsch-paths for the dual problems
citation_details.description: The authors cite this paper to establish a connection between prior works, noting that it showed the equivalence of an algorithm by Hung and Rom [5] to one by Balinski [2]. This helps position their own algorithm as a natural extension of Balinski's signature method.
citation_details.context: When applied to the assignment problem, both algorithms are identical to an algorithm of Hung and Rom [5]. In [6] it has been shown that the latter algorithm is equivalent to an algorithm of Balinski [2]. In this sense our strongly polynomial algorithm seems to be the natural extension of Balinski's signature method which is based on the fact that the Hirsch-conjecture is true for dual transportation polyhedra.

citation_details.parsed_title: Optimization algorithms and point-to-set maps
citation_details.description: The author cites Huard's work on a unified convergence theory for projection methods, but notes that this theory does not cover Rosen's method. This establishes a gap in the literature that the current paper addresses by providing a convergence proof specifically for Rosen's method.
citation_details.context: In resent years substantial efforts have been made in the study of the unified convergence theory of nonlinear programming algorithms [3, 8, 10, 11, 13, 17], but none of the results obtained can successfully be applied to Rosen's method. Huard [8] applied his result to a large class of projection methods, but it does not include Rosen's method.

citation_details.parsed_title: A combinatorial equivalence between a class of multicommodity flow problems and the capacitated transportation problem
citation_details.description: The author cites their own previous work [3], which showed that a specific class of multicommodity problems can be reduced to capacitated transportation problems. The current paper aims to provide a unifying theory for and generalize that result.
citation_details.context: In [3], the author has shown that one of these classes, namely $m$ -source, 2-sink, $r$ -commodity transportation problems ( $m, r \geq 2$ ) can be reduced to more "compact" representations as ordinary capacitated transportation problems. In this paper we provide a unifying theory for this result which applies to more general cases, and generalize the result in [3] to a larger class of multicommodity transportation problems.

citation_details.parsed_title: Graphic matroids and the multicommodity transportation problem
citation_details.description: The author cites reference [6] as one of the works establishing that certain multicommodity network flow problems can be transformed into equivalent single commodity problems. This provides the background for the transformations discussed in the paper.
citation_details.context: Several classes of multicommodity network flow problems have been shown to have the property that they can be transformed into equivalent, single commodity, uncapacitated flow problems [4, 6].

citation_details.parsed_title: An implementation of Karmarkar's algorithm for linear programming

This establishes a direct relationship between the two algorithms, which was not done in the original work.
citation_details.context: Our second result is that the dual-affine-scaling algorithm as described by Adler et al., in [1] is the same algorithm as the primal algorithm applied to the dual problem.

citation_details.parsed_title: New approaches for optimizing over the semimetric polytope
citation_details.description: The paper describes an approach from [20] that significantly speeds up the computation of LP-based bounds by dualizing most cycle inequalities and using a bundle method. However, the authors identify a research gap, noting that this approach has not been used in a framework to find exact solutions for Max-Cut.
citation_details.context: Yet another approach is proposed in [20]. It is assumed that the graph has a node r adjacent to all other nodes. If this is not the case, 0-weighted edges are added to the graph to meet the assumption. Then the following subset of (5) is considered: $$ \left. \begin{array}{l} s _ {r j} + s _ {r k} + s _ {j k} \leq 2 \\ s _ {r j} - s _ {r k} - s _ {j k} \leq 0 \\ - s _ {r j} + s _ {r k} - s _ {j k} \leq 0 \\ - s _ {r j} - s _ {r k} + s _ {j k} \leq 0 \end{array} \right\} \quad \text {f o r a l l} \{j, k \} \in E, r \neq j < k \neq r. \tag {7} $$ These inequalities define the r -rooted metric polytope of G ( M r (G) ). The optimization of a linear function over M r (G) can be done efficiently, as it amounts to solving a maximum flow problem in a graph derived from G . Therefore, the inequalities (7) are kept explicitly in the constraint set while all the other cycle inequalities are dualized. The Lagrangian dual is then solved with a bundle method pretty much in the same way as described in Sect. 4.1. In [20] time savings of up to two orders of magnitude with respect to simplex or barrier-based cutting-plane algorithms are reported for graphs of up to 150 nodes. The primal and dual infeasibilities of the solutions are comparable with those obtained with the simplex or the barrier algorithm. Experiments to obtain exact solutions for (MC) using this approach have not been carried out.

citation_details.parsed_title: Methods of nonlinear 0-1 programming
citation_details.description: The paper refers to [24] as a survey that covers techniques for solving nonlinear 0-1 programming problems developed before 1980.
citation_details.context: A survey of techniques developed before 1980 can be found in [24].

citation_details.parsed_title: Solving quadratic (0, 1)-problems by semidefinite programs and cutting planes
citation_details.description: The paper describes the work of Helmberg and Rendl [27] as a key baseline method. Their approach uses a Branch-and-Bound scheme with a bounding procedure based on solving the semidefinite relaxation strengthened by cutting planes using an interior point code.
citation_details.context: Helmberg and Rendl [27] apply this semidefinite relaxation with cutting planes (solved by an interior point code) in a B&B scheme. They consider the basic semi-definite relaxation (10), strengthened by some hypermetric inequalities. Inequalities are added while solving the relaxation (i.e., after some Newton steps), as well as after the exact solution of the relaxation has been obtained. Then the optimization process is restarted again.

citation_details.parsed_title: Semidefinite programming and combinatorial optimization
citation_details.description: The paper cites [41] as a reference for the equivalent semidefinite programming formulation of the Max-Cut problem, which involves optimizing a trace function over positive semidefinite matrices with specific constraints.
citation_details.context: An equivalent formulation of (MC) is given by $$ z _ {\text{M C}} = \max \left\{\operatorname{tr} L X: \operatorname{diag} (X) = e, \operatorname{rank} (X) = 1, X \succeq 0 \right\}, \tag{8} $$ (see, e.g., [41]), where $X$ is an $n \times n$ real matrix, $\operatorname{tr} A$ denotes the trace of the matrix $A$ , i.e., the sum of its diagonal elements, and $\operatorname{diag}(A)$ maps a matrix $A$ of order $n$ into the $n$ -dimensional vector made of its diagonal components.

A method for globally minimizing concave functions over convex sets
Global minimization of large scale constrained concave quadratic problems by separable programming
Adaptive cubic regularisation methods for unconstrained optimization. Part I: motivation, convergence and numerical results
citation_details.description: The authors identify this reference as Part I of their work, which introduced the Adaptive Regularisation with Cubics (ARC) framework. The current paper is a continuation that further analyzes the methodology proposed in [1].
citation_details.context: In this paper and its predecessor [1], we explore a third alternative: employing a local cubic overestimator of the objective as a regularisation strategy for the step computation.

citation_details.parsed_title: Accelerating the cubic regularization of Newton's method on convex problems
citation_details.description: The authors cite Nesterov [10] for developing more advanced methods that improve the complexity bounds of cubic regularization specifically for convex optimization problems.
citation_details.context: Subsequently, Nesterov [10] has proposed more sophisticated methods which further improve the complexity bounds in the convex case.

citation_details.parsed_title: Cubic regularization of Newton's method and its global performance
citation_details.description: The authors cite Nesterov and Polyak [11] for establishing key complexity results for a similar cubic regularization method. This work serves as a benchmark, as the authors' goal is to match these complexity bounds under more general and practical conditions.
citation_details.context: More recently, Nesterov and Polyak [11] considered a similar idea, although from a different perspective. They were able to show that, if the step is computed by globally minimizing the cubic model and if the objective's Hessian is globally Lipschitz continuous, then the resulting algorithm has a better global-complexity bound than that achieved by the steepest descent method, and proved superior complexity bounds for the (star) convex and other special cases.

citation_details.parsed_title: Linear programming with multiple objective functions: STEP method
citation_details.description: The authors classify the work by Benayoun et al. [4] as a feasible region reduction method, known as the STEM-method. This approach uses the decision maker's preferences on how to alter a solution to create new constraints, thereby reducing the feasible region.
citation_details.context: Feasible region reduction methods (STEM-method by Benayoun et al. [4])—The DM indicates how she/he would like to change the (current) solution. The responses are used to construct constraints, which reduce the feasible region. A series of index specifications (regarding which objectives to worsen and which to improve, and by how much) is required.

citation_details.parsed_title: Nonlinear multiple objective optimization: an algorithm and some theory.
citation_details.description: The authors identify the work by Roy and Wallenius [20] as an extension of their earlier research to handle nonlinear problems, and they use it as a baseline for comparison. The paper's new algorithm is benchmarked against this method, which uses a GRG-based approach and tradeoff information.
citation_details.context: Roy and Wallenius [19,20] extended the earlier work of Zionts and Wallenius to handle problems with nonlinear constraints and objectives. The ZW procedure used the simplex method as a basis for moving between adjacent efficient extreme points. In a similar fashion, the GRG approach by Abadie and Carpentier [1] for solving nonlinear optimization problems is used as the basis for the Roy and Wallenius algorithm. Their procedure uses the same type of tradeoff information as does the original ZW method.

citation_details.parsed_title: An interactive weighted Tchebycheff procedure for multiple objective programming
citation_details.description: The authors describe the Interactive Weighted Tchebycheff Procedure by Steuer and Choo [24] as a related method for nonlinear problems. They note its similarity to their own work in that it is based on generating and comparing well-dispersed solutions.
citation_details.context: Furthermore, Steuer and Choo [24] have developed the Interactive Weighted Tchebycheff Procedure, which is based on the generation and comparison of well dispersed solutions, but is applicable to problems with nonlinear constraints and objectives.

citation_details.parsed_title: A general saddle point result for constrained optimization
citation_details.description: The author cites this work as a recent study on the saddle point properties of the penalty Lagrangian. It is noted that this prior work was conducted without assuming convexity but included a non-negativity restriction on the dual variables, which the current paper does not.
citation_details.context: Recently, Arrow, Gould and Howe [2] have studied its saddle point properties in the absence of convexity, but under the restriction that yi ≥ 0 .

On projected Newton barrier methods for linear programming and an equivalence to Karmarkar's projective method
citation_details.description: The author acknowledges that Freund [10] also developed a full-dimensional version of Karmarkar's algorithm. However, they state that Freund did not prove its equivalence to the original algorithm, a contribution which the current paper provides.
citation_details.context: Freund [10] has independently found a full-dimensional version of Karmarkar's algorithm, but does not prove its equivalence to the original Karmarker algorithm.

citation_details.parsed_title: A new polynomial time algorithm for linear programming
citation_details.description: The paper describes the algorithm from Iri and Imai [14] as a global Newton method that achieves quadratic convergence. However, it is pointed out as a limitation that this algorithm is not known to converge in polynomial time.
citation_details.context: The "multiplicative penalty function" algorithm of Iri and Imai [14] is a global Newton method for the modified "penalty function" $\hat{g}(x) = (m + 1) \log (\langle c, x \rangle - c_0) - \sum_{j=1}^{m} \log (\langle a_j, x \rangle - b_j)$ . Iri and Imai show that their algorithm has quadratic convergence in the limit for nondegenerate linear programs, but at present this algorithm is not known to converge in polynomial time.

citation_details.parsed_title: A polynomial-time algorithm, based on Newton's method, for linear programming
citation_details.description: The author describes Renegar's algorithm as a Newton's method approach for linear programming. This method involves taking steps for a parametrized barrier function where the parameter is updated at each iteration.
citation_details.context: The "Newton's method" linear programming algorithm of Renegar [19] involves taking a Newton's method direction step for one member of a parametrized family of barrier functions defined by a parameter $\mu$ , where the parameter is varied at each step of the algorithm.

citation_details.description: The authors point out that while Berbee et al. did account for both constraints being hit, their analysis was flawed because it was based on the false assumption that the hit points are statistically independent. This paper's new analysis corrects this specific issue.

citation_details.parsed_title: On projected Newton barrier methods for linear programming and an equivalence to Karmarkar's projective method
citation_details.description: The author notes that a similar algorithm was described in the cited work, which frames Karmarkar's algorithm as a barrier-function method. The algorithm presented in this paper can be derived from the cited one by setting the barrier parameter to zero.
citation_details.context: A similar algorithm has also been described in [2]. These authors show that Karmarkar's algorithm can be viewed as a special case of a barrier-function method for solving nonlinear programming problems. If the barrier parameter is set to zero in computing their Lagrange multipliers, the algorithm described in this paper is obtained.

citation_details.parsed_title: A new polynomial-time algorithm for linear programming
citation_details.description: The paper's algorithm is presented as a variation on Karmarkar's original algorithm, designed to overcome some of its limitations. The proposed method applies to the standard form of linear programming and does not require the minimum value of the objective function to be known in advance.
citation_details.context: The algorithm described here is a variation on Karmarkar's algorithm for linear programming. It has several advantages over Karmarkar's original algorithm. In the first place, it applies to the standard form of a linear programming problem and produces a monotone decreasing sequence of values of the objective function. The minimum value of the objective function does not have to be known in advance. Secondly, in the absence of degeneracy, the algorithm converges to an optimal basic feasible solution with the nonbasic variables converging monotonically to zero. This makes it possible to identify an optimal basis before the algorithm converges.

citation_details.parsed_title: Sensitivity analysis for nonlinear programming using penalty methods
citation_details.description: The author cites Fiacco [12] as a foundational work that studied the sensitivity of Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) solutions under specific regularity and complementarity conditions. This work is presented as part of the classical results in sensitivity analysis for nonlinear optimization.
citation_details.context: The sensitivity of KKT solutions was studied by Fiacco [12] and Fiacco and McCormick [14] under linear independence constraint qualification, second-order sufficient condition, and strict complementarity condition.

citation_details.parsed_title: First and second order analysis of nonlinear semidefinite programs
citation_details.description: The author references Shapiro [37] for establishing the differentiability of the unique optimal solution for a nonlinear convex semidefinite optimization (SDO) problem. This result was achieved under Slater and nondegeneracy conditions by applying the implicit function theorem.
citation_details.context: Under Slater and nondegeneracy conditions, by applying the implicit function theorem [11], Shapiro [37] established the differentiability of the unique optimal solution for a nonlinear convex SDO problem.

citation_details.parsed_title: Consecutive and alternating vectors: Polyhedra and algorithms

citation_details.context: We refer the reader to (4.6)-(4.9) in [4], as well as to the literature on total dual integrality, for instance [6, 9, 10].

citation_details.parsed_title: Some proximity and sensitivity results in quadratic integer programming
citation_details.description: The authors cite this work as an example of existing proximity results for quadratic optimization problems. They point out that the proximity bound in [14] is less tight than the one presented in their own paper, highlighting a limitation of the prior result.
citation_details.context: This is a tighter proximity theorem than the one existing in the literature for constrained linear [5], quadratic [14] and nonlinear [16] optimization problems, all of which have \|\| \mathbf{z}^{*} - \mathbf{x}^{*}\ |_{\infty} < n\Delta , where \$\Delta\$ is the largest subdeterminant of the constraint matrix.

citation_details.parsed_title: A polynomial algorithm for an integer quadratic nonseparable transportation problem

citation_details.context: In [2], for linear problems (i.e. $C = 0$ ) an implementation of a discretization method is described which may be briefly characterized as follows: Starting with the solution of the problem $\mathrm{QSIP}(G_0)$ , $G_0 \subset T$ a first coarse grid, a number of refinement steps is performed on grids $G_0 \subset G_1 \subset \dots \subset G_k \subset T$ . To solve $\mathrm{QSIP}(G_i)$ one or more problems $\mathrm{QSIP}(T_i^j)$ are solved with $T_i^j$ (small) subsets of points near the active set of the solution of $\mathrm{QSIP}(G_{i-1})$ . The purpose of this short note is to report on an implementation of such an algorithm in the nonlinear case.

citation_details.parsed_title: A unified framework for primal-dual methods in minimum cost network flow problems
citation_details.description: The paper cites [12] as part of the RELAX family of codes, an efficient serial method for avoiding the 'jamming' problem in dual coordinate ascent. However, the authors note that these codes are difficult to adapt for massively parallel computing, a limitation that motivates the methods proposed in the current paper.
citation_details.context: One way of avoiding the jamming problem is embodied in the RELAX family of serial computer codes (see [12, 17, 46]). Essentially, these codes make dual ascents along directions that have a minimal number of non-zero components, which means that they select coordinate directions whenever possible. Only when jamming occurs do they select more complicated ascent directions. These codes have proved remarkably efficient in practice; however, adapting them to exploit a massively parallel computing environment appears to be a very intricate task, due to the difficulties of coordinating many simultaneous multiple-node price change and labeling operations.

citation_details.parsed_title: Superlinearly convergent variable metric algorithms for general nonlinear programming problems
citation_details.description: The authors cite Han's algorithm to highlight a limitation in a competing approach. They argue that in Han's method, the conditions for achieving superlinear convergence are not well integrated with the requirements for ensuring global convergence, a drawback their proposed method overcomes.
citation_details.context: We contrast this with the algorithm of Han [12, 13]. Han proves global convergence for an algorithm based on a successive programming approach with a superimposed exact penalty used with the line search. Global and superlinear convergence do not mesh together, however—superlinearity is achieved only in the case where the stepsize is one; as we demonstrate in Section 4, a stepsize of one will not guarantee a decrease in the penalty function (a condition required for globality). citation_details.parsed_title: Incremental Proximal Methods for Large Scale Convex Optimization
citation_details.description: The author discusses incremental methods, such as those in [11], as a dual approach to the random methods proposed in the paper. It is also noted that the incremental algorithms from [11] can be applied to the same problem by reformulating it as a penalized problem.
citation_details.context: Informally speaking, when the constraint set collection {x∣gi(x)≤0} , i∈M , is finite, the random methods of this paper could be viewed as a dual to the incremental methods, which have been studied starting with Kibardin [34] and later on by Luo and Tseng [39], Bertsekas [8], Tseng [52], Solodov [49], Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis [13], Nedic and Bertsekas [41], Kiwiel [35], Sundhar et al. [47], and recently by Bertsekas [10,11]. The incremental methods apply to a constrained minimization of the sum of finitely many functions. The random incremental algorithm proceeds by randomly selecting one component function and performing a (sub)gradient step for the selected component while always projecting on a given constraint set. In contrast, the randomized projection method minimizes a single objective function given the collection of constraint sets. The algorithm proceeds by always using the (sub)gradient direction to minimize the given objective, followed by a step that "incrementally reduces infeasibility" with respect to the collection {x∣gi(x)≤0} , i∈M . The recent work by Bertsekas in [10,11] shows that the incremental subgradient algorithms and their prox-type variants can be applied to the problem considered in this paper. In particular, it is shown that the original constrained problem can be re-cast as an equivalent penalized problem under suitable conditions. We note however that the algorithms discussed in this paper apply to a larger class of problems where the collection {x∣gi(x)≤0} , i∈M , need not be finite.

citation_details.parsed_title: Analysis of mathematical programming problems prior to applying the simplex algorithm
citation_details.description: The paper cites this work as an example of reported results in the ongoing search for an algorithm to find a near maximal number of GUB rows. This establishes the context that the problem is an active area of research which the current paper aims to contribute to.
citation_details.context: The solution time for most large-scale linear programming problems is greatly reduced when a large collection of the rows are made into GUB sets [4]. Indeed, the greater the percent of GUB rows for a given model, the faster the solution time. Hence, it is desirable to design an algorithm that quickly finds a near maximal number of GUB rows. Such a process is termed "GUBbing" the model. The search for such an algorithm is being conducted and some results have been reported [1]. Further, systems such as MPS III and MPSX include a gubbing procedure.

citation_details.parsed_title: Reinversion with the preassigned pivot procedure
citation_details.description: This work is cited for providing the definition of a 'spike column' and for its analysis of agenda algorithms and the role of spikes. These are foundational concepts for the 'min spike problem' which the authors use to reframe and solve the 'max GUB problem'.
citation_details.context: Another problem, whose relation to this "max GUB problem" we shall establish, arises during basis reinversion; it is called the "min spike problem". A spike column of a square matrix is one with one or more nonzeros above the main diagonal [2, p. 205]. To maintain sparsity in the representation of the inverse (usually some factorization, such as the product form of the inverse [7]), Markowitz [6] pioneered the notion of an agenda algorithm which prescribes the order of entrance plus pivot row assignment of each column. Hellerman and Rarick [2, 3] and Kalan [5] further analyzed agenda algorithms and the role of spikes in the rearranged basis. These agenda algorithms rearrange the basis matrix so as to nearly minimize the number of spikes.

citation_details.parsed_title: A method of conjugate subgradients for minimizing nondifferentiable functions
citation_details.description: The author uses Zangwill's convergence theory to provide a formal proof for the convergence of their algorithm's minor cycles. They show that their method satisfies the required conditions of Zangwill's convergence theorem for feasible direction methods.
citation_details.context: Our particular "demonstration" method is, in Zangwill's nomenclature, a feasible direction method, to which his convergence theorem A [27, Ch. 4] can be applied directly. The premisses of this theorem require the objective function and the (related) function defining directions to be continuous, and the searched segments to be bounded and closed. Since our minor cycle operates with (continuous) gradients and the segments searched within simplices are in fact compact, these conditions are satisfied by our method; its convergence thus follows by Zangwill's theorem.

citation_details.parsed_title: A new polynomial-time algorithm for linear programming
citation_details.description: The author describes Karmarkar's 1984 paper as a famous example of providing a total complexity estimate for a numerical method, which improved upon previous results for linear programming. The paper proposed minimizing a special potential function and was noted for its performance on large-scale problems and its connection to logarithmic barrier functions.
citation_details.context: The most famous examples of that style of research are the papers by Khachiyan [14] in 1979, who proved the polynomial complexity of the linear programming problems, and by Karmarkar [11] in 1984, who improved Khachiyan's complexity results.4 We will discuss the latter achievement in more detail. In [11] the linear programming problem was considered in the following form: min $\langle c,x\rangle$ s.t. $Ax = 0$ $$ \langle e, x \rangle = 1, \tag {5} $$ $$ x \geqslant 0 \in \mathbb {R} ^ {n}, $$ where $e \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is a vector of all ones. It is assumed that $Ae = 0$ and that the optimal value of problem (5) is zero. In order to solve this problem, Karmarkar proposed to minimize a special potential function $$ \Psi_ {K} (x) = \langle c, x \rangle^ {n} \left[ \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} x _ {i} \right] ^ {- 1}, $$ (compare with the Rosenbrock potential (2)), by a Newton-type method applied to $\ln \Psi_K(x)$ . This result attracted a lot of attention not only because of the excellent complexity estimate: it was declared that this method outperforms the standard simplex algorithm on large-scale linear programming problems (LPP). Very intriguing was the similarity of the Karmarkar potential with the old logarithmic barrier functions.

citation_details.context: In this event, as Glassey [8] observed, the linear complementarity problem solved at each iteration has a solution $(p,x)$ such that $x_{ij} > 0$ for some $j$ implies that $x_{ki} = 0$ for every $k$ , and $x_{ki} > 0$ for some $k$ implies that $x_{ij} = 0$ for every $j$ . citation_details.parsed_title: Iterative methods for variational and complementarity problems

citation_details.context: More recently Pang and Chan [11] showed that iterative techniques can be used to solve nonlinear problems with a sequence of linear subproblems. Their elegant analysis is applicable to a wide variety of variational inequality problems, of which the spatial equilibrium model is only one. They show that under reasonable assumptions iterative techniques can solve a wide variety of nonlinear variational inequality problems with a linear convergence rate.

citation_details.parsed_title: Semidefinite representation of convex sets
citation_details.description: The authors cite Helton and Nie [10] for using sos-convexity to provide sufficient conditions for the semidefinite representability of semialgebraic sets and for providing the formal definition of sos-convexity.
citation_details.context: Despite the relative recency of the concept of sos-convexity, it has already appeared in a number of theoretical and practical settings. In [10], Helton and Nie use sos-convexity to give sufficient conditions for semidefinite representability of semialgebraic sets. In [13], Lasserre uses sos-convexity to extend Jensen's inequality in convex analysis to linear functionals that are not necessarily probability measures, and to give sufficient conditions for a polynomial to belong to the quadratic module generated by a set of polynomials [14]. More on the practical side, Magnani et al. [16] have used sum of squares programming to find sos-convex polynomials that best fit a set of data points or to find minimum volume convex sets, given by sub-level sets of sos-convex polynomials, that contain a set of points in space.

citation_details.parsed_title: Some NP-complete problems in quadratic and nonlinear programming
citation_details.description: This work is cited to establish that global minimization of general polynomials is NP-hard, highlighting a gap that motivates the study of convex polynomials as a more tractable subclass.
citation_details.context: It is well known that in the absence of convexity, global minimization of polynomials is NP-hard [18, 21, 23]. However, if we somehow know a priori that the polynomial is convex, then every local minimum is global and simple gradient descent methods can find a global minimum.

citation_details.parsed_title: Matrix sum of squares relaxations for robust semidefinite programs.
citation_details.description: The authors cite this paper as one of the sources for the formal definition of a sum of squares (sos) matrix, which is a foundational concept for the paper's main topic of sos-convexity.
citation_details.context: The definition of an sos-matrix is as follows [7, 12, 31]. Definition 1 A symmetric polynomial matrix $P(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x]^{m \times m}$ , $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ , is an sos-matrix if there exists a polynomial matrix $M(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x]^{s \times m}$ for some $s \in \mathbb{N}$ , such that $P(x) = M^T(x)M(x)$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: Generalized linear complementarity problems

citation_details.context: The theory of complementarity problems and variational inequalities involving copositive plus matrices is a well-developed theory. See Lemke [18], Gowda and Seidman [17] for complementarity problems and Goeleven [13] for variational inequalities.

citation_details.parsed_title: Complementarity formulations and existence of solutions of dynamic multi-rigid-body contact problems with Coulomb friction
citation_details.description: The authors note that their own paper does not cover dynamic contact effects and refer to Pang and Trinkle [29] as a recent work that does. They describe it as proposing a nonlinear complementarity formulation for dynamic multi-rigid-body contact problems.
citation_details.context: Dynamic contact effects are not treated here. Nevertheless they can be studied by analogous nonsmooth modelling tools as well. For a recent work in this direction the reader is referred to [29]. In their article, Pang and Trinkle propose a nonlinear complementarity formulation of a multi-rigid-body contact problem. The existence of solutions is obtained under feasibility-type conditions.

citation_details.parsed_title: The complementarity problem
citation_details.description: The author cites Karamardian [7] as a key prior work on the nonlinear complementarity problem, but notes its methods were only applicable in specialized cases. The current paper's main theorem is presented as a unification and generalization of these earlier, limited approaches, thereby filling a gap in the literature.
citation_details.context: The nonlinear complementarity problem (that is, where f is assumed to be continuous) has been studied beginning with Cottle [2] and then continued mostly by Karamardian [7, 8]. Cottle [2] and Karamardian [7], for very specialized cases, have both used methods that shared a spirit in common with theorem 1 (also see Wilson [12]). Karamardian's approach has always been via the Kakutani fixed point theorem. Our results, embodied in theorem 3, accomplish considerable unification of these methods.

citation_details.context: In one of his fundamental papers on the theory of blocking pairs of polyhedra [9], D.R. Fulkerson conjectured as to a characterization of the blocking polyhedron associated with all $k$ -sets independent in each of two matroids on the same ground set.

citation_details.parsed_title: Packing rooted directed cuts in a weighted directed graph

citation_details.context: In making this conjecture, Fulkerson noted that the polyhedron (2.3), (2.4) is a common generalization of the blocking polyhedron associated with permutation matrices and that associated with spanning aborescences having a common root (see [7, 11]), and that it is related to the result of [10] on disjoint common partial transversals.

Nonlinear programming without a penalty function or a filter
Cubic regularization of Newton method and its global performance
citation_details.description: This work is cited for introducing the cubic regularization of Newton's method (CNM), which is the foundational methodology the current paper aims to accelerate. The original method from [6] has a global convergence rate of O(1/k^2) on convex problems, which the new proposed method improves.
citation_details.context: In [6] a cubic regularization of the Newton's method (CNM), which can be applied to a general smooth unconstrained minimization problem, was proposed. The main advantage of this scheme consists in its natural geometrical interpretation: At each iteration we minimize a cubic model, which appears to be a global upper estimate for the objective function. This key feature ensures predictable global behavior of the process.

citation_details.description: The paper lists BDIFF [10] as an example of an existing descent-based algorithm for solving complementarity problems. citation_details.context: Among the algorithms included in this class are PATH [5,15], MILES [17], SMOOTH [3], NE/SQP [14], and BDIFF [10]. citation_details.parsed_title: Homotopies for computation of fixed points
citation_details.description: The author cites this work as part of the development of the homotopy method, which was created to overcome the limitations of earlier fixed-point algorithms. This method is presented as a significant advancement that addressed issues like inefficiency and poor use of prior information.
citation_details.context: However, the early algorithms elaborated by Scarf [13, 14] and Kuhn [5], although quite practical for a crude approximation, appeared to be not enough efficient when a high level of accuracy was required. A serious defect of these algorithms was that they did not make a rational use of prior information about the location of the point to be sought. To overcome this difficulty, many efforts have been made these last years. Among the results in that direction, we should mention the sandwich method due to Merrill [12], Kuhn and MacKinnon [10], and the homotopy method developed by Eaves and extended by Eaves and Saigal ([2, 3], see also [5] where a detailed bibliography on the subject is given).

citation_details.parsed_title: Approximation algorithms for combinatorial fractional programming problems.
citation_details.description: The authors describe the work of Hashizume et al. [11] as an extension of Megiddo's approach, but highlight its significant limitation. The cited work's requirement for an approximation algorithm that handles negative weights makes it inapplicable to the class of problems considered in this paper.
citation_details.context: The result of Hashizume et al. [11] is of similar flavor to what we do here. They proved that an $\alpha$ -approximation to a combinatorial problem with a rational objective can be derived from an $\alpha$ -approximation for its linear counterpart. However, they need a rather strong assumption, namely, the existence of a polynomial-time algorithm for the linear version of the combinatorial problem that gives an $\alpha$ -approximate solution even if negative weights are allowed. As they show, such an algorithm exists for the knapsack problem, allowing them to deduce approximation results for the fractional knapsack problem. Note however that this does not hold for most optimization problems, in particular, for the ones we consider here. For instance, for the problems considered by Gubbala and Raghavachari [10] with $k = 2$ , there is no constant factor approximation algorithm, unless $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}$ , if we allow the weights to be arbitrary. Indeed, if we put weight $-(n - 1)$ for a specific edge $e = (u, v)$ and weight 1 for all other edges, then the optimal 2-connected subgraph has weight 0 if and only if there is a Hamiltonian path from $u$ to $v$ , and has weight at least 1 otherwise. This implies that there cannot be an approximation algorithm for the problem if we allow negative weights, unless $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}$ . Therefore, the results by Hashizume et al. cannot be applied to those problems (among others).
