citation_details.parsed_title: Implicit representation of generalised variable upper bounds in linear programming
citation_details.description: The author introduces Schrage's [2] paper as the basis for their work, noting that it generalized the Variable Upper Bounds procedure for specific constraints (GVUB constraints). Schrage's method, which this paper aims to improve, showed that an implicit representation of these constraints could yield significant computational savings.
citation_details.context: In a recent paper Schrage [2] has generalised his Variable Upper Bounds procedure to constraints of the form $$ \sum_ {j \in S _ {r}} x _ {j} + \sum_ {k \in T} a _ {r k} y _ {k} = a _ {r 0} \quad (\text {r o w} r) $$ where the $S_r$ are disjoint, the $a_{rk}$ non-positive, and the $a_{r0}$ non-negative. These constraints are called GVUB constraints, and Schrage showed that the implicit representation of such constraints will often result in substantial computational savings in the (revised) simplex algorithm.

citation_details.parsed_title: A set intersection theorem and applications

citation_details.parsed_title: The complexity of recognizing linear systems with certain integrality properties

citation_details.context: Recently Ding et al. [2] proved that in general the problem is co-NP-complete, even if $A$ is the incidence matrix of a graph.

citation_details.parsed_title: Fractional covers for forests and matchings

citation_details.parsed_title: An algorithmic framework for convex mixed integer nonlinear programs

citation_details.parsed_title: An outer-approximation algorithm for a class of mixed-integer nonlinear programs

citation_details.parsed_title: The Steiner tree problem II: properties and classes of facets

citation_details.parsed_title: A partition based relaxation for Steiner trees
citation_details.description: The paper discusses a recent, alternative LP relaxation from Konemann et al., noting it is as tight as the bidirected cut relaxation but uses a different structure. The authors contrast this with their own geometric approach and point out it does not prove an upper bound on the integrality gap.
citation_details.context: Very recently, Konemann et al. [17] introduced another LP relaxation for the minimum Steiner tree problem which they show is as tight as the bidirected cut relaxation, and showed that the algorithm of Robins and Zelikovsky can be interpreted as a primal-dual algorithm on their LP. However, even their interpretation does not prove any upper bound on the integrality gap of their relaxation as they also compare with the optimum Steiner tree and not the optimum LP solution. Nevertheless, they show upper bounds for their relaxation for a larger class of graphs called $b$ -quasi-biPARTite graphs.1 We stress that their LP seems quite different from ours – while we have variables for edges of the tree, they maintain variables and constraints for special sub-trees called full components much in the spirit of [20]. It is an interesting question to study the relationship between their LP and ours.

citation_details.parsed_title: A dual ascent approach for Steiner trees on a directed graph

citation_details.context: Wong [22] used this relaxation to study the Steiner arborescence problem, and Chopra and Rao [6, 7] studied the properties of facets of the polytope defined by the relaxation.

citation_details.parsed_title: A finite branch-and-bound algorithm for nonconvex quadratic programming via semidefinite relaxations.

citation_details.parsed_title: An outer-approximation algorithm for a class of mixed integer nonlinear programs.
citation_details.description: The paper is cited as an example of recent work on nonlinear disjunctive programming. The authors then point out that this work, like much of the literature, assumes problem boundedness, a gap their own work addresses.

Beginning with the seminal work of Egon Balas [3], there is a vast literature on disjunctive programming, with the recent work of Grossman et al. [8,14,24] treating the nonlinear case. Nevertheless much of this literature, including the cited references, assumes boundedness of the problems; in contrast, a main contribution of our work is on problems where such boundedness is not assumed.

citation_details.parsed_title: Logic-based benders decomposition

citation_details.parsed_title: Optimality conditions for quadratic programming

citation_details.parsed_title: Convex relaxations of non-convex mixed integer quadratically constrained programs: projected formulations

citation_details.parsed_title: Matching, Euler tours and the Chinese postman
citation_details.description: The author cites this paper as an example of an algorithm that solves generalizations of the matching problem. It is mentioned as one of several works that utilize the "blossom shrinking" operation, a key technique in this field.

citation_details.description: This paper is cited as one of the foundational works that extended the concept of affine policies, specifically applying them to linear systems theory within the field of robust optimization.
citation_details.context: Affine policies have been studied extensively in the literature for two-stage and multi-stage adaptive optimization problems. They were introduced in the context of stochastic optimization in Rockafellar and Wets [17] and then later in robust optimization in Ben-Tal et al. [4] and also extended to linear systems theory in Ben-Tal et al. [2] and Ben-Tal et al. [3]. Affine policies have also been considered extensively in control theory of dynamic systems (see Bemporad [1], Kerrigan and Maciejowski [13], Lofberg [16], Bertsimas and Brown [6], Skaf and Boyd [18], Ben-Tal and Nemirovski [5] and the references therein). In all these papers, the authors show how to reformulate the multi-stage linear optimization problem such that an optimal affine policy can be computed efficiently by solving convex optimization problems such as linear, quadratic, conic and semi-definite. Kerrigan and Maciejowski citeKM04 first consider the problem of theoretically analyzing the properties of such policies and show that, under suitable conditions, the affine policy has certain desirable properties such as stability and robust invariance. Goulart and Kerrigan [12] show that under certain conditions, the class of policies that are affine in the uncertain parameters in the current state are equivalent to the class of affine policies with memory of prior states. Bertsimas et al. [9] show that an affine policy is optimal for a multi-stage problem where there is a single decision variable with upper and lower bounds and a single uncertain parameter in each stage. Bertsimas et al. [8] consider linear dynamical systems under uncertainty and show using numerical experiments on classical multistage inventory management problems that affine policies give near-optimal solutions. Kuhn et al. [15] consider one-stage and multi-stage stochastic optimization problems, give efficient algorithms to compute the primal and dual! approximations using affine policies, and determine a posteriori performance bounds for affine policies on an instance by instance basis in contrast to the a priori performance bounds we derive for a class of instances. To the best of our knowledge, there are no a priori performance bounds known for affine policies in a general setting such as the one considered in $\Pi_{\text{Adapt}}(\mathcal{U})$ .

citation_details.context: We use the data structure of Section 2, with the value of each vertex being its label. Step 1 takes a find-min-val operation, step 2 a link, step 3 a cut, and step 4 one change-val per updated label. The total number of label updates over the entire algorithm is $O(nm)$ , as is the number of pivots [10,14], where $n$ and $m$ are the numbers of vertices and edges in the problem network, respectively. It follows that the amortized time per pivot is $O(\log n)$ , and the total running time of the algorithm is $O(nm\log n)$ . This matches the bound of Goldberg, et al. for the Goldfarb-Hao algorithm but considerably simplifies one part of the implementation. Each arc $(i,j)$ in the network, including the arcs of $T$ and their reversals, has a cost $c_{ij}$ that is part of the problem specification and a reduced cost $c_{ij}^{\pi} = c_{ij} - \pi_i + \pi_j$ ([19,20], Section 1). citation_details.description: The author introduces the simplicial decomposition algorithm from Von Hohenbalken [8] as one of the two core algorithms being analyzed. Its key advantages, such as not needing dual variables and using the simplex method for subproblems, are highlighted.
citation_details.context: In two recent papers [8, 9], Von Hohenbalken has described a simplicial decomposition algorithm for solving a nonlinear minimization program with a pseudoconvex objective function and a convex compact feasible set. The algorithm requires no dual variables and therefore eliminates the undesirable feature of having to operate on a formulation with extra variables. Another advantage of the algorithm when applied to linearly constrained problems (such as quadratic programs) is that the powerful simplex method of linear programming can be employed to solve the subprograms.

citation_details.parsed_title: Solving matching problems with linear programming
citation_details.description: The authors cite this work to demonstrate the power of polyhedral methods, noting that its strong cutting plane algorithm for maximum matching was competitive with, or even superior to, existing polynomial-time algorithms. This supports the paper's choice of a cutting plane approach.
citation_details.context: A recent study also suggests that these methods might be successful in solving problems for which "good" algorithms are already available. Grötschel and Holland (1984) implemented a strong cutting plane algorithm for the problem of finding a maximum matching in a graph. This problem can be solved in polynomial time (Edmonds, 1965). The Grötschel and Holland algorithm uses a characterization of the matching polytope developed by Edmonds (1965) and a procedure of Padberg and Rao (1982) for choosing cuts to be added (i.e., solving the so called separation problem). Surprisingly, Grötschel and Holland's algorithm solved large scale problems as well as or better (in terms of running time) than Edmonds' polynomial time algorithm.

citation_details.parsed_title: On the symmetric travelling salesman problem I: Inequalities
citation_details.description: This work is cited as providing the theoretical foundation for landmark computational studies on the traveling salesman problem. The facets of the traveling salesman polytope described in this paper were used as the cutting planes in those successful solution methods.
citation_details.context: The work of Crowder and Padberg (1980) and Padberg and Hong (1980) for the symmetric traveling salesman problem are landmark studies on the use of results from polyhedral theory for actual problem solving. These researchers were able to solve large traveling salesman problems to optimality using a combination of cutting planes, fixing variables using reduced cost information, and branch and bound strategies. More recently, Padberg and Grinaldi (1987) reported solving a larger (532-city) traveling salesman problem. The cutting planes used in these studies were derived from the facets of the traveling salesman polytope described by Grötschel and Padberg (1979a, 1979b).

citation_details.description: The paper cites [4] for providing a polynomial-time algorithm to check membership in the metric polytope. The author also notes a practical limitation of this method related to numerical stability when applying it to check the metric condition (PSDM).
citation_details.context: For graphs with no $K_{4}$ -minor, the existence of a PSD completion is characterized by the metric condition (PSDM). Checking membership in the metric polytope $\mathrm{MET}^{\square}(G)$ can be done in polynomial time (for any graph) [4]. Yet there is some difficulty in checking condition (PSDM). Indeed, even if $x$ is rational valued, $\pi^{-1}$ arccos $x$ is quite unlikely to remain rational! Thus we can only work with a rational approximation of $\pi^{-1}$ arccos $x$ . This means that we may encounter problems of numerical stability for deciding whether (PSDM) holds when $\pi^{-1}$ arccos $x$ happens to be very close to the boundary of $\mathrm{MET}^{\square}(G)$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: An exact duality theory for semidefinite programming and its complexity implications
citation_details.description: The author cites Ramana [44] for providing complexity results on the semidefinite programming feasibility problem. Ramana's work develops an exact duality theory showing that the problem is in NP if and only if it is in co-NP, which has significant implications for its classification.
citation_details.context: It is one of the major open questions in the field of semidefinite programming to determine the complexity status of problem (F). It is not known whether (F) is in NP. Some complexity results are given by Ramana [44]. In particular, he develops an exact duality theory which enables him to show that (F) belongs to NP if and only if (F) belongs to co-NP. Therefore, if NP ≠ co-NP then (F) is neither NP-complete nor co-NP-complete.

citation_details.description: The companion paper [2] provides the worst-case iteration complexity analysis for the ARC family of methods. citation_details.context: Worst-case iteration complexity bounds for the ARC family of methods are derived in [2]. Due to the direct correspondence between the count of (major) ARC iterations and the number of function- and derivative(s)-evaluations, these bounds also apply to the latter. When requiring the mild Cauchy condition on the step, and some stronger assumptions on the objective than in the global convergence results, we obtain an upper bound on the total number of iterations the ARC algorithm takes to drive the norm of the gradient of $f$ below $\epsilon$ that is of order $\epsilon^{-2}$ , which is the same as for the steepest descent method [21, p. 29]. This to be expected since the Cauchy-point condition requires no more than a move in the negative gradient direction. The steepest-descent-like complexity bound can be improved when $s_k$ is the global minimizer of the model (1.4) in a subspace containing the gradient $g_k$ and an appropriate termination criterion is employed. In particular, assuming $H(x)$ to be globally Lipschitz continuous, and the approximation $B_k$ "sufficiently close" to $H(x_k)$ along $s_k$ , we show that the ARC algorithm has an overall worst-case iteration count of order $\epsilon^{-3/2}$ for generating $\| g_k \| \leq \epsilon$ , and of order $\epsilon^{-3}$ for achieving approximate nonnegative curvature in a subspace containing $s_k$ . These bounds match those proved by Nesterov and Polyak [23, Sect. 3] for their Algorithm 3.3. However, our framework, at least for the first-order results, is more general, as we allow more freedom in the choice of $s_k$ and of $B_k$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: A note on the prize collecting traveling salesman problem
citation_details.description: The authors cite Bienstock et al. [7] as an example of prior work on prize-collecting problems. They then distinguish their own work by highlighting a gap: these earlier models make rejection decisions independently for each element, whereas their model makes collective decisions for sets of elements (markets).
citation_details.context: Previous work exists where classical combinatorial optimization problems were extended to consider rejection or selection decisions, such as the prize-collecting traveling salesman problem (see Balas [3] and Bienstock et al. [7]), the prize-collecting Steiner tree problem (see Goemans and Williamson [16] and Goemans [15]), the multi-processor scheduling problem with rejection (see Bartal et al. [5]), and the facility location problem with service rejection penalties (see Charikar et al. [10]). Geunes et al. [14] considered a single-item, single-location, capacitated order selection model where each market is specified by a single demand in a single period, and provided a polynomial-time optimization algorithm based on dynamic programming. However, in all of these models, the rejection or selection decisions are made independently for each element (node, job, order). Our market choice models are different and more general in that rejection/selection decisions are made with respect to a collection of elements as a set. (This is captured through the notion of markets.) For example, in the ELS problem with market choice, selecting a market means that we commit to satisfying the demands of that market in all periods. In particular, our approach is clearly applicable to the more specialized prize-collecting variants of the problems mentioned above, and is potentially applicable to market choice variants of additional covering problems.

citation_details.parsed_title: Integrated market selection and production planning: complexity and solution approaches
citation_details.description: The authors cite Van den Heuvel et al. [26] to justify their methodological choices. The cited work proved that the ELS problem with market choice is NP-hard, motivating the need for an approximation algorithm, and that the profit maximization version is inapproximable, justifying the authors' focus on the cost minimization formulation.
citation_details.context: In the ELS problem with market choice, we are given a collection of markets, each of which is associated with a potential revenue and a sequence of demands over the planning horizon. The decision is made in two stages. First, a decision is made regarding which markets to select and commit to, and which to reject. Then in the second stage, one constructs the minimum-cost production plan to satisfy all of the demands of the markets that were selected in the first stage. In fact, in the second stage we solve a classical ELS problem, in which the demand in each period is equal to the aggregated demand in that period of all selected markets from the first stage. The goal is to find a policy that minimizes the overall lost revenue of the markets that were rejected and the production costs incurred by satisfying the demands of the markets that were selected. In subsequent work to this paper, it has been recently shown by Van den Heuvel et al. [26] that the ELS problem with market choice is NP-hard. Thus, introducing the issue of market choice gives rise to computationally more complex models. Another, perhaps more natural, objective that one may consider in this setting is to maximize the total profit, i.e., the revenue of all the selected markets minus the cost of satisfying them. However, in [26] it has been shown that is NP-hard to approximate this problem within any constant factor. As a result, it is not likely that one can derive meaningful analytical results on this model. As we already mentioned, we derive a constant approximation algorithm for the minimization problem described above.

citation_details.parsed_title: An approximation technique for robust nonlinear optimization

citation_details.context: To put our work into perspective, we briefly recall two antithetic paradigms of dealing with uncertain parameters in optimization problems. On the one hand, the robust optimization approach aims to achieve the best possible value of the objective function under all possible circumstances (choices of the parameter), either in a worst-case [1,4] or in an average sense [2, Chapter. 6.4] and [3] and the references therein. The solution is thus designed to be acceptable for all conceivable values of the parameter, and it is not altered even if the actual value of the parameter became known. This paradigm is reflected by the bi-level structure of worst-case robust optimization problems.

citation_details.context: In Part I of our paper (this issue, pp. 27-56), we described clustering methods for the global optimization problem $$ \min _ {x \in S} f (x) \tag {1} $$ in which a strictly descent local search procedure $P$ was applied to a subset of a sample drawn from a uniform distribution over $S$ , so as to find all the local minima of $f$ that are potentially global. In the $k$ -th iteration of each method, the sample of size $kN$ was first reduced by removing the $(1 - \gamma)kN$ points with the highest function values. Three methods to deal with the reduced sample were presented (Density Clustering, Single Linkage and Mode Analysis), of which the last two turned out to have particularly attractive properties with respect to efficiency and accuracy. As far as the former is concerned, it could be shown that the number of local searches would remain finite (with probability 1), even if the sampling would continue indefinitely. With respect to the latter, we showed that (with probability 1) a local minimum would be detected in each level set component in which a point had been sampled. One such component may, however, contain several local minima; we are only assured of finding one of them. The purpose of this paper is to show how this final deficiency can be dealt with. citation_details.parsed_title: A parallel implementation of the nested decomposition method for multistage stochastic linear programs
citation_details.description: The paper is cited as a reference for the nested decomposition method. This method iteratively solves dynamic programming equations for multistage problems by passing solutions to successor nodes and cuts to father nodes in a scenario tree.
citation_details.context: The techniques for generating cuts allow to solve the dynamic programming equations (20) in the following way. At iteration $k$ with each node $i$ we associate the problem $$ \min _ {x _ {i}} \left\{c _ {i} \left(x _ {i}\right) + \sum_ {j \in \mathcal {S} (i)} p _ {i j} \underline {{V}} _ {j} ^ {k} \left(x _ {i}\right) \mid W _ {i} x _ {i} = b _ {i} - D _ {i} x _ {a (i)} ^ {k} \right\}, \tag {24} $$ in which $\underline{V}_j^k$ , $j \in S(i)$ , are polyhedral models of $V_j$ constructed from the cuts accumulated so far, and $x_{a(i)}^k$ is the current solution of the problem associated with the father $a(i)$ . The solution $x_i^{k+1}$ of (24), if it exists, is passed to the successor nodes $j \in S(i)$ ; the objective or feasibility cut generated is passed to the father node. Cuts received at iteration $k$ are used to update the models $\underline{V}_j^k$ to $\underline{V}_j^{k+1}$ , and the iteration continues [2,3].

citation_details.context: The spirit of Algorithm 1 is to find a collective solution $z(\cdot)$ for all players by an interactive procedure, which is different from the idea of the best response method (BRM) in the literature. Stochastic versions of the BRM include the sampled best-response algorithms for $\mathcal{G}^{\mathrm{prMD}}$ in Pang, Sen, and Shanbhag [5] and the inexact best response methods for SNEPs in Shanbhag, Pang, and Sen [14]. In principle, the best response methods are based on a special reformulation of the game (4)-(7), which requires convexity and differentiability. Thus, the model in [5] has no $x_{i}^{T}S_{i}(\xi)y_{i}(\xi)$ in the objective of $\psi_{i}$ , the recourse action is not dependent on other players' second-stage strategies $y_{-i}$ , and the matrix before $y_{i}$ in the objective and constraint are independent of $\xi$ . As long as the best-response mapping is continuous and contractive, the Nash equilibrium may be achieved. Notice that the optimization involved in the best-response mapping turns out to be a two-stage stochastic programming problem. In other words, when applying BRM to solve a two-stage stochastic game, at every iteration each player needs to solve a two-stage stochastic optimization problem based on the information about others' strategies in the previous iteration.

citation_details.context: A topic related to this paper is considered in [18, 20, 19], which discuss polynomial optimization problems over the simplex, $f ^ {\min } \doteq \min \left\{f (x): \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} x _ {j} = 1, x \geq 0 \right\}$, where $f(x)$ is a general polynomial of degree $\rho$ . Given $\epsilon > 0$ the authors describe an algorithm that computes a feasible solution $\hat{x}$ such that $f (\hat {x}) - f ^ {\min } \leq \epsilon \left(f ^ {\max } - f ^ {\min }\right)$, where $f^{\mathrm{max}}$ is the maximum of $f(x)$ over the simplex. We first note that a guarantee of the form (3.10) cannot be attained for the problems (1.1) studied in this paper (even for fixed $\rho$ and $\epsilon$ ) in polynomial time unless $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}$ . A simple example is given by the problem $\min \{0: \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i = 0, x_i^2 = 1 \forall i\}$ , where the $w_i$ are integers (the subset sum problem). Here, $f^{\mathrm{max}} = f^{\mathrm{min}} = 0$ and guaranteeing feasibility is NP-hard. Through an additional elaboration, this example can be equivalently rewritten, using $O(n)$ variables, so that the intersection graph has tree-width 2. This construction additionally justifies the approximate feasibility guarantee given by our method. Even though the approximation setups in [18, 20, 19] and in this paper are different, we can compare the complexity incurred in achieving the respective accuracies $\epsilon$ . In the case of the algorithms in [18, 20, 19] the workload needed to attain (3.10) can be estimated as $O(n^{O(1 / \epsilon)})$ for each fixed $\rho$ , where the $O(\cdot)$ notation includes other dependencies $\epsilon$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: Sensitivity results in stochastic optimal control: A Lagrangian perspective
citation_details.description: The paper adopts the functional framework proposed in [2] to analyze stochastic optimal control problems. The authors also use an identification between Lagrange multipliers and adjoint states proved in [2] and address a smoothness-related difficulty that was also highlighted in that work.
citation_details.context: Our main motivation to prove the existence of Lagrange multipliers under Gâteaux differentiability assumptions on the data arises from stochastic optimal theory. The first application of our results deals with first order necessary optimality conditions for stochastic optimal control problems in continuous time. Following the functional framework proposed by Backhoff and Silva in [2], our abstract results allow us to provide a direct proof of the existence of Lagrange multipliers at any local solution of the control problem. Having in mind the importance of Lagrange multipliers in sensitivity analysis in optimization theory (see, e.g., [5, Chapter 4]), the study of their existence in stochastic control plays an important role. As pointed out in [2], the main difficulty in deriving the existence result, from standard variational principles, is that the smoothness of the equality constraint that defines the dynamics of the controlled diffusion process is difficult to check. The results in sections 3 and 4, which assume only Gâteaux differentiability of the mapping that defines the constraints and a uniform surjectivity property of the Gâteaux derivative in a neighborhood of the optimal solution, allow us to avoid this issue. Moreover, by means of the identification between Lagrange multipliers and adjoint states, proved in [2], we recover the weak Pontryagin minimum principle proved first in [3] by using different techniques. A detailed discussion and extensions of this result are provided in section 5.1.

citation_details.parsed_title: Optimal stopping under probability distortion
citation_details.description: The authors identify Xu and Zhou [35] as the seminal work that initially proposed and studied the optimal stopping problem under probability distortions. They describe the specific assumptions and methodological approach of Xu and Zhou [35], which relied on the Skorokhod embedding technique for a specific class of processes and distortion functions.
citation_details.context: The stopping problem (10) was initially proposed and studied by Xu and Zhou [35] under different assumptions. First of all, the authors allow for all finite stopping times w.r.t. to some filtered probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, (\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \geq 0}, \mathrm{P})$ ; that is, they consider infinite horizon optimal stopping problems. Second, they impose a special structure on the process $(Y_t)_{t \geq 0}$ ; namely, it is supposed that $Y_t = u(S_t)$ for an absolutely continuous nonnegative function $u$ on $[0, \infty[$ and for a one-dimensional geometric Brownian motion $(S_t)_{t \geq 0}$ . Third, the authors focus on strictly increasing absolutely continuous distortion functions $g$ . Thus, on the one hand, they allow for more general nonconcave distortion functions and this is the main advantage of Xu and Zhou [35], as it allows one to study behavioral finance models. On the other hand, their analysis does not cover the case of Average Value at Risk (cf. Example 1), where the distortion function is not strictly increasing (see, however, Xu [34] for some extensions). More formally, in Xu and Zhou [35] the optimal stopping problems of the form $$ \sup _ {\tau \in \mathcal {T} ^ {\infty}} \mathscr {E} ^ {g} (u \left(S _ {\tau}\right)) \tag {12} $$ are studied, where $\mathcal{T}^{\infty}$ denotes the set of all finite stopping times. A crucial step in the authors' argumentation is the reformulation of the optimal stopping problem (12) as $$ \begin{array}{l} \sup _ {\tau \in \mathcal {T} ^ {\infty}} \mathscr {E} ^ {g} (u (S _ {\tau})) = \sup _ {F \in \mathscr {D}} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} g (1 - F (x)) u ^ {\prime} (x) d x \\ = \sup _ {F \in \mathfrak {D}} \int_ {0} ^ {1} u (F ^ {\leftarrow} (u)) g ^ {\prime} (1 - u) d u, \\ \end{array} $$ where $u'$ and $g'$ are derivatives of $u$ and $g$ , respectively, and $\mathcal{D}$ denotes the set of all distribution functions $F$ with a nonnegative support such that $\int_0^\infty (1 - F(x)) dx \leq S_0$ . The main idea of the approach in Xu and Zhou [35] is that any such distribution function may be described as the distribution function of $S_{\tau}$ for some finite stopping time $\tau \in \mathcal{T}^\infty$ and this makes the application of the Skorokhod embedding technique possible (for a comprehensive survey on Skorokhod embedding, see Obloj [27]). Hence, the results essentially rely on the applicability of Skorokhod embedding technique to the stochastic process $(Y_t)_{t \geq 0}$ . The analysis in Xu and Zhou [35] can probably be carried over to the case of bounded stopping times (see, e.g., Ankirchner and Strack [4] for some discussion on the Skorokhod embedding for more general sets of stopping times).

Using the necessary optimality conditions in Bao and Mordukhovich [1, Theorem 5.3] and our proof technique, one can show that (II)(iii) and (II)(ii) can also serve as constraint qualifications for the necessary optimality conditions for MPECs with various notions of relative Pareto minimizers, as defined in Bao and Mordukhovich [1].

citation_details.parsed_title: Optimality conditions for bilevel programming problems
citation_details.description: The author discusses the "value function approach" and the "partial calmness condition" from Ye and Zhu [30, 31]. This previous work is presented as an important but ultimately insufficient method for solving BLPPs, highlighting its limitations and motivating the current paper's combined approach.
citation_details.context: In Ye and Zhu [30, 31], the following value function approach is taken to reformulate the BLPP. Define the value function of the lower-level problem as an extended valued function $V \colon R^n \to \overline{R}$ by $$ V (x):= \inf _ {y} \{f (x, y): g (x, y) \leq 0 \}, $$ where $\bar{R}:= R \cup \{-\infty\} \cup \{+\infty\}$ is the extended real line and $\inf \{\varnothing\} = +\infty$ by convention. Then it is obvious that problem (BLPP) can be reformulated as the following problem involving the value function: $$ \begin{array}{l} (\mathrm {V P}) \quad \min _ {x, y} F (x, y) \\ \begin{array}{l} \text {s. t.} f (x, y) - V (x) \leq 0, \end{array} \\ g (x, y) \leq 0, \\ G (x, y) \leq 0. \\ \end{array} $$ It is easy to think that because the reformulation (VP) is exactly equivalent to the original BLPP, the problem will be solved if the nonsmooth necessary optimality condition is used on the problem (VP). The problem turns out to be not so simple, because the nonsmooth MFCQ does not hold at any feasible solution of the problem (VP), so the KKT condition may not hold. To deal with this difficulty, Ye and Zhu [30, 31] proposed the partial calmness condition. The value function approach was further developed in Ye [27, 29] using other constraint qualifications, such as the Abadie constraint qualification. For the case where the value function is convex, Ye [27, 29] showed that the resulting KKT condition takes a simpler form in which only one solution of the lower-level optimal problem is involved. Under the partial calmness condition, this simpler KKT condition was proved to hold under the assumption of inner semicontinuity of the solution mapping of the lower-level program (Dempe et al. [9]).

citation_details.parsed_title: Substitutes, complements and ripples in network flows
citation_details.description: The authors identify a significant gap left by Granot and Veinott (1985), which is the problem of efficiently selecting a well-behaved optimal solution when multiple exist. They critique the perturbation method proposed in the cited work as computationally impractical and potentially ambiguous, a problem which the current paper addresses.
citation_details.context: Next we address the problem, left open by Granot and Veinott, Jr. (1985), of efficiently finding well-behaved selections when multiple optimal solutions exist—an existence result does not guarantee that a solution obtained by a given optimization algorithm will indeed possess the desired properties. This is an important issue when multiple solutions exist for more than a small number of “exceptional” parameter values, a situation which does occur in practice. For example, even for linear network flow problems situations arise where multiple solutions are the norm rather than the exception (for example, in the maximum flow problem, all flows but those on a minimum cut can have several values). To address this problem Granot and Veinott, Jr. (1985) assign a perturbation parameter to every variable/cost pair that render the costs strictly convex and then taking the limits one perturbation at a time. In practice, their approach entails heavy computations as one would have to solve a large number of Monotropic Problems in order to obtain limits with reasonable accuracy, leading to prohibitive solution times for all but the simplest models. Moreover, the solutions they obtain may depend on the order of taking the limits, thus both the practical efficiency and the intuitive explanation of the optimal solution are lost. This problem is addressed and solved in §4.

citation_details.context: To overcome this issue, [40] was the first to propose a different distributed approach, namely, a subgradient-push algorithm that combines the distributed subgradient method [47] with the push-sum protocol [27].

citation_details.parsed_title: On distributed averaging algorithms and quantization effects
citation_details.description: This paper is cited to provide theoretical backing for a technical claim within the authors' analysis. Specifically, it supports the assertion that Assumptions 3.2 and 3.3 together imply the properties of Assumption 3.1.
citation_details.context: In particular, the following two assumptions taken together imply Assumption 3.1 [43].

citation_details.parsed_title: Distributed Subgradient Methods for Multi-agent Optimization
citation_details.description: The authors identify [47] as proposing a foundational distributed subgradient algorithm for general networks. This method is presented as a baseline which is intuitive and simple but slow, as it requires diminishing step-sizes for exact convergence.
citation_details.context: To handle more general (possibly time-varying) networks, a distributed subgradient algorithm was proposed in [47], while its stochastic variant was studied in [56] and its asynchronous variant in [36] with provable convergence rates.

citation_details.parsed_title: On the Convergence of Decentralized Gradient Descent
citation_details.description: This paper is cited as an example of a decentralized gradient descent method that suffers from a steady-state error. This limitation is presented as the motivation for the development of more advanced algorithms like EXTRA.
citation_details.context: References [62, 61, 60] use a difference structure to cancel the steady state error in decentralized gradient descent [47, 75], thereby developing the algorithm EXTRA and its proximal-gradient variant.

citation_details.parsed_title: The Entropic Penalty Approach to Stochastic Programming
citation_details.description: The cited paper introduced the 'Entropic Penalty' approach for stochastic programming, which connects penalty functions to the principle of Expected Utility. The authors note this approach was limited to the exponential utility function, a gap which the current work addresses by generalizing the method to arbitrary concave utility functions.
citation_details.context: In a recent paper, [2], a special type pf penalty function $P_{E}$ , called "The Entropic Penalty", was employed to solve (SP-E) via the unconstrained penalty type problem $$ \inf \left\{g _ {0} (x) + p P _ {E} (x) \right\} \tag {EP} $$ where $p > 0$ is a penalty parameter. The special interest in the entropic penalty approach is due to its intimate relation with the principle of Expected Utility. Indeed, for stochastic programs with stochastic right-hand side (with $g(x, b) \coloneqq b - g(x)$ ): $$ \inf \left\{g _ {0} (x): g (x) \geqslant b \right\} \tag {SP-RHS} $$ it is shown in [2] that the dual problem of $(EP)$ consists of maximizing the certainty equivalent of the classical Lagrangian dual of $(SP - RHS)$ : $$ h _ {b} (y): = \inf _ {x} \left\{L _ {b} (x, y) = g _ {0} (x) + y ^ {T} g (x, b) \right\} $$ i.e., the dual of $(EP)$ is $\max_{y\geq 0}u^{-1}Eu(h_b(y))$ where $u$ is the exponential utility function.

citation_details.parsed_title: Strongly stable stationary solutions in nonlinear programs
citation_details.description: The author cites Kojima [24] as an influential and foundational work on nonlinear programs (NLPs). This work is mentioned as the starting point for a line of research addressing parametric sensitivities of NLPs when the active set changes.
citation_details.context: Tracing back to the influential works of Kojima [24] on NLPs and Robinson [35] on generalized equations, a series of results have been obtained in the literature to address parametric sensitivities of NLPs in the presence of active index set changes [17, 38, 25, 6], culminating in a practical method to calculate directional derivatives of the primal variable solution in the form of an auxiliary convex quadratic program (QP) with a linear program embedded [33].

citation_details.parsed_title: Dependence of solutions of nonsmooth differential-algebraic equations on parameters
citation_details.description: The author uses Lemma 3.1 from the cited work [40] as part of the proof for Theorem 3.4. This lemma helps establish that an auxiliary mapping is a Lipschitz homeomorphism under certain conditions for L-smooth functions.
citation_details.context: Next, statement (i) follows from [40, Lemma 3.1] and [3, Theorem 7.1.1]. Statement (ii) holds by the following arguments: the $PC^r$ function $\mathbf{r}$ is immediately furnished from [34, Corollary 20] and the auxiliary mapping $\mathbf{f}$ is therefore $PC^r$ at $(\mathbf{x}^0,\mathbf{y}^0)$ by construction. As the zero $(\mathbf{x}^0,\mathbf{y}^0)$ of $\mathbf{g}$ implies the implicit function $\mathbf{r}$ , $\mathbf{f}$ admits a local inverse $\mathbf{f}^{-1}$ at $(\mathbf{x}^0,\mathbf{y}^0)$ which satisfies $\mathbf{r}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{y}}^{-1}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{0}_m)\forall \mathbf{x}\in N_{\mathbf{x}^0}$ by [37, Lemma 3.2.1]. Moreover, since $\mathbf{f}_{\mathbf{x}}^{-1}$ is the identity mapping, $\mathbf{f}^{-1}$ is $PC^r$ at $\mathbf{x}^0$ since $\mathbf{r}$ is $PC^r$ on $N_{\mathbf{x}^0}$ .

citation_details.parsed_title: A Light-Traffic Theorem for Multi-Server Queues
citation_details.description: The authors cite Burman and Smith (1983) for their work proving a light traffic limit theorem for multiserver queues. This work is presented as part of the existing literature, from which the authors differentiate their own more general methodology.
citation_details.context: Burman and Smith (1983) prove a light traffic limit theorem for multiserver queues which was conjectured by Boxma, Cohen, and Huffels (1979).

citation_details.parsed_title: On Solving Linear Complementarity Problems as Linear Programs
citation_details.description: The author cites this paper by Cottle and Pang as providing an alternative approach to the equivalence between linear complementarity problems and least element problems, a topic the current paper extends to the nonlinear case.
citation_details.context: For another approach to the equivalence treated in the present work and in [8], see the papers [6] and [7] of Cottle and Pang.

citation_details.parsed_title: A Least Element Theory of Solving Linear Complementarity Problems as Linear Programs
citation_details.description: The author points to this work, which presents a least element theory for linear complementarity problems, as an alternative approach to the equivalence problem that the current paper investigates for nonlinear operators.
citation_details.context: For another approach to the equivalence treated in the present work and in [8], see the papers [6] and [7] of Cottle and Pang.

citation_details.parsed_title: On the convergence rate of incremental aggregated gradient algorithms
citation_details.description: The paper cites IAG [9] as an example of a fast incremental gradient method that achieves a linear convergence rate for strongly convex problems. This method is presented as part of the existing literature on first-order methods which the authors compare their work against.
citation_details.context: In the past few years, fast incremental gradient methods with improved rates of convergence have been developed [5, 9, 26, 29]. Of these, SAGA [5] with averaging addresses the merely convex case and achieves a sublinear convergence rate $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{N}{k}\right)$ , where $N$ denotes the number of blocks, while in the presence of strong convexity, nonaveraging variants of SAGA and IAG [9] admit a linear convergence rate assuming that the function satisfies some suitable smoothness conditions.

citation_details.parsed_title: A modified BFGS method and its global convergence in nonconvex minimization
citation_details.description: The paper cites [12] to support the methodological principle that bounding the eigenvalues of the Hessian approximation matrix is crucial for achieving global convergence. This concept is fundamental to the design and analysis of the proposed quasi-Newton method.
citation_details.context: In particular, the boundedness of the eigenvalues of $H_{k}$ is an important factor in achieving global convergence in convex and nonconvex problems (cf. [1, 12]).

citation_details.parsed_title: IQN: An incremental quasi-Newton method with local superlinear convergence rate
citation_details.description: The paper identifies that the incremental quasi-Newton (IQN) method from [18] is limited by its reliance on the strong convexity assumption. This limitation presents a research gap that the current paper aims to fill by developing a method for non-strongly convex objectives.
citation_details.context: In both the full and limited memory variants of the SQN methods in the literature [3, 18, 20], it has been uniformly assumed that the objective function is strongly convex.

citation_details.parsed_title: On stochastic subgradient mirror-descent algorithm with weighted averaging
citation_details.description: The paper references [21] to establish the convergence rate of averaging-based stochastic approximation schemes, which are a common baseline approach for merely convex problems. The authors contrast their non-averaging method with this standard technique.
citation_details.context: For example, averaging SA schemes achieve a rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{M}{\sqrt{k}}\right)$ , where $M$ is an upper bound on the norm of the subgradient (see [21, 22]).

citation_details.parsed_title: Block-coordinate gradient descent method for linearly constrained nonsmooth separable optimization
citation_details.description: The paper cites [28] for providing foundational theoretical work on exact regularization for convex programs. This work on regularization conditions and error bounds informs the methodological approach of the paper, which uses an iterative regularization scheme.
citation_details.context: Friedlander and Tseng [7] and Tseng and Yun [28] established the necessary and sufficient conditions of exact regularization for convex programs and derived error bounds for inexact regularized convex problems.

citation_details.parsed_title: Stochastic quasi-Newton methods for nonconvex stochastic optimization
citation_details.description: The paper mentions [30] as a recent development in the field, which extended stochastic quasi-Newton (SQN) methods to nonconvex problems. This is cited as part of the literature review to contextualize the paper's own contribution within the broader landscape of SQN methods.
citation_details.context: Recent extensions have included an SQN method [30] for solving nonconvex stochastic optimization problems and a constant step size variance reduced SQN method [14] for smooth strongly convex problems characterized by a linear convergence rate.

citation_details.parsed_title: A theoretical and empirical comparison of gradient approximations in derivative-free optimization
citation_details.description: This paper is cited for its effective "linear interpolation" gradient estimator. The authors' proposed AdaZORO algorithm uses a descent method with this estimator as a fallback when gradient compressibility is not present.
citation_details.context: In the absence of gradient compressibility AdaZORO reduces to a fixed step-size descent method using the "linear interpolation" gradient estimator shown to be effective in [3].

citation_details.parsed_title: Global convergence rate analysis of a generic line search algorithm with noise
citation_details.description: The paper is cited as an example of prior work on the convergence of inexact gradient descent. The authors state that these existing results are not directly applicable to their specific analytical setting, motivating their new theoretical results.
citation_details.context: Although there are many prior results in the literature characterizing the iteration complexity of (prox-) gradient descent using an inexact gradient [4, 19, 39, 46], they do not precisely fit our situation.

citation_details.parsed_title: A zeroth-order block coordinate descent algorithm for huge-scale black-box optimization
citation_details.description: This work is cited as part of a recent line of research that uses finite differences to approximate directional derivatives. These approximations are then used in regression schemes to estimate the full gradient.
citation_details.context: Recently, several works [3, 9, 10, 14, 48] have considered finite differences $y_{i} = \frac{f(x_{k} + \delta\mathbf{z}_{i}) - f(x_{k})}{\delta}$ as noisy approximations to the directional derivatives $\mathbf{z}_i^\top \mathbf{g}_k$ and investigated various regression schemes for recovering $\mathbf{g}_k$ from these linear measurements.

citation_details.parsed_title: Stochastic first-and zeroth-order methods for nonconvex stochastic programming
citation_details.description: This paper is cited for establishing the query complexity of the Random Search algorithm for convex functions, which is O(d/ε²). This result serves as a standard baseline for comparison in zeroth-order optimization.
citation_details.context: The former approach yields higher complexity; [20] showed if $f$ is Lipschitz differentiable and convex then Random Search finds an $\varepsilon$ -optimal solution in $\mathcal{O}(d / \varepsilon^{2})$ queries, while [21] showed any algorithm for this problem necessarily requires $\Omega (d / \varepsilon^2)$ queries.

citation_details.parsed_title: Curvature-aware derivative-free optimization
citation_details.description: This paper is mentioned as an example of a coordinate-descent-style approach within the broader field of zeroth-order optimization.
citation_details.context: We mention also the work of [17], which requires only one query per iteration (but at the cost of a slower convergence rate) and the coordinate-descent-style approaches of [23, 44].

citation_details.parsed_title: The effect of deterministic noise in subgradient methods
citation_details.description: This work is cited as part of a body of literature that analyzes gradient descent methods using biased gradient estimators. This area of study is noted as being closely connected to the convergence analysis of zeroth-order methods.
citation_details.context: Finally, we note the many works [4, 8, 19, 26, 32, 39] that study gradient descent: $x_{k + 1} = x_k - \alpha \hat{\mathbf{g}}_k$ , where $\hat{\mathbf{g}}_k$ is a biased estimator of the true gradient $\mathbf{g}_k$.

citation_details.parsed_title: Random gradient-free minimization of convex functions
citation_details.description: This paper is cited as a foundational work on the Random Search algorithm. This method is noted for using a randomized gradient estimator that requires only two function evaluations per iteration.
citation_details.context: To overcome this, randomized estimators were employed in SPSA [43] and Random Search [34, 35] that use only two queries per iteration.

citation_details.parsed_title: Proximal Subgradients, Marginal Values and Augmented Lagrangians in Nonconvex Optimization
citation_details.description: The paper cites [26] to support the claim that for a locally Lipschitz function, the set of lower semigradients is nonempty for a dense subset of its domain. This is a known result that the paper builds upon.
citation_details.context: If f is locally Lipschitz then ∂−f(x) is nonempty for a dense subset in Rm (see [26, Theorem 1] and [17, Théorème 2], for more general results).

citation_details.parsed_title: Reneging phenomena in single channel queues
citation_details.description: The paper is cited as an additional reference on queueing models with impatience under the FIFO discipline. This existing body of work is presented to contrast with the less-studied area of processor-sharing queues, thereby highlighting a research gap that the current paper aims to fill.
citation_details.context: There is a large literature on queueing models with impatience under the FIFO discipline. An early paper by Barrer [1] considers an example arising in a military application. Stanford [27] surveys the literature in this domain (see also Stanford [26] and Boots and Tijms [5]). This body of work focuses primarily on exact performance analysis. Ward and Glynn [29] have recently obtained a diffusion approximation for single channel queues. There are also various studies of multiserver queues with abandonments, motivated by call center applications; see the survey by Ronald and Massoulie [3], Gans et al. [10], and references therein.

citation_details.parsed_title: Polymatroids and mean-risk minimization in discrete optimization
citation_details.description: This work is cited for demonstrating that a key function is submodular when random coefficients are uncorrelated (i.e., the matrix is diagonal). The authors use this as a starting point for their own generalization to non-diagonal matrices.
citation_details.context: In a special case, $\Lambda$ is assumed to be a diagonal matrix, and so the random coefficients $\tilde{t}_{ij}, j \in [J]$ , for the same $i$ are uncorrelated. In this case, [4] successfully showed that $g(y)$ is submodular. As a result, we can strengthen a DCBP by incorporating extended polymatroid inequalities in the form $\pi^{\top}y \leq T$ , where $\pi \in \mathrm{EP}_g$ . Unfortunately, the submodularity of $g(y)$ quickly fades when the off-diagonal entries of $\Lambda$ become nonzero, e.g., when $\Lambda$ is associated with a general covariance matrix.

citation_details.parsed_title: The submodular knapsack polytope
citation_details.description: This paper is mentioned as part of recent work that proposed specific types of inequalities for solving submodular knapsack problems, providing background for the current paper's focus on valid inequalities.
citation_details.context: Recently, [5, 1, 7] proposed cover and packing inequalities for efficiently solving submodular and supermodular knapsack sets with 0-1 variables.

citation_details.parsed_title: Models for minimax stochastic linear optimization problems with risk aversion
citation_details.description: The authors reference this work as an example of a distributionally robust optimization model that uses moment information to define ambiguity sets, which is central to the current paper's approach.
citation_details.context: Moment information has been widely used for building ambiguity sets in various distributionally robust optimization models (see, e.g., [6, 11, 34]).

citation_details.parsed_title: On mixing sets arising in chance-constrained programming
citation_details.description: This reference is cited as part of the established literature on the Sample Average Approximation (SAA) approach, which the authors contrast with their own distributionally robust method that does not require full distributional information.
citation_details.context: For generic chance-constrained programs, the SAA approach and valid inequalities for the related MILPs have been well studied in the literature (see, e.g., [20, 21, 17, 19]).

citation_details.parsed_title: A sample approximation approach for optimization with probabilistic constraints
citation_details.description: This work is cited for introducing the sample average approximation (SAA) method, which is presented as a major alternative research direction to the distributionally robust approach taken in the paper.
citation_details.context: In another promising research stream, the probability distribution $\mathbb{P}$ of $\tilde{t}_{ij}$ is replaced by a finite-sample approximation, leading to a sample average approximation (SAA) of the chance-constrained model [20, 24].

citation_details.context: The SAA model is then recast as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP), on which many strong valid inequalities can be derived to accelerate the branch-and-cut algorithm (see, e.g., [21, 17, 19, 32, 18]).

Lemma 3.3 employs a different transformation approach to show the projection property for $\mathcal{D}_2$ when these moments are ambiguous in the sense of [11].

citation_details.description: The paper is cited as an example of the rich, foundational literature on Lagrangian duality and Farkas type results. The authors contrast this with the lack of similar results for semi-infinite programming, which motivates their work.
citation_details.context: The other is the Lagrangian duality and Farkas type results for problem (1.2), which are fundamental in convex optimization and other fields, such as game theory, set containment problems, etc. The literature on these areas is very rich (see, e.g., [6, 7, 12, 17, 20, 21, 33]), but there is little for semi-infinite programming except the work of Fang, Li, and Ng [12], where the Lagrangian duality and Farkas lemma for semi-infinite programming are characterized in terms of epigraphs of the conjugate functions of the involved functions. In this paper, applying our main results on FM qualification for system (1.1), we establish some sufficient conditions for ensuring the strong Lagrangian duality and Farkas lemma, which seem new as far as we know.

citation_details.parsed_title: A null-space primal-dual interior-point algorithm for nonlinear optimization with nice convergence properties
citation_details.description: The paper adopts the QP subproblem formulation from Liu and Yuan [21]. This method involves relaxing the linearized constraints based on two prescribed conditions to ensure progress.
citation_details.context: Supposing that $x^{k}$ is the current iterate, Liu and Yuan [21] propose to solve the QP subproblem $$ \min \left(g ^ {k}\right) ^ {T} d + (1 / 2) d ^ {T} B _ {k} d \tag {2.1} $$ $$ \text {s. t.} A _ {k} ^ {T} d = A _ {k} ^ {T} d _ {p} ^ {k}, \tag {2.2} $$ where $d_p^k \in \Re^n$ approximately minimizes $\| h^k + A_k^T d\|$ and satisfies the following two prescribed conditions: Condition (a). $\| d_p^k\| \leq \kappa_1\| A_kh^k\|$ , where $\kappa_{1} > 0$ is a constant. Condition (b). If $\| h^k \| \neq 0$ , $\| h^k \| - \| h^k + A_k^T d_p^k \| \geq \kappa_2 \| A_k h^k \|^2 / \| h^k \|$ , where $\kappa_2 \in (0,1)$ is a constant.

citation_details.parsed_title: Newton-Type Methods for Non-Convex Optimization under Inexact Hessian Information
citation_details.description: The authors critique the methods in [17] for requiring the accuracy of stochastic estimates to depend on the final desired optimization accuracy, rather than being chosen dynamically. They argue this is a key limitation, as their own work uses a dynamic approach where the accuracy holds with a fixed probability, independent of the final solution accuracy.
citation_details.context: Like in this paper, in the works [19, 17], it is assumed that at each iteration the stochastic gradient and/or the stochastic Hessian approximate their true values with sufficiently high accuracy and this holds with some probability $p$ . However in [19, 17] unlike our work, the accuracy of the stochastic gradient and/or the stochastic Hessian is not chosen dynamically but instead depends on the final desired optimization accuracy $\epsilon$ . They choose, at each iteration, the approximate stochastic gradient and/or Hessian to be essentially the true gradient and/or Hessian with a small error and their choices of the stochastic gradient/Hessian hold with probability $p$ that depends on the optimization accuracy $\epsilon$ . As such, the analysis of their methods reduces to the deterministic setting and yields expected complexity bounds that hold with high probability. First, they provide no complexity analysis when the stochastic gradient/Hessian fails to be essentially the true gradient/Hessian. Secondly, the probability $p$ relies heavily on $\epsilon$ . In contrast, we derive our expected complexity bounds using stochastic gradient estimates that, at each iteration, dynamically change and the stochastic estimates hold for a fixed probability, independent of the optimization accuracy.

citation_details.context: The paper [13] studies the case of nonlinear parametric model and proposes the knowledge gradient with discrete priors (KGDP). KGDP overcomes the computational issues, but requires that we represent the uncertainty about the unknown parameters using a finite number of samples, where one of the samples has to be the true parameter. citation_details.context: We use a globalization technique that is based on a multidimensional filter framework. Originally, the filter concept was developed by Fletcher and Leyffer [26] in order to globalize SQP methods for nonlinear programming problems without using penalty functions. The original version of the filter method works with a two-dimensional filter, where each entry consists of the objective function value and a measure for the constraint violation at a given point. The filter globalization concept has rapidly established itself as one of the most important and efficient globalization techniques in nonlinear programming. citation_details.parsed_title: Estimates of the Duality Gap in Nonconvex Optimization
citation_details.description: The author introduces the work of Aubin and Ekeland, who estimated the duality gap using the 'lack of convexity' concept. The author then points out a gap in their work, noting that their generalization to non-linear mappings involved a perturbed problem rather than the original one, which this paper aims to address.
citation_details.context: In [1] Aubin and Ekeland consider the following optimization problem $$ \mathfrak {o} = \inf \left\{F (x, A x): x \in X, A x \in Y \right\} \tag {P} $$ where $X$ and $Y$ are convex subsets of a locally convex Hausdorff vector space $E$ and of $\mathbb{R}^m$ , respectively; and where $A: E \to \mathbb{R}^m$ and $F: X \times Y \to \mathbb{R}$ . They define the dual as $$ v ^ {*} = \sup _ {p \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \inf _ {x \in X} L (x, p) \tag {P*} $$ where $L(x,p) = \inf \{F(x,q) + \langle p,Ax - q\rangle:q\in Y\}$ Moreover, after having introduced the definition of lack of convexity of a function $f$ , say $\rho(f)$ , they establish, under a suitable regularity condition and assuming $A$ to be a linear continuous mapping, the following inequalities $$ 0 \leqslant v - v ^ {*} < \rho (F). \tag {1} $$ Conversely, their generalization to the case where the mapping $A$ is no longer linear turns out to involve not exactly $v$ , but the value of a similar perturbed problem. In fact, estimate (1) becomes $0 \leqslant w - v^{*} \leqslant \rho(F)$ , where $$ w = \inf \left\{F (x, A x; \rho (- A), \rho (A)): x \in X, A x \in Y \right\} \quad \text {a n d} $$ $$ F (x, A x; \rho (- A), \rho (A)) \triangleq \inf _ {q} \left\{F (x, p): \rho (- A) < q - p < \rho (A) \right\}. $$

citation_details.parsed_title: Augmented Lagrangians and applications of the proximal point algorithm in convex programming

citation_details.context: Over the last decade, we are witnessing a resurgence of Lagrangian-based methods. This surge of interest is due to the flexibility that they provide in exploiting special problem structures that abound in modern and disparate applications (e.g., image science, machine learning, communication systems). Augmented Lagrangian methods (also known as multiplier methods) which are a typical prototype, were invented about half a century ago by Hestenes [18] and Powell [23], are the core of the analysis and development of many extensions of Lagrangian-based schemes capable of tackling optimization problems with various types of structures and constraints. This is reflected by a rich and very large volume of literature on various practical and theoretical aspects of many Lagrangian-based methods. Two classical references providing the central developments and ideas underlying Lagrangian-based and related decomposition methods are the books of Bertsekas [3], and Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis [4], which include a comprehensive list of relevant references for these developments until the nineties. Here, one should also mention the pioneer works of Rockafeller [25, 26] on the convergence analysis of proximal AL methods. For more modern developments, results, and applications, see e.g., the more recent works [5, 28], [12, 7, 27], and references therein.

It is readily seen that their construction may be formulated through the setwise inner derivatives introduced above.

citation_details.parsed_title: Reinforcement learning in robust Markov decision processes
citation_details.description: The authors describe the work of Lim et al. [20] on adaptively constructing uncertainty sets for robust MDPs using online learning. They point out that this work is limited to rectangular uncertainty sets due to computational tractability, a gap the current paper addresses.
citation_details.context: Several works (Bertuccelli et al. [9], Lim et al. [20], Hanasusanto and Kuhn [16]) have studied uncertainty set construction for robust MDPs. In early work of robust MDPs such as in Nilim and El Ghaoui [23], the authors have discussed ways to construct statistically meaningful uncertainty sets based on sampled trajectories. Similar task for continuous state and action spaces is addressed in Hanasusanto and Kuhn [16]. Recently, several works have studied constructing uncertainty sets adaptively so that the learning factor is incorporated into the robust MDP framework: Bertuccelli et al. [9] consider the case where the model parameters are fixed yet unknown and propose a method that iteratively constructs uncertainty sets using past samples and then solves and runs the minimax policy from the resulting robust MDP formulations. They show that if all state-action pairs are sampled sufficiently many times, the resulting policy converges to the optimal policy of the MDP. Lim et al. [20] consider a case where the model parameters may further be inherently uncertain, in that they may change from time to time and the true uncertainty sets are unknown, and develop a method based on online learning such that the accumulated reward approaches to the optimal one of the robust MDP where the true uncertainty sets are given. Because of computational tractability issues, these work all focus on the rectangular cases.
